item.title: Agentic system personalizes physical controls to help users “DJ their art”
item.description: “TangiMap” uses an AI agent to reprogram how buttons, knobs, and sliders are used, helping users do things like edit photos and perform music in a more dynamic, tactile way.
item.dc:creator: Alex Shipps | MIT CSAIL
item.content:encoded:
In 2017, Apple removed the home button from its iPhones. Users lost a convenient, tangible control — part of a larger shift to digital buttons, knobs, and sliders we also see in cars (like with radio presets and air conditioning) and kitchens (see smart fridges).

We can’t leave physical controls behind entirely, though. They tend to be more convenient and efficient — think of how you can use a physical gaming controller without looking at it — and, at times, more precise, like when you use a dial to get the volume just right. But tangible controls are typically preprogrammed to do a specific thing, minimizing their usefulness.

A new system called “TangiMap,” co-developed by an MIT graduate student and researcher at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), helps bring tangible control back to your software. The system personalizes the physical controls on everyday devices by mapping digital widgets onto tangible inputs, turning things like editing photos, animation, performing music, and creating 3D models into more dynamic and tactile experiences. Just as a DJ’s pads switch between triggering cues, loops, and samples, TangiMap gives a device’s controls entirely new roles.

But how, exactly? TangiMap relies on an AI agent, or semi-autonomous programs that “think” and complete well-defined tasks, to find and act on context about the software you’re using, your tendencies, and the device used to control that program. To gather the required context, the agent can draw on sources such as the program’s API (the rules that let programs talk to each other), an MCP server (a standard that connects AI agents to apps), or a screenshot interpreted by a vision-language model. Then, the agent uses a large language model to put all the info it's gathered into a file before mapping specific digital functions to physical controls.

“TangiMap builds on our broader vision of reprogramming common objects to be more dynamic,” says Yunyi Zhu ’20, MEng ’21, a doctoral student in the MIT Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and a CSAIL researcher whose advisor is MIT Associate Professor Stefanie Mueller. “Here, AI agents help us adapt physical controls to whatever we’re working on. We want to bring back physical controls so we can interact with our devices eyes-free, the way you adjust a car’s volume without looking away from the road. Physical controls also let you adjust several settings at once, like tweaking brightness and contrast together when editing an image, which is hard to do on a screen.”

The system helped the researchers turn a standard mixer into a photo-editing controller. That way, they could adjust color in Adobe Lightroom, with a complementary visualization of those controls displayed on their screen. The team did the same with sound-mixing software, so that performers can adjust their music in real-time with their own inputs to knobs and faders. 

The researchers also reprogrammed a simpler mixer to work with the 3D modeling program Blender. Their interface included an area where users can type in a prompt, and once the model was generated, users could adjust features like shininess on a mixer using physical controls. Within Adobe’s Character Animator software, TangiMap connected specific expressions and movements to buttons on a control pad so users could animate (or “puppeteer”) a cartoon character live.

Zhu and co-author Chang Xiao, an assistant professor at Boston University, presented their tool at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology earlier this month.

Zhu and Xiao created a custom user interface (UI) for each application. While that adds another layer of personalization to the creative process, the team is hoping to create a more streamlined system that helps the designer to generate the UI for their device by taking a picture.

The researchers are also considering the physical aspects of user interactions. They want to use more ergonomic devices and also ensure that TangiMap accounts for where users position their hands when doing different tasks. For example, users typically hold a mixer differently when they’re using it to make music than, say, when playing a video game. You may want controls mapped closer or further apart, depending on what you’re doing.

Zhu is hoping to do a user study to get more feedback about TangiMap, and whether this kind of “smart DJing” could indeed improve those experiences. But the dynamic reprogramming she ultimately envisions is even more ambitious.

“The same way our phones and computers generalize to a range of tasks, we want other objects to be more intelligent,” she says. “I would like to build physical items that use an AI agent as a brain to decide what to reprogram into. They could understand what to transform into, given a specific situation.”

A chemical jar, for instance, could tell you if it’s sealed correctly when asked, and when you want to see what it’s typically used for, the container would instead display that information. While that kind of versatility and interactivity is a ways off, more powerful agents and more intricate fabrication pipelines could bring everyday objects to life.

Their work was supported, in part, by Google’s Gemini Academic Program Award.

item.title: What if excess renewable energy could power new industrial processes?
item.description: Excess electricity from solar and wind generation could become widely available across the U.S. and then tapped to manufacture materials or run data centers, scientists say.
item.dc:creator: Adam Zewe | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
As the U.S. expands its reliance on renewable energy, a considerable amount of excess electricity will be generated by solar and wind power plants. A new study explores how this energy could potentially be harnessed by certain technologies or production processes, reducing costs and increasing energy efficiency.

Researchers from MIT and Georgia Tech studied future situations in which the build-out of solar and wind farms has scaled up enough that 80 percent of the electricity supplied to customers in the U.S. is generated from renewable sources. They modeled systems with different mixtures of wind and solar power capacities.

They found that solar and wind farms could produce as much as 10 percent more power than the grid could immediately use or store in electricity systems that cost-effectively meet demand with 80 percent renewable energy. If not utilized, this excess electricity would go to waste.

This finding holds true even when the cost of energy-storage devices like batteries is low, and it remains largely consistent across the U.S. in many future scenarios. 

The researchers’ model reveals when excess electricity will likely be available. It shows that periods of excess will generally occur in the spring and fall and usually persist for several hours at a time. 

This predictability presents an opportunity for some industrial processes that, with the right scheduling and capacity scaling strategy, could use this otherwise excess energy. Examples include raw materials grinding and even electrified steel production. The excess could also be tapped to help meet the growing electricity demands of data centers. 

While it can be more challenging to run industrial processes intermittently than continuously, the predictability of potential excesses helps, the authors say. Additionally, strategies like designing less-capital-intensive machinery, or even sharing equipment across manufacturing sites, could also be useful. 

“In this era where there is a need for additional electricity, where demands are growing to support data centers and other end users, we wanted to understand what this excess electricity will potentially look like so we can design processes to benefit from these excesses. Our work can help technology developers and other stakeholders plan for future infrastructure needs and start innovating toward these technologies now,” says Jessika Trancik, a professor in the MIT Institute of Data Systems and Society (IDSS) and a senior author of this study.

She is joined on the paper by lead author Micah S. Ziegler, a former IDSS postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Georgia Tech; Aliza Khurram, a former IDSS postdoc now at the Toyota Research Institute; and Shannon Y.S. Hwang a PhD student in IDSS. The research appears today in Joule.

Examining excess

Wind and solar energy are variable resources because they are dependent on weather. During periods when supply exceeds demand, operators often take measures to either store the excess or reduce energy production altogether.  

But “another way to think about that curtailed energy is as an opportunity to use this excess electricity for some other processes,” Trancik says.

“Excesses could instead be used productively in a range of processes including making materials and training AI models,” Ziegler adds. 

To help engineers design processes to utilize this resource, the MIT researchers modeled the dynamics, durations, and frequencies of excess energy events. 

They used an energy systems model to study systems that combine wind, solar, and energy storage to meet different percentages of electricity demand in many future scenarios. The model can also simulate how these systems might operate hourly over decades.

They fed this model 40 years of data that captured weather extremes and fluctuations in wind and solar resources across the United States. They also incorporated technology-related factors, such as the cost of building different types of batteries or other kinds of energy storage, as well as electricity demand profiles for specific regions.

“All these costs are changing, so we wanted to study many different combinations of technologies to help people plan amid all this uncertainty about what the future power system is going to look like,” Trancik says.

They designed the model to handle this enormous amount of data, while balancing the level of detail so the problem was computationally tractable. 

In the end, the researchers found that significant amounts of excess energy would be generated in electricity systems that meet a significant portion of demand with renewable energy. Even when systems are designed to minimize the costs of delivering renewable energy, the amount of potentially excess power available would regularly double the amount used to meet demand.

“We found that considerable excess energy could be available even in systems with very low-cost storage, including at costs an order of magnitude lower than what battery storage costs today,” Ziegler explains. 

“There is a huge amount of renewable energy that might be wasted in these cost-optimal systems, and there is not as much sensitivity to location as one might have thought. This energy is broadly available across the U.S.” Trancik says.

The model shows that the greatest potential periods of excess energy would occur in the spring, with smaller amounts of excess available in the mid- to late fall. These excess periods typically continue for seven to 12 hours, usually occur midday through the afternoon, and sometimes last for multiple days.

Leveraging surplus energy

Because these excess energy patterns are somewhat predictable, scientists and engineers could design processes to capitalize on this resource, Trancik says.

“In many of the scenarios, excess energy was often available for seven to 12 hours continuously, which suggests this duration could be a good target for technology developers and system planners when they design and schedule processes,” Ziegler explains. “When the same characteristic is found consistently across a wide range of possible energy systems, it can be considered more robust to our uncertainty about the future.”

For example, some industrial machinery, like electric arc furnaces in steel production or mills for grinding raw materials, could be switched on and operated during these times.

This electricity could also power equipment to manufacture products used seasonally, like fertilizer or concrete, which tend to be used more during spring, summer, and fall, and less during the winter. This coincides with several periods where more excess electricity is available. The energy could also power flexible computing, such as AI training processes that can be scheduled for times of day, or even months, when excesses are more likely available. 

The researchers hope these results inform the development of technologies designed to utilize excess renewable energy, like periodic manufacturing processes that efficiently operate for a few hours at a time.

In the future, they plan to study the costs of developing infrastructure, equipment, and technologies that can benefit from these excesses.

“In many places today, we enjoy inexpensive electricity, but there could be more constraints on the system going forward. This excess renewable energy could be a resource that we might utilize to meet increasing demands,” says Trancik. 

“If we can develop cost-effective ways to use this excess energy, we could potentially reduce some costs of transitioning to low-carbon energy resources,” Ziegler adds.

This research was funded by the MIT Climate Grand Challenges as part of the Weather and Climate Extremes project, and by the MIT Portugal Partnership Research Seed Fund Program, the MIT Technology and Policy Program, Georgia Tech, the MIT Energy Initiative, and the National Science Foundation (NSF).

item.title: Arianna Doss: Prescribing change
item.description: When she isn’t scoring on the soccer field, the MIT senior and 2027 Rhodes Scholar works toward a future as a physician and policymaker advancing health equity.
item.dc:creator: Gitana Savage | MIT News correspondent
item.content:encoded:
Growing up in Houston, Arianna Doss lived just minutes from the Texas Medical Center, the largest medical complex in the world. But in her experience, proximity to medical innovation did not necessarily mean access to quality care for members of her community.

The contrast, which she witnessed as a resident of the city’s historically Black Third Ward, shaped how Doss came to understand health care in the United States: as a system deeply influenced by social and political factors.

Now a senior at MIT studying biological engineering and political science, Doss hopes to address those disparities from several angles. She plans to become a physician, potentially specializing in obstetrics and gynecology or emergency medicine, while also pursuing a career in health policy and public service. Recently selected for a Rhodes Scholarship, Doss will pursue a master’s degree in comparative social policy, followed by a master’s in global health science and epidemiology, at Oxford University next fall.

At MIT, her interests have taken her from a public health course in South Africa to Capitol Hill, where she worked on federal maternal health legislation. Along the way, she has found ways to bring together her interests in science, politics, and social justice.

During her first year at MIT, Doss applied on a whim to an Independent Activities Period class called “Evolution of an Epidemic,” led by Professor Bruce Walker, director of the Ragon Institute. The course took students to Johannesburg and Durban, South Africa, for two and a half weeks to study the HIV epidemic. The experience helped Doss recognize that she could pursue medicine without abandoning her interest in the broader systems shaping public health.

“It really unlocked something in me,” she says. “It helped me realize that I can go into medicine and be patient-facing, while also working in public health to make a larger, more policy and population-wide impact as well.”

That intersection became especially clear during her work on Capitol Hill.

Through the MIT Washington program, which provides funding for students pursuing policy-related internships in Washington, Doss secured a position as a maternal health intern for U.S. Representative Lauren Underwood.

The experience gave Doss an opportunity to see how policy decisions could influence the health of patients well before they entered a hospital. Doss has explored that closer to home through her involvement with Link Health, a nonprofit that partners with community health organizations to help patients enroll in public benefits. As a patient navigator, she helps clients with processes that can be difficult to navigate, particularly for people facing language barriers or unfamiliarity with government systems.

Outside the classroom, Doss has found another way to bring her advocacy interests together, through soccer.

A lifelong soccer player and three-year starter on MIT’s women’s varsity team, she chose the Institute, in part, because she wanted to continue competing at a high level while pursuing an engineering education. She was drawn to the prospect of playing alongside students who shared her interest in science and engineering.

“I wanted to be on a soccer team that also had people who were going to be in STEM,” she says. “I didn’t want to be the only engineer on the team.”

For Doss, soccer has provided a welcome counterbalance to the demands of MIT, not least because of the team’s winning record. For every one of her four years on the team, the Engineers have won the NEWMAC tournament title and played in the NCAA Championship Tournament. 

“Life at MIT is difficult. It’s rough. It would be a lot rougher if I didn’t have soccer as an outlet,” says Doss, who was recently named NEWMAC player of the year.

But her experience as a student-athlete has also raised some questions of belonging. She had anticipated finding a larger community of Black athletes at MIT, and that left her wondering where she would find that sense of connection.

Doss and several friends began discussing ways to bring Black athletes together across MIT’s varsity teams. In April, they launched the MIT Alliance for the Advancement of Black Athletes, with Doss serving as president. The organization, which is open to all, aims to build connections among Black student-athletes and create a stronger sense of community across teams. 

Looking ahead, Doss plans to attend medical school after her master’s work at Oxford. Ultimately, she hopes to practice medicine while continuing to influence public health policies, especially those that can be implemented on the community level. Her interests include mitigating racial health disparities in areas such as maternal health and chronic disease, as well advancing public health through better access to high-quality education, housing, and safety-net programs.

“A physician who understands our complex political systems is a more effective advocate, while a policymaker with clinical experience is a more impactful public servant,” she said. “I plan to be both.”

item.title: Many languages, one common neural code
item.description: Analyzing speakers of 21 languages, an MIT study using multilingual AI finds the human brain may represent meaning in much the same way.
item.dc:creator: Rubina Veerakone | McGovern Institute for Brain Research
item.content:encoded:
Languages take on thousands of forms. Some are tonal, like Vietnamese, where shifts in pitch convey distinct meanings. English relies on precise word orders, but this matters less for Russian, where words can be swapped without changing the intended message. 

Despite so much variety in the linguistic kingdom, an MIT study has found that the human brain may process all sorts of languages in a universal way.

Artificial intelligence made this finding possible. In the study published today in Nature Neuroscience, the researchers used multilingual models to predict how the human brain responds to various languages. Those models also helped the researchers detect a shared brain process across people who collectively spoke 21 different languages.

“Of course, there are many differences in the ways humans converse with each other. But our team found that there is something fundamentally similar in how the brain communicates,” says Evelina Fedorenko, who is an investigator at MIT’s McGovern Institute for Brain Research, an associate professor of brain and cognitive sciences, and the senior author of the paper.

The study is the first to use multilingual models to predict brain responses across many languages. As researchers develop AI language tools to diagnose brain disorders, this work can extend their benefit to speakers of more languages, and may one day even keep endangered ones from vanishing.

Parsing the linguistic mind

Language allows us to share our thoughts about the outside world and the ones we create in our minds. That power lives within a network of brain regions located in the left hemisphere.

“Every language is managed by these same parts of the brain,” explains Andrea Gregor de Varda, the lead author of the new study, a postdoc in the Fedorenko lab, and fellow in the K. Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center.

While scientists know that all languages activate the same parts of the brain, de Varda and Fedorenko wanted to know if that meant the brain processes them in the same way.

For example, they wondered, does the brain of someone who speaks Korean operate comparably to the brains of a Hindi or Spanish speaker?

It’s extremely hard to answer that question if you lack the right tools, de Varda says. And they needed one capable of creating a common code for comparing all sorts of languages — a task that is well-suited to artificial intelligence.

Where AI meets the brain

Large language models (LLMs) — such as those powering ChatGPT and Claude — interpret language much like the human brain, although they weren’t designed to do so. That surprising similarity is allowing de Varda and others in the field to wield these tools as a piercing lens into the human mind. Such studies often explore LLMs’ ability to learn or make sense of linguistic elements, such as grammar and meaning, to glean insights into how the brain might handle communication. But early LLMs used to work within a single language. The MIT researchers thought another class of models might help expand that scope.

“Multilingual language models are LLMs that can process hundreds of languages at once,” explains Fedorenko. Like other AIs of their kind, multilingual models ingest words or phrases and output numbers that scientists can extract. “Those numbers show how the model represents that bit of language,” she says. Now the team could study many languages at once using a single numerical code from the models. But the extent to which the models aligned with the human mind still lurked in the unknowns. De Varda believed he could coax an answer into light through a computational approach.

Using machine learning, he merged two data sources: the multilingual models’ code and scans of people’s brains as they performed linguistic tasks. The product was an AI tool known as an encoding model. It takes a multilingual model’s code, say, for a sentence, and predicts how the human brain might light up in response to the same input.

Encoding models at the time only existed for a handful of languages including English, French, and Chinese. But de Varda sought to test whether those models could be extended to more — and importantly, understudied ones. Doing so could reveal new aspects in which AI mirrors the human brain, and even detect a shared neural component across speakers of various languages.

A mental bridge between languages

The Fedorenko lab already had preexisting brain imaging data from speakers of 12 languages: Afrikaans, Dutch, Farsi, French, Lithuanian, Marathi, Norwegian, Romanian, Spanish, Tamil, Turkish, and Vietnamese. They recruited speakers of nine additional ones for their new study — Italian, Portuguese, German, Russian, Polish, Hindi, Arabic, Mandarin, and Korean — and recorded their brain activity while they listened to stories from “Alice in Wonderland” in their native language. By coupling that brain imaging data with outputs from multilingual models, the team created encoding models for those 21 languages.

“We found that the encoding models accurately predicted brain responses in all of the languages we studied — even in Marathi and Lithuanian, that, in contrast to English, we only have a limited amount of data on,” says Fedorenko. “The fact that there’s this emergent similarity between models and humans across so many languages is really quite exciting.”

Another finding was more interesting still. Even though the researchers trained an encoding model in a single language, it could predict brain activity for a language it had never seen before. For example, an encoding model trained to predict brain responses in French could also predict responses in Vietnamese, without ever being trained in Vietnamese. It was a truly fascinating discovery, de Varda says, because this was only possible if all the speakers’ brains were representing language in a shared way: a neural thread binding human communication.

What was that shared component? Dissecting different linguistic features across all the languages suggested that it has something to do with meaning. “That’s the intended power of communication, right? To share meaning; new information or our feelings about the world. So it’s fascinating we see that reflected in this work,” says Fedorenko.

In science, this new study gives brain researchers some explanations for long-held curiosities among them. In society, it could steer emerging technologies into a more inclusive direction. Scientists are starting to explore clinical uses of AI language tools, such as those that can detect cognitive decline based on brain activity patterns during language. But most of those studies, and the methods clinicians use today, are in common and well-studied languages like English. By showing how AI and the human brain overlap across many diverse languages, this new research may be a step toward clinical tools that do not leave most speakers out.

In another vein, reversing the Fedorenko lab’s approach might help preserve languages on the brink of extinction. “Say you had one single speaker of a language that is dying out. You might imagine a case in which we can train a model in the opposite direction: give it images of that speaker’s brain, and it could translate those into language,” notes Fedorenko.

De Varda adds that there are features that clearly differ between languages, too, and that those must be somehow represented in the brain and even LLMs. Defining those differences in future research, he says, might unearth new fragments of knowledge to complete the puzzle of the linguistic mind.

As researchers develop AI language tools to diagnose brain disorders, this work can extend their benefit to speakers of more languages, and may one day even keep endangered ones from vanishing.

item.title: J-PAL North America launches Medicaid Learning Lab to help state agencies test, learn, and improve health care delivery
item.description: The lab will support four state Medicaid agencies in building capacity to use evidence in their decision-making.
item.dc:creator: Victoria Moura | J-PAL North America
item.content:encoded:
This fall, J-PAL North America, a regional office of MIT's Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab, has launched the Medicaid Learning Lab (MLL) in collaboration with the SCALE Lab at the Yale School of Public Health. Through April 2027, this fully funded program will support an inaugural cohort of four state Medicaid agencies: the Delaware Department of Health and Social Services; the Louisiana Department of Health; MassHealth; and TennCare. 

A kickoff convening in September brought together more than 20 Medicaid leaders, researchers, and collaborators and was the first opportunity for participants to meet in person before the program's online sessions began. Speakers included researchers from the J-PAL network: Amy Finkelstein, co-scientific director of J-PAL North America and the John and Jennie S. MacDonald Professor of Economics at MIT; Jacob Wallace of Yale University, scientific advisor to the MLL and faculty co-director of the SCALE Lab; and Rebecca Myerson, associate professor at Emory University.

Practitioners also spoke, including Bill Halsey, director of healthcare policy and innovation at the Connecticut Department of Social Services; Allison Espeseth of Covering Wisconsin; and Hannah Maniates, director of Medicaid programming at the National Association of Medicaid Directors. 

Halsey described why testing and learning in Medicaid matters: “Often in Medicaid, we will implement a new program and only years later will we evaluate it. If we have a test-and-learn mentality, where we set up a rigorous evaluation methodology before implementing a new program, we can establish a rapid-learning cycle and generate actionable insights in a shorter time frame." 

Maniates named the questions agencies most often bring to researchers: What makes member outreach effective? What works for automatic renewals? And how do changes in enrollment affect utilization?

The MLL is the latest iteration of J-PAL North America's Learning Lab model, following the Climate Action Learning Lab, which has now run twice with state and local climate leaders, and the AprendeLab in Puerto Rico. The MLL also builds on J-PAL North America's prior work to launch randomized evaluations with Medicaid agencies in South Carolina, Wisconsin, Connecticut, and Maine.

Connecticut's evaluation efforts demonstrate where MLL participants' engagement can lead: a single J-PAL-supported evaluation of adolescent vaccination outreach grew into a sustained partnership between the state's Department of Social Services and Yale researchers, with data scientists now embedded in the agency. 

Closing the convening, Wallace told the cohort that Connecticut may look like the exception, but it is not. Their evaluation was initiated from the same place that MLL participants currently stand, working to identify one program and one question worth answering.

The MLL is launching at a time when Medicaid leaders are under growing pressure to improve health outcomes while controlling costs. Medicaid and the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) together cover more than 74 million people and account for roughly 30 percent of average total state spending, and new cuts and implementation requirements mean state leaders are being asked to do more with less. The program will support participating agencies in using evidence to determine what works, make informed trade-offs, and direct dollars toward programs with proven impact. 

The MLL is structured to address some of the common evaluation challenges faced by agencies: a lack of standard evaluation frameworks, a mismatch between immediate evaluation costs and longer-term benefits, and challenges in establishing researcher partnerships capable of producing a well-designed study. By helping agencies overcome these hurdles and invest in rigorous evaluation, J-PAL North America seeks to generate findings that can both inform individual agency decision-making and serve as a shared resource to help every state allocate resources more effectively.

Finkelstein, who co-chairs J-PAL North America's U.S. Health Care Delivery Initiative, opened the convening by tracing the inspiration for the MLL back to the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment, which she led and which produced the first randomized evidence on the effects of Medicaid coverage. That evidence exists only because a budget constraint led Oregon to allocate coverage slots by lottery. "Programs of Medicaid's consequence should not have to wait for an accident," she said.

Through April 2027, MLL participants will engage with other cohort members, researchers, and J-PAL staff in workshops and sessions grounded in real-world randomized evaluations in the Medicaid context. Each agency will also receive individualized, structured technical assistance from J-PAL staff to identify evaluation ideas and develop preliminary randomized evaluation designs. Each team will work to identify a program to prioritize for evaluation, develop a program theory of change, and outline a preliminary randomization plan. This work will be informed by a forthcoming playbook on randomized evaluations in Medicaid, co-developed by the SCALE Lab at Yale and J-PAL North America, which draws on Connecticut's experience embedding evaluation in its Medicaid program.

Selected agencies will be connected with researchers from the J-PAL network to co-develop a randomized evaluation concept. These projects will be eligible to submit proposals to J-PAL's Health Care Delivery Initiative for funding awards of up to $400,000. All participants will also join a standing practitioner network for continued peer exchange. 

"We have seen some of the pain points in getting studies or randomized evaluations off the ground, so we are excited and intrigued to learn how other states overcome some of those barriers," said Sara Garrity-Gentile, director of strategy at MassHealth and MLL inaugural cohort member.

The MLL will conclude at a summit next spring, where each team will present its evaluation opportunity to the cohort. This program is made possible thanks to a grant from Arnold Ventures. Medicaid agencies, researchers, and funders interested in future cohorts can learn more about the Medicaid Learning Lab and the U.S. Health Care Delivery Initiative on the J-PAL website.

item.title: AI-driven technique could help engineers design analog chips faster and with less expense
item.description: The “SLIC” training method enables a small LLM to compete with much more resource-intensive models in complex circuit design tasks.
item.dc:creator: Adam Zewe | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
A new technique developed by MIT researchers could help engineers use artificial intelligence to streamline the design and innovation of analog integrated circuits, semiconductor chips that perform vital functions like communication and power management in electronic devices.

In the future, this method could allow engineers to prototype faster, explore a wider range of chip designs, and discover new design schemes that might improve the performance and energy efficiency of robots, medical monitors, or industrial sensors.

Designing analog integrated circuits that meet specific requirements is usually a cumbersome manual process due to the enormous number of possibilities. Frontier generative AI models have shown success in automating the process, but using these resource-intensive, cloud-hosted models could expose proprietary circuit design and semiconductor foundry data to malicious users.

The MIT method, called Small LM Iterating on Circuits, or SLIC (pronounced “slick”), enables engineers to train a small language model to perform analog circuit design as well as or better than a frontier large language model (LLM). 

This small model is inexpensive and efficient enough to run on a laptop. Because it’s trained and deployed locally, it can use a company’s circuit design data without raising privacy risks. 

When compared to complementary baselines and open-weight frontier LLMs, a small model trained by SLIC more effectively generated designs that achieved the circuit objectives. 

“We’ve provided an alternative option to automate analog circuit design. With our technique, engineers can train a small, locally deployable model, using their own confidential data, and then deploy it in their own environment to ensure their assets remain protected,” says Yan Xu, an electrical engineering and computer science (EECS) graduate student and lead author of a paper on this technique.

She is joined on the paper by senior author Ruonan Han, a professor of EECS and a member of the MIT Research Laboratory of Electronics; Zhengqi Gao PhD ’26; Wenjie Lu PhD ’18, a former MIT postdoc who is now a principal research scientist at Analog Devices, Inc.; Xin Zhang, a research manager at IBM Research; Duane S. Boning, the Clarence J. LeBel Professor in EECS and MIT vice provost for international activities; and others at IBM Research and Analog Devices. The research will be presented at the 2026 Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems. 

“Through some specialized training and area-specific research, we can use much smaller models that consume far fewer resources to achieve almost the same results as flagship models in analog circuit design,” says Han. “This opens many more possibilities in the design of complex chips, especially if we care about costs, data privacy, and customization.”

Mimicking human learning

Analog integrated circuits enable a device to interact with the physical world. For instance, these circuits boost incoming wireless signals in smartphones and process outputs from sensors that track a car’s engine temperature. 

Real-world signals tend to be unpredictable, so engineers must balance a wide and complex array of targets and tradeoffs to maximize analog circuit performance. This has made the design problem especially challenging for AI models.

“To design a circuit, engineers find a good starting point based on their intuition and then, drawing on their knowledge of circuit design, tune a few knobs toward the performance they want,” says Xu. “There is no universal way to solve every circuit design problem.”

Even if a powerful, cloud-based model could design a circuit as well as a human, most companies would be reluctant to send their foundry-specific data to external AI service providers.

With SLIC, the MIT researchers created a training method that teaches a smaller, less expensive, faster language model to design analog integrated circuits that meet user specifications. 

The SLIC model uses a few billion parameters, making it several thousand times smaller than frontier models that use trillions of parameters and require enormous amounts of computational resources. 

“We tried to mimic the behavior of how a human learns to design a circuit,” Xu says.

They used a technique called multi-turn reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where a model works through a multi-step task while adapting to environmental feedback. 

When given an analog circuit optimization task, SLIC uses a large LLM to generate several demonstrations of the open source design process. Then SLIC then uses these demonstrations to guide the small model in mimicking this design process. 

After the small model gains some initial knowledge about circuit design, SLIC lets it practice by tackling a new design problem on its own.

The model makes an initial guess of the design parameters, performs simulations, evaluates the results, and iteratively refines the design using knowledge it gained about analog circuits.

Once a design achieves the user’s goals, SLIC prioritizes additional marginal gains. This means the model keeps learning to make improvements that boost performance even when several designs meet the user-defined targets. 

An interpretable process

Importantly, because SLIC employs models that describe their reasoning using natural language, the user can understand the decisions it makes along the way.

“Although the whole process is automated, the user can see what is going on inside the model. This could help the user gain some new ideas about circuit design, and it also adds a lot of confidence about the decision-making process,” Han says.

An engineer could utilize SLIC by adapting the researchers’ trained model to their data using a fine-tuning process. Or they could employ the SLIC training process to build their own model with company data, allowing for more customization.

“We are seeing an increasing demand for analog chips, but the speed of design has not kept up. This research is trying to bring new capabilities to AI to solve a problem that industry has been stuck on for decades,” Lu says.

When the researchers tested SLIC’s ability to design a circuit that met desired performance metrics, their small model came close to matching the performance of the latest GPT model (GPT-6-Astra). It did this while using a fraction of the computational resources. 

The researchers also found that the SLIC model maintained its performance when tackling previously unseen circuit structures and adapting to more advanced technology nodes (design and manufacturing rules) and real commercial processes.

Because SLIC teaches a model the general chip design process, the system is not tied to any company. This makes it a more scalable approach that could be used by many organizations for a range of circuit applications.

“The knowledge the model has gained about circuit design is universal in nature. That is the powerful aspect of this tool,” Han says.

In the future, the researchers want to explore self-improving models that can independently learn to handle more diverse topologies and design targets. They also want to use SLIC to build a multi-agent framework, in which many small language models work on different parts of a complex circuit design task.

“Yan’s work shows that a locally deployable model can learn transferable design behavior and iterate with a circuit simulator to improve a design, which could reduce repetitive manual tuning for engineers. This is the kind of work the MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab makes possible. We see it as opening the door to more sophisticated custom design, including RF and microwave circuits, in the settings where industry actually works,” says Zhang.

This research is funded, in part, by Analog Device, Inc., IBM, and the John L. Ocampo Endowment Fund of MACOM Technology Solutions.

item.title: A tiny superconducting sandwich could help computers use less energy
item.description: MIT researchers combined superconducting and magnetic layers in a tiny device offering persistent memory and signal control for more energy-efficient computing.
item.dc:creator: Julianna Mullen | Plasma Science and Fusion Center
item.content:encoded:
Scientists at the MIT Plasma Science and Fusion Center (PSFC) have created a tiny superconducting device that could help future computers store and process information using far less energy.

Today’s computers, supercomputers, and data centers need more of everything to keep up with demand: more energy, more capacity, and more speed to perform increasingly complex tasks. Feeding those computers’ processors with information — fast — is part of the challenge.

That’s where random access memory, or RAM, comes in. It’s a computer’s working space, keeping the information needed for current tasks close at hand. Without enough RAM, a computer slows down as it repeatedly retrieves information from hard drives or other longer-term storage.

Most familiar RAM is volatile: Turn off the power, and its contents disappear. There’s also nonvolatile memory, like the kind in a flash drive, which retains information without power. But there are trade-offs. Flash memory, for example, is slower to write than conventional RAM, and repeated writing and erasing eventually wear it out. Other forms of nonvolatile memory have different strengths and limitations.

In an effort to create faster, more energy-efficient computers, researchers have been developing superconducting computers, which rely on superconductors — a material that, when cold enough, exhibits no electrical resistance — instead of the traditional semiconductors to write information. In theory, the switch to superconductors allows for much quicker information processing with less heat emitted. But, processing is only as good as the memory that can supply those processors. It’s been a challenge to develop fast, high-capacity memory that also works at the extremely cold temperatures needed to operate superconducting computers.

Researchers at the PSFC have made a device that could help. In their recently published Physics Review Letters paper, titled “Magnetic Exchange-Coupled Superconducting Devices with Broken Symmetry for Cryogenic Memory,” senior research scientist Jagadeesh Moodera and his colleagues, including first author and postdoc Josep Ingla-Aynés, describe the device, which is a tiny sandwich made of an ultrathin superconducting film between two magnetic layers that can act as a memory cell. The magnets determine whether the film’s superconductivity is switched on or off.

"Integrating these devices can lead to processors operating at high speed and low energy,” says Moodera. “This development addresses the current lack of suitable cryogenic memory and control components, allowing for the advancement of cryogenic electronics technologies, including quantum computing and networking."   

At the memory cell’s operating temperature, depending on whether a current can pass through or not, a computer can distinguish between two states and read them as a 0 or a 1, which is a bit, the smallest unit of data in a computer. 

Writing a bit means, in this case, changing the magnetic alignment in the memory cell’s film: If the magnetization is pointing in opposite directions, the current can pass through; if it’s the same direction, the film becomes resistive. The researchers change the magnetic alignment by applying a small magnetic field and an electrical pulse that briefly heats the selected cell, making its magnetization easier to switch. Once set, the magnetic alignment stays in place without a continuing pulse or applied field. Each cell remembers. Moreover, it takes less energy to change that magnetic alignment in these cells and encode the bit than it does in traditional semiconductor cells. 

The device still needs to stay extremely cold to operate, but each bit does not need a continuous electrical supply to preserve its state — it’s nonvolatile memory. 

The researchers demonstrated that they could switch one cell without changing a neighboring cell, which is key when building memory in which individual bits can be selected and rewritten. The thought is that smaller cells could allow more information to fit into a compact space and could reduce the time and energy needed to write it.

According to Ingla-Aynés, “Any useful memory must have the ability to change one bit without disturbing all the information around it. Showing that we could switch a single cell without losing the neighbor's memory state was an important step toward bringing this superconducting layered device closer to a practical memory technology.”

The sandwich has another useful trick: It can also control where electrical signals go.

At a lower temperature, the device acts as a superconducting diode, which is like an on/off switch for delivering electricity in a certain direction. Within a particular range of currents, the device lets current flow without resistance in one direction while presenting resistance in the other. Changing the magnetic alignment can reverse that preferred direction, or create a resistive “off” state. Those settings could be used to direct or block the electrical pulses that carry information through superconducting circuits.

Having both capabilities in the same layered structure opens possibilities for combining memory and signal control on a superconducting chip. With that technology, superconducting computers could become a practical, energy-efficient alternative to the traditional computers currently relied upon for energy-intensive applications like AI. Moreover, while the devices store regular bits rather than quantum computers’ qubits, both quantum and traditional computers need reliable ways to hold information and move signals; the devices could potentially provide memory and signal control for quantum computers’ supporting electronics. Placing these devices near the cryogenic systems needed for superconducting operation could help reduce heat and electromagnetic interference that can disrupt the qubits’ fragile quantum state.

The researchers have demonstrated that their device can be used as an individually switchable, nonvolatile memory cell that could potentially serve as a building block for a new generation of highly efficient computers. The next challenge is to make these devices smaller and combine them into arrays capable of storing large amounts of information, while also quantifying just how much energy savings is possible in a system comprised of these devices.

item.title: New approach enables physically consistent AI models of chaotic systems
item.description: Enforcing physics-based constraints prevents AI models from generating unreliable predictions for complex nonlinear systems in weather, climate, and turbulent flows.
item.dc:creator: David Chandler | Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems
item.content:encoded:
Modeling of complex, chaotic processes such as weather and climate patterns and turbulent flows in aviation or in ocean currents has advanced enormously in recent years. However, such models are still prone to drift into physically impossible predictions over time.

Now, researchers with MIT’s Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS) have found a way to introduce physics-based restrictions on machine learning models that can ensure that such models never exceed realistic bounds, based on what is actually possible in the real world. This new approach, using information that is now being made freely available by the team, could significantly improve the usefulness and reliability of such models, which besides climate and weather are also used in a wide range of industrial processes, aeronautics, and hydrology.

The new findings are published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) in a paper by MIT graduate student Sunbochen Tang and MIT professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis. 

“Lack of guarantees for a bounded response has always been a major obstacle on formulating data-driven models for complex nonlinear systems,” says Sapsis, a professor of mechanical engineering and LIDS affiliate. The approach the team has developed, he says, “paves the way for applying the most advanced machine-learning architectures for prediction and control in a plethora of real-world problems, even those characterized by intrinsic instabilities.”

Developing reliable models for complex dynamical systems is important across many domains. In fluid dynamics, turbulent flows can disrupt air travel, reduce the efficiency of wind turbines, and affect fuel economy of vehicles. Similarly, in weather forecasting, the chaotic nature of atmospheric dynamics makes accurate long-term predictions difficult. 

“Tiny differences in the starting conditions can lead to dramatically different outcomes in a chaotic system,” Azizan says. “That makes predicting its behavior far into the future extremely difficult.” And yet, there are always physical constraints on the kinds of changes that are possible in the real world.

“Chaos does not mean anything can happen. These systems often remain bounded, and their models should, too.” But how to introduce those boundaries into the models has been a thorny problem, says Azizan, the Hayes Associate Professor in the Department of Mechanical Engineering and the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society, and a principal investigator in LIDS.

“A model can match the data over a short period and still fail when you let it run for a long time,” he says. “Small errors can accumulate until the simulation produces values that grow without limit,” producing predictions that could never actually occur in real systems.

“It’s a fundamental problem with many of the existing machine learning models,” he says. “It’s a question that comes up frequently in different domains: how can we embed physical constraints into these models in a way that preserves their flexibility, but ensures physically meaningful outputs?”

“We want to preserve the chaos without the artificial runaway behavior that the real system does not have,” he says. “Our approach gives the model room to learn complex dynamics while guaranteeing that its trajectories stay bounded.” This is the first work that establishes such formal guarantees for machine learning models of chaos.

Previous attempts to prevent unrealistic results from such models have often been based on “imposing penalties or incentives during training,” says Tang, a doctoral student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and LIDS, using functions that are often designed based on privileged information about the system. But as these only apply during the training process for the model, “there’s no guarantee that the model will satisfy the underlying constraints intended by such incentives at test time” once it is dealing with new inputs when it is actually used. “The model could still produce unbounded predictions,” he says.

To illustrate why simply imposing arbitrary limits would not be a satisfactory solution to the prediction stability issue, Tang explains, “you can cap the predictions, for example, by setting an arbitrary limit on physical quantities, such as 100 degrees for temperature. That’s one possible way to keep predictions bounded, but it could restrict the model from representing complex and nontrivial features that should be learned directly from the data.”

He says that “what sets our approach apart is that we formulate energy-based constraints. We let the model learn an energy-like function,” based on real-world chaotic systems, where energy dissipation helps keep trajectories bounded despite their complex behaviors. “Specifically, the model learns an energy-like function, along with a boundary where its chaotic behavior should be confined to. We then add a projection layer, a component that adjusts how the model predicts the system will evolve, to enforce energy dissipation as a hard constraint. Outside this boundary, the energy-like quantity must decrease, so the simulated system is drawn toward the bounded region. That way, we can establish theoretical guarantees that the model prediction remains bounded over arbitrarily long forecast windows.”

The team tested their approach on a variety of different well-known physical systems, ranging from simple textbook cases to highly complex multidimensional systems, and found that their approach closely matched the true outcomes, while conventional approaches soon deviated into impossible predictions.

Azizan adds that “the fundamental difference between our approach and the existing approaches is what we call hard constraining versus soft constraining.” While many of the current approaches “try to incentivize the model to satisfy the constraints, they’re not treated as hard constraints. Our approach is based on the concept of hard-constrained neural networks,” so that what comes out “is always physically consistent, even if it’s a completely new case the model hasn’t seen.”

“AI models shine in scenarios where there’s a large amount of data available,” Azizan says, for example with images or with text, both of which are abundantly available on the internet. However, he says, “for a lot of physical systems, data is not as abundant.” For such cases where the data is limited, he says, “these physics-constrained approaches can help a lot, because the physics of the problem is another source of information.”

The new approach is broadly useful for any chaotic systems. “This is readily applicable to a wide range of neural network architectures,” Tang says. They plan to continue testing it on ever-larger systems. “We’re trying to see how well this would work on data-driven models of realistic weather systems.”

“The projection layer is modular: it is model-agnostic and can work with different neural network architectures,” Azizan says. “We hope other researchers and practitioners will build on it and test it on larger and even more complex problems.” The paper, along with open-source code, is now accessible online at PNAS.

A follow-up work this year by members of the team was presented at the Learning for Dynamics and Control conference. The paper won the conference’s Best Paper Award.

“Trustworthy and reliable AI needs more than just evidence that a model usually works,” Azizan says. “For high-stakes applications, you need guarantees about the properties that must always hold. In this work, we established one such guarantee: boundedness. Our broader goal is to make principles part of how AI models are built, not just how they are tested.”

The findings could support more reliable predictions of long-term patterns in climate systems and turbulent flows.

item.title: Following the “mathocalypse,” mathematicians consider the future
item.description: A panel discussion at MIT explored AI’s implications for mathematical discovery and the people who make it their profession.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Chu | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
It’s been a tumultuous year for math. Big open questions that have occupied mathematicians for decades are now being solved in a matter of hours by artificial intelligence agents that companies deploy by the thousands to work on a single problem in tireless lockstep. 

AI’s relentless rise is raising existential questions for the field: How will the tools affect humans’ understanding of mathematical concepts? In the face of AI’s brute-force productivity, will mathematicians still have jobs? And what will all this mean for mathematics as an intellectual pursuit? 

At MIT, mathematicians grappled with these and other questions at a panel discussion on Monday titled “AI and Society: The Future of Math.” Leading mathematicians from MIT, Harvard University, Northwestern University, and New York University — each experts in their respective fields — sat down for a conversation that touched on the quality of AI math, how AI is challenging long-established research norms, and the evolving opportunities for mathematicians, whether they embrace the machines or remain “AI vegans.”

The wide-ranging discussion, which took place in a packed lecture hall in MIT’s Building 3, was moderated by science writer Kevin Hartnett, author of “The Proof in the Code,” and featured Jacopo Borga, the Cecil and Ida Green Career Development Assistant Professor of Mathematics at MIT; Michael Hopkins, the George Putnam Professor of Pure and Applied Mathematics at Harvard University; Bryna Kra, the Sarah Rebecca Roland Professor of Mathematics at Northwestern University; and Tristan Buckmaster, professor of mathematics at New York University's Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences.

As the panelists shared their various and at times conflicting perspectives on AI’s impact, one thing was clear:

“Math has changed more in the last two months than in the last 100 years,” said Kra, who cautioned that AI’s power will change what it is to be a mathematician and what it will take to advance human knowledge in meaningful ways. “It’s like the first sentence in ‘A Tale of Two Cities’: ‘It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.’ It’s a really exciting moment … and also scary.”

AI’s sprint

Artificial intelligence has made steady strides over the last decade thanks in large part to mathematicians themselves, who out of curiosity have been honing AI models to solve problems with known solutions. These early exercises proved successful, most notably in 2025. That summer, at the International Mathematical Olympiad, Google DeepMind’s AI models achieved gold-medal status by quickly finding solutions to most of the problems that were posed to the world’s best high school mathematicians. 

Around that same time, other mathematicians found that some AI systems could solve problems with known solutions, but in ways that were slightly improved compared to the solutions that human mathematicians had derived. 

In 2026, AI’s power took a quantum leap. In several instances, scientists found that models could solve open-ended research questions — mathematical problems that had no known answer. Then, in September, OpenAI made a field-shaking announcement: The company focused thousands of its AI agents on a singular challenge, and after 88 hours, the agents produced a proof related to the Navier-Stokes equation — a Millienum Prize Problem that is one of seven unsolvable mathematical Holy Grails. 

OpenAI’s sudden interest in the Navier-Stokes challenge coincided with work by Tristan Buckmaster, one of the panelists. After a year of progress, he and his collaborator, at rival AI behemoth Anthropic, were on the cusp of solving the problem when OpenAI made its announcement.

OpenAI’s sprint to be first to the proof opened up a huge debate, about whether proper credit was given, whether the mathematicians’ data was leaked, how the AI agents arrived at their solution, whether that solution makes any meaningful sense, and above all, how AI will change mathematical research. 

A month later, the company doubled down, releasing 722 manuscripts, organized into categories that ran the gamut of mathematical topics. The manuscripts claimed to have used AI entirely to solve many of math’s major, unsolved problems — an achievement that has widely been coined the “mathocalypse.” 

But many mathematicians insist that it isn’t just about whether a problem can be solved, but also, how. And, they say, when they’ve looked into the details of AI proofs, it’s not clear how the agents arrived at their conclusions. 

“The papers themselves are nonsense,” Hopkins said during Monday’s discussion, noting that AI-generated proofs contain “strange ideas.” He continued: “There still is a sense of AI math versus human math.”

“For math to be important, it has to have human understanding,” Buckmaster added. 

New norms

For mathematicians like Kra, this moment in math’s history presents an opportunity to let go of certain long-held norms of mathematical research, such as competition among research groups and the prestige of being the first to prove an idea, also known as priority.

“It shouldn’t matter that you’re first,” Kra said. “Speed should not be a priority. It’s not about the proof production anymore. We need to find other ways to assess understanding.”

However, “We can throw away priority, but people are going to want to be pioneers,” Hopkins countered, noting the challenge that mathematicians will now face in making in-roads where AI has already clear-cut. 

Kra, however, struck a hopeful counterpoint: 

“You can be a pioneer in different ways, for instance in communicating [how a proof came to be],” said Kra, who helped this year to draft the Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics — a statement signed by mathematicians around the world that calls for action to address the risks that AI poses to mathematical research. “Communication of math is even more important now.” 

Indeed, the panelists have already seen a subtle shift in what is expected of a mathematician, at all levels, from undergraduate students to early and established career mathematicians. 

“The interview is becoming more important,” said Kra, noting that it’s no longer enough to accept, hire, or promote a mathematician based on ideas they have written or published — they have to also show that they understand and can explain those ideas to another person. 

Human math

AI is also making mathematicians question the role of academic journals, which have long been the benchmark for evaluating and validating mathematical advances.

“Ninety percent of how we’ve judged [mathematicians] are through journals,” says Jacopo Borga, who is an early-career mathematician at MIT. “I’m not sure that’s how we should do this anymore. We should come up with a new metric and let it evolve.”

Kra, who is a managing editor of a specialty journal, is seeing a huge increase in the number of papers submitted, primarily reporting results that were generated or assisted by AI. To deal with the deluge, that particular journal has had to hire an additional managing editor. 

Where journal editors have traditionally prioritized publishing new proofs that push the field forward, Kra sees that, in response to AI “slop,” some publications are putting more value on exposition — the section of a paper that explains the reasoning behind a conjecture or proof. For now, humans have the advantage over AI in communicating mathematical ideas.

“There’s a real art to exposition, if you can explain something in a clear and elegant way,” Hopkins echoed. 

Kra noted that there are experimental journals coming online now, that are designed to highlight uniquely human contributions to mathematics. For instance, there are journals that publish expositions, such as papers that explain an old result in a new way that modern mathematicians can understand.

“There is a lot of opportunity to curate and translate knowledge,” said Hopkins, who shared that one of his students has been working to prove a theorem from the 1970s. The original language and construction from that decades-old theorem, he said, was just as foreign as some of AI’s proofs today. 

In noting novel approaches journals are taking in response to AI, Kra also mentioned Mathematical Discourse, a new peer-reviewed “video journal” that will feature videos of people giving talks about mathematical research. The journal’s preliminary site states that “giving a mathematical talk captures the human side of mathematics in a unique way, and supporting these human aspects of our discipline will be ever more important in the coming years.”

“A new kind of mathematician”

The rise of AI may be hitting especially hard for students, who are still learning the fundamentals in the presence of so many AI shortcuts. 

“Mathematics is probably the slowest science you can do,” said Borga, to appreciative laughs from the audience. “Students today are bombarded by [conflicting messages of] what they should do, and are overwhelmed. We need to give them space to learn.”

How they should learn could be a matter of personal belief. 

“There is a big faction of my group who are ‘AI vegans’ [people who do not use AI], while others are using it,” said Hopkins, who is finding ways to support both groups.

He also highlighted one particular student, who seemed to be a sort of “horse whisperer of AI.” This student has good mathematical instincts, Hopkins said, but struggles with execution. They are motivated by curiosity, rather than being first to a solution, and have a way of prompting AI to produce interesting insights. 

“This may be a new kind of mathematician,” Hopkins said. 

As AI forces the field of mathematics to adapt and change its centuries-long ways of pursuing knowledge, Borga and others see the moment as a new beginning, rather than math’s end.

“The castle is collapsing,” Borga says. “There’s open ground to explore.”

“AI is going to affect everyone (beyond mathematicians),” said Buckmaster, who urged students to stay the course “rather than escape or jump ship to another field. … Think of new ways to be creative and communicate your ideas,” he said. “Just do what you love.”

The panel discussion, co-sponsored by the Department of Mathematics, is the first of a planned series hosted by MITHIC and SERC exploring how AI is reshaping our personal and professional lives.

item.title: AI helps researchers investigate how thousands of medical studies share code
item.description: An MIT and Dana-Farber Institute-led team used large language models to examine nearly 4,000 studies and hundreds of code repositories, revealing gaps in the information needed to scrutinize and reuse published research.
item.dc:creator: Bwiza Gihana Deborah | Institute for Medical Engineering and Science
item.content:encoded:
The data and code that underpin a research study can tell us what was actually done, and how. In a medical study, for example, how were patients selected for inclusion? How were missing values handled? How were the results evaluated? 

Access to a study's data and code help researchers to answer these questions, to examine the methods, and to build on the work. 

“Studies involve many choices about how to prepare data, develop models, and evaluate performance. These are sometimes called ‘researcher degrees of freedom,’” says Tom Pollard, a research scientist at MIT's Laboratory for Computational Physiology and Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. “The choices we make affect the results, and a methods section in a paper can only capture so much detail.”

While sharing code can be a first step, in order for code to be understood and reused, it must be sufficiently structured and described. The problem is that, right now, there is little guidance for researchers on what constitutes a well-organized, well-described collection of code. 

This is where an international team led by researchers at MIT and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute sought to help, by examining how code is currently shared in clinical prediction studies. Such studies develop or evaluate models to estimate patient outcomes, such as the risk of developing a disease. Because these models inform decisions about patient care, researchers need to be able to scrutinize how they were built and tested.

Using large language models (LLMs), the researchers examined nearly 4,000 papers to identify statements about shared code. They then followed the statements to assess hundreds of associated code repositories.

Their review revealed two key gaps: Code sharing remains uncommon, and making code public does not consistently mean providing the documentation and supporting information needed for reuse. The open-access findings, recently published in Nature Medicine, are informing TRIPOD-Code, a reporting guideline being developed to clarify what researchers should share.

Following the code

TRIPOD-Code builds on TRIPOD and TRIPOD+AI, checklists that help researchers report how clinical prediction models were developed and evaluated. To understand current code-sharing practices, the team identified studies citing either guideline. The review included almost 4,000 studies that developed, updated, or validated prediction models, and whose full texts were available through PubMed Central’s open-access collection. 

“The challenge was that the information was highly inconsistent. First, we had to identify whether or not a paper shared code” says Thomas Sounack, the study’s first author. He adds that authors “discuss and link to code from a paper in many different ways.”

The team used an LLM to help screen papers, identify statements about code availability, and extract links. Software then retrieved the linked repositories — online collections of code and related files — for further assessment.

The workflow went beyond checking whether a link existed. It also assessed repositories against characteristics such as completeness of documentation, software requirements, and terms of reuse.

“The real benefit of LLMs is their ability to process unstructured information such as text. These models helped us work with information that was scattered across papers and software repositories, rather than neatly organized in a table,” says Pollard, who is a senior author of the study. “That allowed us to examine how code was being shared in much more detail across a large collection of studies.”

Human reviewers evaluated the work of the LLMs. Two researchers independently checked 500 papers and a separate sample of repositories, resolving disagreements before comparing their assessments with the automated results. 

Agreement was stronger for concrete characteristics, such as whether a license file was present, than for judgments about the adequacy of documentation. Because classification errors remain possible, the authors emphasize the overall patterns rather than treating every count as exact.

Inconsistent code sharing

Only about 1 in 8 studies reported sharing code. Where code was shared, the contents of repositories varied widely.

Some repositories were “extremely well-organized and -documented, while others gave almost no guidance at all,” Sounack says. Good code sharing, he explains, means “giving enough information to understand what the code does and be able to run it to reproduce the results reported in the paper.”

Practices also varied substantially across journals and countries. Among journals, the proportion of studies sharing code ranged from zero to more than 70 percent. Some journals with low sharing rates nevertheless had written code-sharing policies, suggesting that policies alone may not be enough to motivate code sharing.

The review also helped to identify examples of effective practice. Some researchers, for example, provided synthetic datasets to assist with code reuse where the original patient records could not be shared publicly.

Setting a standard for code sharing

Researchers who share code are already making an effort to make their work transparent. But clinical prediction research brings together people from medicine, statistics, and computer science, whose expectations for documenting and sharing code may differ.

TRIPOD-Code aims to establish a consensus. Through an expert review process, the team is developing guidance on which elements of shared analytical code should be considered essential.

“We want to give researchers practical guidance on how to share code, and give journals clearer expectations to communicate to authors,” Pollard says. “The review gives us evidence to inform those discussions."
