item.title: Ultrasound imaging without the gel
item.description: A new dry material could replace the traditional goopy gel for wearable ultrasound patches.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Chu | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
Engineers at MIT and the Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology’s Wearable Imaging for Transforming Elderly Care project (SMART WITEC) have developed a dry and stretchy material that could eliminate the need for a wet and sticky gel in ultrasound imaging. 

Ultrasound technicians typically spread a cold gel onto a patient’s skin before imaging the area with an ultrasound probe. The gel fills in tiny gaps between the probe and the skin so ultrasound waves can travel efficiently through the skin to generate clear images of a patient’s underlying structures. 

Members of MIT’s Zhao Lab are designing wearable ultrasound patches that could provide continuous imaging, at home or on the go. But one sticking point has been the gel. Their previous designs have included a layer of hydrogel — a mostly water-based material that seals up the space between the skin and a small ultrasound probe. But within a day or two, the gel can dry out, along with its ability to transmit sound waves. 

“In a doctor’s office, a technician can simply apply more gel if needed. But for a wearable device, gel-based designs can limit their long-term usability,” says Xuanhe Zhao, the Uncas and Helen Whitaker Professor of Mechanical Engineering at MIT. 

The MIT team has developed a liquid-free alternative to gel that efficiently transmits ultrasound waves, which they report today in the journal Science. Because the material is dry from the start, its performance remains stable over long periods. In experiments, the engineers found that the rubbery material enabled a wearable ultrasound device to generate clear, continuous images over nine days, even during vigorous exercise.

As a demonstration, the team fixed a small wearable patch, about the size of a key fob, to a volunteer’s neck. The patch contained a small ultrasound probe, and the dry and stretchy layer that stuck directly to the skin. The entire patch was connected to a small portable tablet that recorded the patch’s ultrasound images as the volunteer took a 30-minute bike ride, from MIT’s campus in Cambridge, Massachusetts, to Bunker Hill in neighboring Charlestown, and back. 

“We are really aiming to address a material challenge in ultrasound imaging,” says study leader Shu Wang, a postdoc in MIT’s Department of Mechanical Engineering.

“If you don’t have a good interface, that will definitely stop you from developing this wearable imaging field,” adds co-lead author and MIT postdoc Runze Li. “This is a very good solution that enables a longer time for imaging.”

In addition to Zhao, Wang, and Li, the study’s MIT co-authors are Chen Gong and Won Jun Song; additional co-authors are Zihan Tang and Ying Li of the University of Wisconsin at Madison; Chwee Teck Lim of the National University of Singapore; and Xiaodong Chen of Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. Zhao, Chen, and Lim are the co-lead principal investigators of the SMART WITEC interdisciplinary research group.

Molecular detangler

Gels and liquids in general are ideal media through which sound waves, including ultrasound, can travel. Think of sonar, and the calls of whales and dolphins, which can travel much farther in water than air. This is mainly due to the makeup of molecules in fluids. Water molecules, for instance, are small and loosely connected, and can slide easily against each other. As a sound wave passes through, there is little friction between the molecules, allowing the wave to travel without losing intensity. 

Soft solids such as most rubbery and polymer-based materials, however, have more interconnected molecular structures. The same sound wave would dissipate when moving through a solid block, as larger, tangled molecules would generate more friction as they shift in response to the incoming wave. 

The MIT team aimed to make a solid, rubbery material that retained a gel’s ultrasound propagating properties. For this, they took a molecular engineering approach. 

“Hydrogel is mainly water, with just a bit of polymer, whereas solid materials like rubber are almost 100 percent polymer molecules,” Wang explains. “We tried to reduce the friction between polymer chains in our material, without adding liquid or lubricant.”

Polymer materials such as rubber and elastic are made from microscopic molecules that chemically bond with other similar molecules to form long polymer chains. In a solid material, these chains form a dense thicket and do not slide easily against each other. 

In looking for ways to reduce the friction between polymer chains, the engineers landed on a “bottlebrush” structure — a molecular configuration that has been explored in other applications including drug delivery and light-reflecting materials. A bottlebrush molecule consists of a main backbone of molecules, with smaller side chains of molecules sprouting away, like the bristles of a pipe cleaner. 

“These hairy extensions don’t easily penetrate other bottlebrush molecules,” Wang notes. “They can easily move around at the ultrasound frequencies, and that’s why there is less friction between them.”

With that reasoning, the team came up with a protocol to fabricate a polymer material made entirely from a molecular bottlebrush architecture. Their first attempts, however, did not quite hold up. 

“The first samples were very soft and crumbly, like tofu,” Wang says. “If the samples were too large, they would not hold their own weight, and if you picked one up, it would just break.”

They quickly found they could reinforce the material by chemically fusing it with a second, loosely connected network of bottlebrush molecules. This additional network essentially held the first, crumbly network of bottlebrush polymers in place, without affecting their low-friction properties. The result was a tougher, rubbery material that the researchers were able to stretch repeatedly without tearing. 

“It’s very much like skin,” says Wang. “It’s very soft but will hold together if pinched or pulled.” 

Imaging workouts

The team fabricated credit card-sized samples of the new material and first tested its ultrasound properties on a “phantom” model — a synthetic structure that is made from materials that mimic a human’s skin and internal structures. In these tests, the material efficiently transmitted ultrasound waves from a probe, through the model, to image the structures underneath. The team kept the setup running continuously and found it kept imaging clearly for around nine days. 

“In principle, this material could go forever, depending on how stable it is,” Wang notes. “The sound properties stay the same. And that was the moment when we thought, oh, this material could work.”

To test the material’s mechanical performance, the team adhered a patch to a volunteer’s chest as they ran on a treadmill. For comparison, the volunteer also wore a sample of a conventional silicone rubber. Throughout a 10-minute run, the silicone rubber became water-logged with sweat, whereas the new material wicked away any sweat buildup. These tests suggest that the new material can hold up over strenuous exercise. 

Finally, the researchers tested the material in the field, attaching it to a small ultrasound transducer applied to a volunteer’s neck. Throughout a 30-minute bike ride that traversed steep inclines, the device maintained continuous and accurate ultrasound imaging of the rider’s blood flow. 

Going forward, the team is working to streamline the fabrication of the material. Then, they hope to enable wearable, long-lasting ultrasound imagers that can be used to track athlete performance and monitoring patient health outside of clinical settings.

“In the hospital, a doctor can replace gel if it dries out,” Li offers. “But if we want ultrasound imaging that goes beyond the clinical scenario, we need a material that lasts longer, and is easier to handle. And we think this really works.”

item.title: Scientists create the first whole-body single-cell atlas of an adult vertebrate
item.description: Researchers mapped gene activity across the entire body of a tiny fish, creating a resource for studying brain regeneration, cellular diversity, and tissue function.
item.dc:creator: Mackenzie White | Whitehead Institute
item.content:encoded:
Viewed from above, Danionella cerebrum offers a rare sight in a vertebrate: its brain, visible through the top of its head. Since the species was formally described in 2021, the tiny, transparent fish has drawn rapidly growing interest for its unique biology.

Scientists at MIT, the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research, and Charité–Universitätsmedizin Berlin recognized another opportunity in the tiny fish: It brought whole-animal single-cell profiling within reach, allowing the team to create the first comprehensive map of cell types and gene activity across an adult vertebrate. That perspective could help reveal how cells in different tissues coordinate their responses — and how changes in one part of the body influence others.

In a study published in Science on Oct. 29, the team profiled more than 600,000 cells from across the fish to build the whole-body map of which genes are active in which cell, known as a single-cell transcriptome atlas. A cell’s transcriptome is the full set of RNA molecules it has made from its DNA at a given time, providing a snapshot of which genes the cell is using.

Together, the data provide a molecular reference for the cell types found throughout Danionella, the patterns of gene activity that distinguish them, and where many of them are located. The atlas also gives researchers a baseline for exploring how injury, aging, drugs, or other changes affect cells across the whole animal.

“Once you have a spatially resolved atlas, you know what cell types exist, but you also know the neighbors of those cell types in this context,” says Kutay Deniz Atabay, who led the work as a postdoc in the lab of Peter Reddien, a Whitehead Institute member and professor of biology at MIT. “This gives you access at multiple different levels of complexity, from molecular to cellular to systems.”

Cell atlases have become increasingly detailed, but extending them across a whole adult vertebrate has been difficult for a simple reason: size. Profiling the cellular diversity of larger animals comprehensively is technically demanding and expensive. Danionella offered a unique way around that problem. Its miniature body — barely 1 centimeter long — makes the experiment possible, while its close relationship to zebra fish allows researchers to draw on genetic tools developed for one of biology’s most widely used model organisms.

Atabay first became interested in Danionella in early 2019, while searching for a small, transparent animal in which he could watch the nervous system regenerate. Its miniature size and accessible brain made it especially promising for that work, and the researchers found that the fish has broad regenerative capacity, including in the brain and fins. Reddien’s lab, meanwhile, had already seen the value of a comprehensive whole-animal cell atlas through its work on planarians, regenerative flatworms whose small size had made such an atlas possible. Together, those interests led to a larger question.

“Deniz and I had the thought: Would it be possible to get a cell-type transcriptome atlas for a complete vertebrate?” says Reddien, who is also an investigator with the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. “Here’s an animal where we’d have a chance.”

To build the atlas, the researchers used single-cell RNA sequencing to measure gene activity in individual cells collected from across the brain, spinal cord, eyes, internal organs, fins, head, and trunk. They paired those data with spatial methods that mapped cell types and patterns of gene activity back to their locations in tissues. The resulting atlas was extensive enough to capture even exceptionally rare cell populations.

Looking across the animal revealed patterns that can be difficult to see when tissues are studied separately. In the nervous system, neurons from the same region often had more similar patterns of gene activity — even when they used different neurotransmitters, the chemicals neurons use to communicate — than when compared to neurons using the same neurotransmitter in different regions. Similar patterns have been observed in other vertebrates, including mammals, suggesting that regional and developmental identity may be an important organizing feature of vertebrate nervous systems.

The atlas also revealed signs that adult cells retain a molecular memory of where they belong in the body. Fibroblasts, a type of connective-tissue cell, maintained region-specific activity of genes best known for establishing different parts of the body during development. Cells in the pectoral and pelvic fins, for example, retained gene programs associated with forelimb and hindlimb development in other vertebrates. What these persistent signals do in adult Danionella remains unknown, but they may help tissues maintain or rebuild the appropriate structures. In planarians, positional information provides molecular guidance that helps regenerating tissues rebuild the correct structures.

The research also used the atlas as a reference for studying Danionella’s remarkable regenerative abilities. After injuring the telencephalon, a region of the forebrain, the missing neurons regenerated and the researchers traced a progression from an early wound and immune response to neural stem-cell activity and the production and maturation of new neurons.

The team has made the atlas publicly available through DigiFish, an interactive resource for exploring cell types and gene activity throughout the animal. Paired with Danionella’s transparency and growing experimental toolkit, the atlas can help researchers identify specific cells and genes to study or manipulate and then follow their activity in the animal.

For Reddien, the advance presents numerous, diverse opportunities for new science. “There’s been this era of genome sequencing, where you get the complete list of all the genes that it takes to make an organism,” he says. “The transcriptomes of cells tell you how that genome is being utilized in the different cell types. To have the transcriptome of every cell type seems like a big turning point in how one would investigate the biology of an organism.”

item.title: If tiny “primordial” black holes exist, here’s how we might find them
item.description: When engulfed by a star, the small but massive object should devour the star from within, leading to a detectable explosion, a new study proposes.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Chu | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
Scientists have hypothesized that, in the fraction of a second following the Big Bang, minute black holes may have been forged within tiny, dense pockets that collapsed under their own gravity. If these primordial black holes are ever found, they could represent a significant component of dark matter — the invisible substance that makes up most of the universe’s matter. 

Now physicists at MIT and elsewhere have worked out a way that astronomers could detect a primordial black hole. The team carried out theoretical calculations and three-dimensional simulations to show what would happen if a lingering primordial black hole were captured by a modern, sun-like star. 

In a study appearing today in the Astrophysical Journal, the team’s simulations reveal a dramatic evolution: When an atom-sized primordial black hole with the mass of an asteroid is caught up in the gravity of a sun-sized star, it should quickly fall into the star’s core. Then, it would begin to devour the star from the inside. 

If the star spins sufficiently fast, the simulations show that a disk of its own stardust should begin to circle as it falls into the black hole. 

“Once the disk forms, this is essentially a death sentence for the star,” says lead author Ore Gottlieb, an assistant professor of physics at MIT. 

Within a matter of seconds, interactions between the black hole and the spinning disk should launch powerful jets of matter that ultimately pierce through the star, making it explode.

That dramatic fate, the researchers calculated, would generate a flash of blue and ultraviolet light, along with gamma- and X-rays. This flash should be bright enough to detect with current telescopes.

“There is hope for us to probe primordial black holes through interactions with stars,” Gottlieb says. “We expect this to be visible, and it’s something we should look into.”

The study’s co-authors are Matteo Cantiello of the Flatiron Institute, Cameron Norton and Matthew Kleban of New York University, and Ken Van Tilburg of Stanford University. 

Quantum quarry

Today, the smallest and lightest primordial black holes would have evaporated away due to Hawking radiation — a quantum effect that was proposed by the physicist Stephen Hawking to describe how black holes can radiate energy and shrink, very slowly, over cosmic time. 

Larger, heavier primordial black holes, however, should still be around, not having had quite enough time to disappear. These lingering relics would be about the size of an atom, and as massive as an asteroid (or about a millionth of the mass of the Earth). Gottlieb and his colleagues wondered: If asteroid-mass primordial black holes indeed exist, how might they interact with stars today? What’s more, could this interaction be a way to detect primordial black holes, and confirm their existence? 

In their new study, the researchers carried out analytic calculations and numerical simulations based on equations of general relativity, hydrodynamics, stellar evolution, and particle physics, to determine how an asteroid-mass primordial black hole could be captured by a star and what events might unfold from there.

They discovered that the gravitational pull from a single star would not be enough to trap a passing primordial black hole. However, the researchers found that gravitational interaction with a companion, such as a second star or planet, could efficiently trap a primordial black hole. 

In this three-body configuration, the team calculated the friction that the black hole would experience as it passes through the stellar material. They found that repeated passages could gradually shrink its orbit, and over a span of thousands to millions of years — nearly instantaneous on cosmic timescales — the black hole would fall into the center of the star. 

“Then, this is where the action begins,” Gottlieb says. 

A critical pull

The team modeled the black hole evolution within the star. How quickly the black hole grows depends on how much energy the black hole releases back into the surrounding star as it heats the gas and slows further infall. 

They found that most of the energy is carried into the black hole, allowing the black hole to grow faster than previously thought. Within several million years, the black hole would have consumed about 1 percent of the star’s mass. If at this critical point, the star spins fast enough, its gas can no longer fall directly into the black hole and instead piles up in a rotating disk of material around a few-meter-sized black hole at the heart of the star. 

“Inside the star, you have a black hole with a disk,” Gottlieb says. “The black hole is also spinning, and it’s twisting space and time.”

As the black hole continues to consume the disk’s spiraling material, it twists and pulls on the disk’s magnetic field.

“This twisted magnetic field will power very strong electromagnetic jets from the poles of the black hole,” Gottlieb explains. “And these jets will just explode the star, within a few dozen seconds. It’s very fast. Once you have a disk, you are done.” 

Finally, the team estimated the color and intensity of light that such an explosion could generate, from start to finish, across the electromagnetic spectrum. 

“We would initially detect some X-rays and gamma rays, then over time optical and infrared emissions, and later on radio emissions,” Gottlieb says. “This is something we could potentially detect, if it’s not happening too far from us. It could be many galaxies away, not just in our backyard.”

He points out that other astrophysical phenomena could produce a similar flash. If astronomers detect such a flash, they will have to combine the signal with other clues to confirm that the source is a primordial black hole. 

“For instance, if the star is a certain mass that is not supposed to explode, it must be something that is happening inside that is a sort of parasite that is consuming the star from the inside,” Gottlieb says. “The broader impact is that we can now place constraints on primordial black holes, and their contributions to dark matter, using observations.”

This work was supported, in part, by the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science Advanced Scientific Computing Research Program, and by the National Science Foundation.

item.title: Study reveals data centers’ long-distance damage to air quality
item.description: Researchers find air pollution from data center electricity use can affect communities far from the facilities, with some of the highest impacts in the Midwest.
item.dc:creator: Adam Zewe | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
The rapid expansion of data centers for artificial intelligence causes negative health and air quality impacts in regions far from where the brick-and-mortar facilities are located, according to a new study by MIT researchers.

The team estimates that additional air pollution from the electricity demands of data centers in 2023 resulted in about 650 premature deaths across the United States. 

Some Midwestern states had among the highest estimated rates of premature deaths per capita attributable to data centers, even though much of the data center electricity demand was concentrated in Virginia and Texas.

The researchers built a modeling framework that captures how the electricity demanded by data centers propagates through the nation’s interconnected power grid. The model also considers how atmospheric conditions impact the formation of air pollution in different regions.

The framework identifies power plants across the country whose emissions increase in response to data center electricity demand. In parts of the Midwest, these emissions combine with atmospheric conditions that favor the formation of fine particulate matter, a pollutant that can cause heart attacks, stroke, and lung disease.

The researchers say these results underscore the importance of considering unintended regional health impacts of data centers, and how the location and operations of these facilities affect public health on a broader scale.

“When people think about the negative impacts of data centers, they usually focus on the neighbors. But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region. Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” says Noelle Selin, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS); director of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy; and senior author of the study.

Selin is joined on the paper by Yuang (Albert) Chen, an MIT graduate student; as well as others at MIT, the University of California at Irvine, and Yale University. The research appears today in Environmental Research Letters.

Capturing regional impacts

The Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that electricity demands of data centers represented about 4 percent of total U.S. energy demand in 2023 and resulted in about 4.4 percent of the nation’s overall emissions. 

That proportion has likely increased as new data centers continue to be built at a rapid pace.

Many prior studies estimate impacts using average electricity-grid emissions. Like those studies, the researchers assume data centers draw power to run computing tasks 24/7. Their approach also identifies which generators respond to that additional demand hour by hour, allowing them to trace where the resulting emissions and health impacts occur, Chen explains.

“Generators that respond to additional electricity demand are often natural gas plants, although the response varies by place and hour,” he says.

To drill down on regional health impacts, the MIT researchers developed a modeling approach that enables them to identify which generators are contributing to data center electricity demand within each modeled region. 

This allows them to incorporate a spatial component into the analysis.

They built an electricity system model that simulates how much electricity each generator produces and pumps into the grid every hour. This model also considers how that electricity is transmitted between regions. 

It gives the researchers data on emissions of nitrogen oxides (NOx) and sulfur dioxide (SO2) for each generator across the United States. NOx contributes to the formation of ground-level ozone, or smog, while both NOx and SO2 contribute to the formation of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) in the atmosphere.

“It was a challenge to gather all the data,” Chen says. “There are more than 10,000 generators in the U.S. grid, and we needed to make sure the data provided for each generator is valid and validated across other data sources.”

The researchers incorporated these data into a chemical transport model. This model simulates how pollutants form and travel through the atmosphere across regions. 

From there, they translated the additional air pollution from data center operations into premature mortality rates using evidence from epidemiological literature.

The model estimates that emissions from data centers caused about 650 premature deaths in 2023 (513 from PM2.5 and 137 from smog), which represents about 5.3 percent of the nation’s total electricity-related mortality. 

“While it is not surprising that any additional source of air pollution will result in mortalities, with data centers, when and where these deaths are occurring are different than you might expect,” Selin says.

A pollution mismatch

The premature mortality rates were highest in Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas, but the bulk of the electricity demand was concentrated in northern Virginia and in Texas. Premature mortality rates in Virginia and Texas are only about half as much as most Midwestern states.

One reason for this mismatch is the interconnected nature of the power grid, Chen says. 

Generators that respond to the increased electricity demand in Virginia are likely located in the Ohio Valley, where there is a higher proportion of older power plants that generate more emissions from burning coal and natural gas. 

“Different regions have different mixes of power. If you turn on a major new demand source, by plugging a data center into the grid, you might have to fire up your really dirty power plant to meet that new demand,” Selin says.

Plus, due to atmospheric conditions, many pollutants generated in these regions are transported to downwind states.

Midwest states like Nebraska and Iowa are traditionally agricultural regions. Additional ammonia in the atmosphere from fertilizer enhances the formation of PM2.5. The estimated health impacts also extend to Kansas, South Dakota, Missouri, and Arkansas, illustrating that the effects can reach states with relatively few data centers.

The study shows that rural populations are expected to have significantly higher mortality risk from data center electricity demand than urban populations, Chen says.

“When people are thinking about data center siting and operations, it is important to consider more than just things like land and energy prices. They should also take air quality considerations into the equation,” he says. “This is a good baseline to think about where we should build data centers and how we should supply those data centers with electricity.”

In the future, the researchers want to consider air quality impacts of onsite generation — a growing trend where data centers incorporate power plants that supply electricity. They could also study the flexibility of data center operations, and how adaptively adjusting electricity demand could impact air quality. 

This research was funded, in part, by the MIT Energy Initiative Society of Energy Scholars and the MIT Martin Family Society of Fellows for Sustainability.

item.title: Confirmed: Numbers tell, but language sells
item.description: When people use statistics to persuade others, they are more likely to summarize the data in words — and it works, researchers say.
item.dc:creator: Peter Dizikes | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
Suppose you are in charge of your firm’s commuting policy and, after some research, you determine that 57 percent of your colleagues drive to work. How would you communicate that number to co-workers?

You could just tell them the number. Or you could characterize it in words. If you want to imply that 57 percent is a large number, you could call it “a clear majority,” or even “approaching two-thirds” (roughly 67 percent). However, if you seek to minimize 57 percent, you might call it “barely over half.” 

Either way, when people are motivated to persuade their audience that a number is particularly high or low, they are considerably more likely to use language to describe the data, rather than simply airing the original numbers. 

Now a new study co-authored by an MIT scholar quantifies this phenomenon: People motivated to persude others about statistical facts are 25 percent to 29 percent more likely to use words describing the numbers in question, instead of the numbers themselves. That is a large enough increase to be termed “substantial,” “significant,” or any number of other words.

“If I’m a well-informed expert and I have incentives to persuade my audience, I’m relatively more likely to choose to use language,” says co-author Victor de Chaisemartin, a doctoral candidate at the MIT Sloan School of Management. 

The language that experts choose when seeking to persuade others is also more slanted than their numeric communications. As the authors note in the paper, people appear to be leveraging the imprecision of language in ways they feel are palatable: Whereas reporting a number incorrectly would be precisely false, it may be more psychologically comfortable to slant a message using language.

And that’s just the half of it. The study also shows that audiences find language-based descriptions of numbers convincing — even when they are told there is an agenda behind them. 

“Language messages are particularly persuasive,” de Chaisemartin says. Telling an audience they are being spun, he notes, “actually doesn’t do very much to mitigate this. That’s interesting. It makes you wonder what’s going through people’s heads, and how they are dealing with information.”

The paper, “Numbers Tell, Words Sell,” is being published in the American Economic Review. The authors are de Chaisemartin; Michael Thaler, a lecturer in economics at University College London; and Mattie Toma, an associate professor at the University of Warwick. 

Floating in data, reporting it in words

As de Chaisemartin describes it, the study’s origins come from a basic observation.

“The world has loads of statistics floating around in it,” he says. “But often if you pick up a newspaper or read something in the media, or if you’re reading a corporate report, you don’t usually see 50 statistics. You’re often going to see a lot of quantitiave data reported in words.”

Indeed, one study of media practices has found that 22 percent of news items include statistics, but that 24 percent of those stories only use words to describe the numbers. Another study of academic research has found that just 37 percent of papers include numbers in their abstracts. 

To conduct the study, the researchers conducted two separate but parallel experiments. In the first one, using the research platform Prolific, 1,000 members of the general public were divided into 500 pairs of senders and receivers of information, communicating the results of simple games and observations. In the second experiment, set up through the University of Warwick’s Policymakers Lab, 146 scholars from academia were paired with policymakers from five countries — primarily central government officials.

Ultimately, the experiments show that when incentivized for accuracy, senders of information choose language over numbers only 13 to 14 percent of the time; that is, experts generally prefer numbers for communicating accurately. But faced with incentives to persuade, the likelihood of senders choosing language increases by 25 to 29 percentage points. 

“It’s a clear-cut hypotheses, it makes sense, and the results bear it out,” de Chaisemartin says.

Applying the findings

While the study is specific in nature, it contains some broader implications. For one thing, de Chaisemartin notes, the findings can help organizations recognize the value of constructing consistent usage standards. Climate scientists, he notes, do this already regarding some forecasts. Security officials, medical researchers, doctors, and scholars may also have good reasons to adopt similar characterizations of likelihoods and other things. 

“There are ways to think carefully about how we set up and report empirical data,” he says. “This could be viewed as one piece of information pushing in that direction.”

De Chaisemartin also suggests that the findings bear on the issue of media literacy generally, and could be used to help people analyze the statistical claims they read in the news. For his part, he is also interested in follow-up questions about what happens when people send information to the same audience repeatedly. 

“That might introduce interesting new mechanisms in this process,” de Chaisemartin says, noting that senders of information might have additional incentives to protect their reputations for accuracy, while audiences could become more discerning over time. 

To be sure, there are many subtleties involved in descriptions of statistics. For example, given that most drivers wear seatbelts, a policy intervention raising the usage rate by two percentage points might not seem huge in absolute terms, but could represent a substantial increase within the remaining room for improvement. In other circumstances, a change of two percentage points might just be a small fluctuation in a sea of data.  

Language descriptions could therefore help contextualize numbers or aid audiences in understanding statistics. However, the present findings suggest caution when interpreting language, since it may also signal that the expert was trying to persuade their audience.

In any event, de Chaisemartin expresses hope that public discourse involving statistics can become consistently healthy and accurate. 

“There’s a space for language and numbers to be complementary, and to provide people with both,” he says.

The research was supported, in part, by the British Academy/Leverhulme Small Research Grants, and the University of Warwick Behaviour Spotlight Small Grant Scheme and Primary Data Funds.

item.title: This featherweight, flying robot carries its own sensors and computers
item.description: The speedy microrobot flies without an attached motion-capture system, moving it closer to applications like agriculture or industrial surveillance.
item.dc:creator: Adam Zewe | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
Over the past decade, MIT researchers have developed aerial microrobots with bumblebee-like speed, agility, and durability, for tasks like precision agriculture or search-and-rescue. But these featherweight microrobots couldn’t carry the electronics needed for navigation, forcing them to remain connected to a motion-capture system in the lab.

Now, the researchers have designed a flapping-wing microrobot with onboard sensors and computation, which can follow a complex trajectory and land precisely on a sunflower outside the lab’s motion capture environment.

While the robot is still connected to an offboard power source, this demonstration highlights the potential of aerial microrobots to be used for precision agriculture in the future. 

For instance, flying microrobots could weave through a field of almond trees or blueberry bushes to carefully pollinate delicate blossoms in regions where natural pollinator populations have been decimated by habitat loss. They could also hover near plants without causing damage, monitoring crop health and spotting pests before they become widespread.

To enable onboard sensing and computation, the researchers developed a method to expand the artificial muscles that power the robot’s wings, increasing the net payload so the tiny robot could carry the necessary electronics.

They also designed a sensor suite that can rapidly estimate the robot’s position and orientation without relying on an offboard motion capture system, and a miniature electronics package to securely hold the tiny computational components on the nimble vehicle.

“This is a really important milestone for the research community. This is the first demonstration of an aerial microrobot that is sensory and compute autonomous. There are many situations, like pollination or industrial surveillance, where you can’t use a larger robot. Small-scale robots are uniquely positioned for these types of tasks, and if this thread of technology becomes successful in the future, it could be very promising,” says Kevin Chen, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), head of the Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory within the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), and co-corresponding author of a paper on the robot.

He is joined on the paper by co-lead authors and MIT graduate students Yi-Hsuan (Nemo) Hsiao, Quang Phuc Kieu, and Zhongtao Guan; co-corresponding authors Jonathan P. How, a Ford Professor of Aeronautics and Astronautics and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS) and the Aerospace Controls Laboratory (ACL) at MIT; Elizabeth Farrell Helbling, an assistant professor at Cornell University; and others at MIT. The research appears today in Science Robotics.

Increasing the payload

The MIT researchers previously developed a swift, agile aerial microrobot with four wings, each powered by a set of soft actuators, or artificial muscles, that flap the wings rapidly so the bot can perform detailed maneuvers. 

The robot, roughly the same size and shape as a microcassette, weighs less than a paperclip.

To bring this tiny robot closer to real-world applications, the researchers need it to carry the additional weight from electronics for onboard sensing and computation, while still being fast, maneuverable, and robust to collisions.

In this research, they developed a method to scale up the artificial muscles without hampering the robot’s performance. They carefully tuned the radius and length of the soft actuators, increasing their size by 50 percent while boosting the robot’s net lift forces by 46 percent. 

“It is very difficult to scale up the actuators without causing the output power of the system to go down, which reduces the lift forces. We tuned the geometry of the robot very precisely so lift proportionally increases with the additional actuator weight,” Chen explains. 

They were able to achieve a lift-to-weight ratio of 1.9, giving the robot more than enough lift force to carry the onboard electronics package they developed, which weighs only 244 milligrams. 

The tiny electronics package contains the sensors, and microcontroller needed for onboard sensing and computation. 

The researchers incorporated an inertial measurement unit to estimate attitude, an optical flow sensor to estimate lateral flight speed and position, and a time-of-flight sensor to measure height.

But without the precision of the attached motion capture system, the robot does not know its absolute position, causing it to drift off course.

Speedy sensing

To overcome this challenge, the team designed a sensing algorithm to calculate the robot orientation, angular velocity, and position extremely quickly, simplifying the calculations to reduce the computational cost.

They found that estimating position continuously at a faster rate yielded higher performance than a more accurate, slower estimation.

“We spent a lot of time optimizing the selection of the sensors and position estimators so the robot would have very low drift. Our robot can now fly with positional accuracy that is comparable to flying with offboard cameras,” says Hsiao. 

They integrated the sensors and computing components into a tiny electronics package, which they attached to a fiberglass substrate so it wouldn’t be thrown off by vibrations of the robot.

“When you are talking about a computer which is that small, everything must be thought through carefully. There are so many factors to consider; it must do both perception and control, while fitting onto the robot and running fast enough that the vehicle will remain stable during flight,” How says.

They tested the offboard computation capabilities of the aerial microrobot through a series of flight demonstrations, including hovering at different heights and following point-to-point trajectories. The robot maneuvered quickly and precisely, with positional errors of only a few centimeters.

In addition, they demonstrated the robot’s potential for artificial pollination by using a joystick to send high-level position setpoints, guiding the aerial vehicle around several plants before carefully landing on a sunflower. 

“This is quite difficult to do, even if you do have a motion-capture system,” Hsiao says.

The researchers analyzed the vehicle’s power expenditures and found the electronics only consume about 6 percent of the total power, with the rest fueling the robot’s artificial muscles and wings. 

They identified ways to further reduce power consumption from the electronics. This would allow for the addition of more components, like a camera that would enable the robot to recognize objects.

The researchers are now working toward two goals: putting a camera onboard for autonomous object recognition and obstacle avoidance; and integrating power electronics and batteries onto the tiny robot, which would enable untethered flight in an outdoor environment. 

This research was funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), U.S. Office of Naval Research, U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research, MathWorks, and a Zakhartchenko Fellowship.

item.title: Joe Higgins to step down as VP for campus services and stewardship
item.description: During his time at the Institute, Higgins has guided MIT’s physical campus through a transformative period, delivering 2030 Capital Plan projects, improving critical facilities, and advancing decarbonization.
item.dc:creator: Office of the Executive Vice President and Treasurer
item.content:encoded:
Joe Higgins will step down as MIT vice president for campus services and stewardship (VPCSS) at the end of January, Executive Vice President and Treasurer Glen Shor announced today in an email to MIT faculty and staff. Higgins is relocating to the West Coast to be closer to family. 

“Joe is an engineer by trade, and he is adept at building extraordinary things,” Shor says. “He has made an enormous mark on our campus and its future, and we are profoundly grateful for his vision, efforts, and highly engaging and collaborative style.”

Higgins joined MIT in 2016 as director of infrastructure operations in the Department of Facilities. His leadership portfolio quickly expanded to include overseeing campus maintenance, utilities, and facilities engineering and implementing the adoption of technology platforms to better support stewardship decisions, improve operations, and more effectively manage risks and costs.

Higgins assumed the newly created role of VPCSS in 2019. The VPCSS portfolio includes the Atlas Service Center; Department of Facilities; Environment, Health and Safety Office; MIT Welcome Center and Open Space Programming; Office of Campus Planning; and the Office of Sustainability.

Over the course of his seven-year tenure, Higgins has adeptly guided MIT’s physical campus through a transformative period, bringing MIT’s 2030 Capital Plan projects from the drawing board to reality; systematically improving the conditions of critical facilities; and making significant strides to advance campus decarbonization efforts.

“The biggest gift has been getting to work with an amazing team of people”

As Higgins prepares to relocate to the West Coast to be closer to his family, he has been reflecting on his MIT “family.”

“The biggest gift has been getting to work with an amazing team of people who are so dedicated to MIT,” says Higgins. “CSS senior leaders are exceptional, and they’ve built exceptional teams that really are the backbone of our campus.”

Case in point for Higgins is how CSS teams responded to the Covid-19 pandemic. They were instrumental to ensuring essential research and operations continued safely at the height of the pandemic, and they were equally imperative to reimagining new ways of working and operating the campus in a post-Covid world.

“No matter how hard the challenge or big the roadblock, the teams at CSS are here to support the Institute 24/7, 365 days a year,” says Higgins. “I’m going to really miss that shared sense of purpose and community that my colleagues display every day.”

As part of Higgins’ family-driven relocation, he has accepted the role of vice president of facilities management at Chapman University in Orange, California.

Stewarding MIT’s physical campus

Higgins has skillfully advanced MIT’s 2030 Capital Plan, helping to elevate the capabilities of Institute buildings to support cutting-edge academic and research endeavors, improve the residential experience for students, and establish a new level of discipline in keeping MIT facilities in suitable condition.

Signature projects that came to life during his tenure include the construction of the MIT Stephen A. Schwarzman College of Computing, the Graduate Junction residence hall, and the Edward and Joyce Linde Music Building; the recently completed renovation of the Metropolitan Warehouse; and a substantial upgrade to the Central Utilities Plant. And there’s more transformation on the horizon: Higgins and his team have been at the forefront of turning Building 39 into a headquarters and hub for the new MIT Quantum Initiative (QMIT) and a home for a new Quantum Systems Lab (QSL). 

“QMIT and QSL represent the next great chapter in MIT’s historic leadership in quantum science and engineering, and Joe and his team made it possible for us to take this leap,” says Ian A. Waitz, vice president for research. “Throughout every phase of the project, they have been incredible partners, creative problem-solvers, and deeply invested in creating an unprecedented facility to enable MIT to pursue transformative applications of quantum science as well as to catalyze a growing regional ecosystem.”

The capital plan is also an important vehicle for addressing deferred maintenance, an area where the Institute has made considerable progress on Higgins’ watch. Facilities condition is tracked through a measure called the “Facilities Condition Index” — the ratio of deferred maintenance to the total cost of replacing building systems. MIT 2030 Capital Plan investments in renewal have reduced MIT’s overall campus Facilities Condition Index by about 40 percent, making the Institute a peer leader on this front in higher education.  

Making progress on campus climate goals

Higgins has also brought passion, vision, and a collaborative spirit to MIT’s climate goals, helping to put the Institute on a path to dramatically reduce its carbon footprint. Over the past decade, the Institute has decreased energy use per square foot by more than 10 percent, even as the campus has grown and research activity has intensified. Rooftop solar power generation has increased by more than five times in the same period, and 33 MIT building projects have earned Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) certification. 

“We completed more than 300 energy-efficiency projects across campus, focusing on our most energy-intensive research buildings, and ultimately touching nearly every corner of MIT,” notes Higgins.

Higgins forged extensive partnerships with leading organizations across Greater Boston and with the City of Cambridge to enable over 450 megawatts of large-scale wind and solar energy projects in regions of the United States heavily reliant on fossil fuels. Together, these steps have put MIT on the verge of achieving net-zero carbon emissions.

“Joe has represented MIT interests and objectives through extremely complex Cambridge processes such as the development of the Building Energy Use Disclosure Ordinance (BEUDO),” says Sarah Gallop, director of MIT’s Office of Government and Community Relations. “His signature collaborative style, combined with his high level of expertise, have helped MIT and the city to achieve greater mutual understanding and to pursue joint initiatives. These include the creation of a virtual power purchase agreement (VPPA) and the implementation of the Greater Cambridge Energy Program (GCEP). Joe is a creative and constructive thinker and really makes things happen.”

Higgins has also laid important groundwork for MIT’s long-term campus decarbonization strategy. This has included his work earlier this year to spearhead MIT becoming an anchor institution in the BosTEN Project, a yearlong study to explore the feasibility of creating what could become the first city-scale thermal network in the United States. The network would help decrease the carbon footprints of major buildings across Boston and Cambridge by harnessing heat from the soil and rock under the Charles River and Boston Harbor, as well as waste heat from buildings and industrial facilities. It would also provide a renewable source of energy that can stabilize and even reduce the costs to heat and cool buildings.

“Joe’s vision and leadership extend beyond MIT’s campus,” says Lindsey Butler, executive director of the Boston Green Ribbon Commission. “He’s been pushing farther so that we can ignite broader strategies and technologies for other institutions and organizations to use. He understands the scale of change we need, and he’s worked overtime to help us go bigger.”

Tapping a seasoned interim leader, launching a national search 

Shor has selected Jon Alvarez, director of campus planning, to oversee the CSS areas while the search for Higgins’ permanent successor is ongoing.

“I am grateful to Jon for accepting the interim role of VPCSS while we conduct this search,” Shor says. “Jon currently leads a team of planners, designers, archivists, and technical professionals. He is a respected, long-serving member of Joe’s leadership team, deeply connected to a range of campus partners, and engaged in several strategic initiatives on which we will continue to make progress during this transition period.”

National executive search firm Isaacson, Miller will lead the search for the Institute’s next VPCSS. Shor is aiming to make an appointment during the upcoming spring semester. 

“I am confident all the CSS areas will continue to serve MIT with dedication and skill while we search for Joe’s successor,” says Shor.

item.title: Designing the next chapter for professional athletes
item.description: MIT Sloan student Collin Johnson, a former NFL player, worked with MIT DesignX faculty to create Founders Academy, a program to help athletes plan their futures off the field.
item.dc:creator: Maria Iacobo | School of Architecture and Planning
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 National Football League (NFL) season is well underway, but you won’t find Collin Johnson on the gridiron. After six seasons as a professional football wide receiver, he elected to crisscross the MIT campus as an MBA student at the MIT Sloan School of Management instead.

While in the NFL, Johnson served on the NFL’s Players Association, the union serving players and their families. There, he found his next passion: supporting players’ transition from their playing days to their post-playing lives. Planning his own shift for when he would retire from football, Johnson founded Beyond-Sports, an education platform that develops programs for current and former professional athletes. 

“I realized a lot of players struggle for different reasons after they stop playing football,” says Johnson. “It may be financial reasons, or finding community, or finding a new occupation.”

After surveying NFL players about possible career paths, Johnson was surprised to find that “entrepreneurship” was at the top of the list. Intrigued, he decided that his fledgling company needed an entrepreneurship program. His research led him to MIT DesignX, the accelerator program based in the MIT Morningside Academy for Design, and Svafa Grönfeldt and Norbert Chang, the faculty director and lecturer, respectively. 

At 10 years old, DesignX has grown from its original program on campus to collaborating with universities and incubation centers around the world, including programs in Italy, France, Dubai, Mexico, Hong Kong, Sweden, and Switzerland. DesignX was recently named by Time magazine as one of the best incubators and accelerators in the United States, ranking highest among design-based programs.

“The field of entrepreneurship is not for the faint of heart, and with the rate of change and the ability to compete, the competition is fiercer than ever,” says Grönfeldt. “At DesignX, we look at how to de-risk the innovation and entrepreneurship process. We take a deep dive into understanding the people we aim to serve with what we create. What are their pain points, what are their needs, and what does any solution have to actually fulfill those needs or address those pain points? That is where the tools of design come in.”

Chang, who took the lead on developing the program with Johnson, says he found Johnson to be mission-driven, in large part because Johnson had just left pro football and was experiencing the transition himself.

“He knew firsthand what it feels like to step away from the game and ask yourself, ‘What’s next?’” says Chang. “He also knew how few resources exist to help athletes answer that question in a serious way. That lived experience shaped everything about the program.”

The result is Founders Academy, a venture-building executive education program designed to help current and former NFL players bring their ideas to life. The cornerstone of the program — a four-day workshop at MIT — was held earlier this summer.

Undaunted by hard work

“Building this program together meant taking the curriculum DesignX normally runs over a semester and condensing it into four days, while keeping its rigor,” says Chang. “That was highly ambitious, and Collin still pushed for more. He was the athletes’ biggest believer.”

Johnson says he recognized the similar mindsets between athletes and entrepreneurs. 

“There is a constant feedback loop that players are exposed to nearly every day,” he says. “We practice and then watch film to see how and where we can improve. We get obsessed with our craft and we iterate and do it again the next day and try to improve. We have agency over our craft — much like entrepreneurs.” 

If the metaphor that the rigors of an MIT education is akin to drinking from a fire hose causes some to hesitate, it did not faze the six current and former professional football players who attended the inaugural program. Grönfeldt says she was delighted with the passion and rigor they brought to the program, and she learned a lot about the life of a football player.

“We only see the glamour side of their life, but to hear them talk about the mental work, determination, and the stamina required is impressive,” she says. “DesignX goes through rapid prototyping, and the process goes very fast. They’re used to speed and not being in their comfort zone. They took to the material, sat down at eight o’clock in the morning, and they were still going at it at 10 o’clock at night. They had an impressive work ethic.”

Been there, done that

Because the DesignX curriculum was condensed and originally not designed for solo entrepreneurial efforts, Chang added a mentorship component to the program. Each student was paired with a mentor who had been through the experience and had tangible experience in their industry. 

“That meant someone who could guide them, pressure-test their thinking, and share hard-won lessons from building companies themselves,” says Chang. “Mentors were also able to open doors and make connections to help accelerate their ventures.”

Johnson did not want to develop a feel-good program for the athletes. He wanted them to see what entrepreneurship actually involves, from defining the problem to building the product to learning the economics of fundraising — including the hard, unglamorous parts. Applicants were required to share a business interest and proposed solution or an existing business they planned to develop. Applications were reviewed by Johnson and DesignX faculty to determine readiness and to match mentors — sourced heavily through Grönfeldt’s and Chang’s networks — with each venture. 

“I found the athletes’ business ideas to be directly related to the curriculum that was taught,” says Johnson. “That was the game changer for them, because they could talk directly with Norbert and Svafa about their ideas. The curriculum really unlocked everything for them.”

To launch the academy shortly before beginning his own journey at MIT Sloan was a huge thrill for Johnson. Making it more rewarding were the rave reviews from the participants. That feedback has given Johnson a path to refining next year’s program with Grönfeldt and Chang. He has already procured Founders Academy as an approved program by the NFL Players Association, which allows future applicants to attend the program with little to no out-of-pocket cost. Participants earn a DesignX certificate when they complete the program.

“Ultimately, I’d like to integrate the mentorship model into MIT’s ecosystem,” says Johnson. “I can see a time when MIT students are serving as mentors to the athletes. It could be a mutually beneficial collaboration. When you think about an MIT doctoral student and an NFL player, at face value, you don’t think they have anything in common. But when they sit down and bond over a problem — we found they have a lot in common.”

item.title: Helping AI text detectors keep up with changing conditions
item.description: A more flexible training method can make AI text detectors more robust when new models emerge or AI-generated text is disguised to appear human.
item.dc:creator: Adam Zewe | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
A teacher who believes a student’s term paper may have been written by a large language model (LLM) can use a tool for detecting artificial intelligence-generated text to help confirm their suspicions. But the teacher may want to think twice before putting all their trust in the detector. 

Researchers from MIT and Cornell University showed that such detection tools, which are AI models themselves, can be fooled by AI-generated text disguised to appear as if it were written by a human. Detectors can also fail to identify AI text due to natural shifts in writing habits over time or the emergence of new LLMs.

In a new paper, the researchers demonstrated how a special training technique makes an AI detector more accurate and resilient to deception, even as human and AI writing constantly changes.

They employed a method called test-time adaptation, which allows a deployed detection model to learn from new, unlabeled data by adjusting its inner workings on the fly. In this way, the model adapts to unseen inputs without being retrained from scratch.

In experiments, a commercial detector could only identify about 27 percent of AI-generated text that had been disguised, while the new approach achieved 93 percent accuracy.

This method could help educators, editors, publishers, and hiring managers flag LLM-generated writing that people try to pass off as human-written. It could also be used by cybersecurity experts to prevent email phishing scams or identify search engine optimization fraud.

“There are many high-stakes contexts where people really care about the identity of the author, from scientific publishing to short story competitions. We’ve shown that test-time adaptation allows your AI detector to be much more robust, even with continual adversarial behavior by AI users,” says study co-author Manish Raghavan, the Drew Houston (2005) Career Development Professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management, who also holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), and is a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS).

He is joined on the paper by lead author Kevin Ren, graduate student at Cornell Tech, and senior author Nikhil Garg, an assistant professor at Cornell Tech. The research will be presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems.

Duping the detectors

The proliferation of LLMs that generate human-like text has led to a plethora of commercial AI-detection tools to help people identify whether a piece of writing was authored by a human.

But these detection tools can fail when the text they evaluate significantly differs from the text they were taught to identify. This is known as a distribution shift.

Detector developers typically train their models by gathering text from the internet that they know to be either AI- or human-generated. They train the model to tell the difference. 

However, once the detector is released, people might change the way they write or the way they use AI to generate text. 

For instance, a human in 2030 may write about different topics using new analogies that weren’t common for someone writing in 2010. A detector trained with 2010 data might be unfamiliar with this new writing style and incorrectly mark human-written text as AI-generated.

The release of a detection model also creates a cat-and-mouse game between its developers and users who want to bypass it. These individuals can run AI-generated text through an automated “humanizer” software tool that modifies it to appear human-written to the detector.

“After the company releases a model, a bunch of ‘humanizers’ pop up to try to beat it, so the company tries to incorporate this humanized text into their training so the detector can identify it, and so on. It’s like rinse-and-repeat. The cycle can go on forever,” says Ren.

The researchers explored whether test-time adaptation (TTA) can make an AI detector resilient to these distribution shifts.

Adaptation in action

In TTA, instead of freezing the model so it can’t change during deployment, researchers allow that model to adapt itself to incoming data after it has been released. For an AI text detector, these data are new pieces of text uploaded by users. 

These data are unlabeled, so the detector developers don’t know which data were written by humans versus AI models. But these new data represent contemporary human and AI writing — exactly what the developers want the model to be able to predict. 

With enough examples, the detector learns to identify patterns to determine which data are AI-generated and which are human-generated.

The researchers studied TTA by creating datasets to contain a certain amount of AI-generated and human-generated text, but they don’t provide those labels to the model. They also used LLMs to generate some examples that resemble text written by AI to specifically evade a detector. 

Then they performed the TTA training process and tested the model on ground-truth data.

In experiments designed to mimic the natural shift in human language over time, a detector that used TTA was 85 percent accurate, while traditional methods only achieved 73 percent accuracy.

And when it came to writing designed to thwart detection tools, existing methods could only identify about 27 percent, while TTA enabled the model to catch more than 93 percent of disguised text.

“TTA has the potential to really help deployed AI-detection models in terms of being able to proactively address this iterative ‘gaming’ behavior by adversarial AI users,” Ren says.

Adapting to shifts in human writing behavior is a more difficult TTA problem, since the shifts are slower and occur in more subtle ways, he adds.

The researchers caution that TTA may not always be an effective solution as future LLMs produce more natural-sounding language and it becomes harder to find verifiable human text to use for training.

“It isn’t entirely clear if this will be a solvable problem,” Raghavan says. “There are some big, open questions about how you should think about science, writing, and art in a world where it is infeasible to tell the difference between human-generated content and AI content.”

In the future, the researchers want to explore similar strategic domains where TTA could be useful and build better benchmarking tools to help engineers improve these AI detection models in a dynamic fashion.

This project used API credits provided by Pangram to use their AI text detectors.

item.title: Putting a spotlight on AI, society, and humanity
item.description: Supported by the MIT Human Insight Collaborative, scholars are exploring how AI is impacting the human experience and reshaping higher education.
item.dc:creator: Danna Lorch | School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences
item.content:encoded:
MIT students are going to office hours less often. They’re spending less time working through problem sets, and with one another. Those were among the findings of MIT’s recent report on artificial intelligence and education, and they are one reason a growing number of MIT faculty are concerned about how generative AI is both changing how people work and affecting how they think, learn, and relate to one another.

For the MIT Human Insight Collaborative (MITHIC), those questions have become a central focus, and MITHIC is working with collaborators across the Institute, including the Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing (SERC), to help MIT address them.

Launched in 2024 as a strategic initiative, MITHIC brings together scholars, artists, educators, and researchers to explore the human dimensions of the defining challenges of our time. Since its launch, MITHIC has supported 67 projects across 31 MIT units, offering a total of $5.5 million in funding.

Roughly a third of those projects are focused on AI, society, and humanity — a topic that MITHIC faculty co-lead Heather Paxson says has become an increasingly important part of the initiative.

“When we refer to AI and society, we’re not only speaking about individual ethical decision-making or how to retrain workers. We’re looking at how AI is reshaping sociality, how we relate to one another,” says Paxson, a professor of anthropology and the associate dean of the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS). 

Eroding “creative friction” 

Building upon this focus, an AI and Society Forum took place on campus earlier this year. Co-organized by MITHIC, SHASS, SERC, and the MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium (MGAIC), the event featured presentations and panels concentrating on jobs, democracy, and AI. 

On campus, the report on AI and education warned that AI is eroding the “creative friction” that has long defined an MIT education: students debating ideas and challenging one another, their professors, and their teaching assistants, in class and out of it.

MITHIC faculty co-lead Seth Mnookin, a science writing professor and head of Comparative Media Studies Program/Writing (CMS/W), said, “The report wasn’t saying that AI is here and we all need to adapt. It was saying that we need to be asking more fundamental questions.”  

“When the United States entered World War II in 1941, the Institute’s newly minted scientists and engineers helped shape that era through science and technology,” Mnookin said. “We’re at a similarly consequential moment with AI. The difference is that this time, the questions that matter most can’t be answered by technologists alone. That’s where the humanities, arts, and social sciences come in.”

Crossing disciplines in the pursuit of answers

MITHIC is supporting a range of interdisciplinary projects through its SHASS+ Connectivity Fund, in which a SHASS scholar partners with a researcher in another part of MIT. 

In the context of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, political science professors Adam Berinsky and Charles Stewart III and MIT Sloan School of Management Assistant Professor Chara Podimata are studying how large language models (LLMs) have become intermediaries of democratic knowledge. 

The ongoing project, which has demonstrated how voters in Alaska’s midterms who conducted their pre-election research using Anthropic’s AI model, Claude, may have received incomplete information about candidates and their views, was recently featured in The New York Times. 

“AI is becoming part of the way people encounter and make sense of political information, and yet we know relatively little about what that information environment actually looks like, how it differs for different user demographics, political identities, and geographies,” Podimata told the Times.

In another project, CMS/W Professor Eric Klopfer and brain and cognitive sciences Professor Pawan Sinha are co-leading research that’s measuring AI’s near- and long-term effects on cognition.

Meeting at the intersection of AI, education, and neuroscience, the professors are examining whether generative AI is increasing the human brain’s consumption of information but offloading cognitive function, or supporting an increase in cognitive function when used as part of the creative process. They recently gathered experts on the topic for an event on the MIT campus, “AI and the Brain.”

In the field of arts and technology, Anna Huang, a professor of music technology holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Joe Paradiso, a professor at the MIT Media Lab, are examining how incorporating AI impacts the creative process and live performance experience.

Their project, “Live Musician-AI Improvisation, Tuning the Social Aesthetics in Human-AI Partnerships” explores the question: what happens when human composers and contemporary machine learning systems improvise to make music together? 

As part of their project, a collective of MIT musicians, ethnomusicologists, and engineers meets for regular sessions to experiment with improvisation frameworks like stopping to discuss how technology impacts authorship and musical direction, ensemble dynamics, and other cornerstones of improvisation. Faculty will ultimately incorporate their takeaways into a future course or practicum on AI-improvisation.

Teaching and scholarship in an AI era

SHASS faculty and academic staff are also leading new MITHIC initiatives to help broaden instruction and community dialogue about the intersection of AI and society. 

Graham Jones, professor of anthropology, and Arvind Satyanarayan, associate professor of computer science, used MITHIC’s SHASS+ Connectivity funding to help launch a course, 6.S061/21A.S02 (Humane User Experience Design), in which students examine how AI systems are designed and grapple with the consequences of AI agents entering into socio-cultural relationships with people through their ability to mimic human thought and speech.

“The crux of our collaboration is the term 'humane.' It’s a bit of a double-entendre, meaning both human-serving or benevolent, and humanlike,” Jones said at the inaugural MITHIC Annual Event. “What’s interesting is that our students are discovering that there’s a fundamental tension between building a system that’s good for people and one that seems human, because real people can develop dangerous dependencies.”

Another project, “Rebuilding Computing and Society at MIT,” is supported by MITHIC’s Education Impact Fund (EIF). Led by Dwai Banerjee, associate professor of science, technology, and society, the initiative revitalized the Computing and Society concentration launched in 2019. The HASS concentration had gone dormant, listing classes no longer being offered and with minimal student interest. The concentration now features current classes across 11 SHASS units in which students can explore computing through different humanistic and social science angles.

Banerjee, who serves as the concentration’s advisor, is also working with lecturer and research affiliate Mariel Garcia-Montes PhD ’26 to find ways to connect the concentration instructors and campus initiatives on computing and society. MIT senior Daniel Gonzalez is also part of the project, developing a research and outreach program that centers undergraduate voices in computing and society efforts across the Institute.

Another MITHIC project funded by the EIF, “Review of Generative AI Assistive and Resistant Communication Assignments and Supporting Workshops,” is led by Michael Trice, a lecturer in MIT’s Writing, Rhetoric, and Professional Communication (WRAP) program.

The project is responding to a consistent SHASS faculty request for additional training and skills needed “to fully address generative AI concerns in their classes.” 

Trice is creating a bank of faculty resources and facilitating workshops and visiting lectures on generative AI and writing. These include a talk given earlier this fall by John Gallagher from the University of Illinois, who presented findings from a large-scale survey on AI-usage and writing conducted with undergraduates at his institution in 2026.

Meeting the moment

MIT leaders agree that MITHIC, now in its third year, is playing a central role in the Institute meeting the moment, as AI presents both extraordinary potential and disturbing risks. 

“There has never been a more important time for constructive collaboration between science and technology and the human-centered disciplines,” MIT President Sally Kornbluth recently said. “Through MITHIC, MIT is giving faculty the support to reach out across disciplines and pursue their dreams.”

Agustín Rayo, dean of SHASS and co-chair of MITHIC, agrees. “MIT is uniquely placed to help us understand this extraordinary moment and to generate the values, tools, and policies that we will need to shape AI so that it becomes a force for good,” he said. “It is essential that we deploy AI technology in a way that elevates human existence, rather than diminishing it.”

At the recent SHASS 75th Anniversary Symposium, Provost Anantha Chandrakasan said given the rapid development of AI, an understanding of the ethical implications and societal impact of implementing new technologies is especially urgent.

“SHASS provides an essential perspective on questions concerning how technology can be developed thoughtfully and deployed responsibly, with the aim of improving human well-being,” said Chandrakasan, who also serves as MITHIC co-chair.

Looking ahead, MITHIC and SERC are developing a series of events that pair humanists or social scientists with colleagues in a single field, starting with mathematics, to examine what AI is changing about how that field produces knowledge and trains its next generation.

“The question isn’t whether AI will change these fields,” Mnookin said. “It’s whether we understand what’s at stake before it does.”
