item.title: Q&A: Why building math muscles remains important in the AI era
item.description: Assistant Professor John Urschel explains why learning the fundamental skills of mathematics is still essential despite the evolution of AI tools.
item.dc:creator: Abby Abazorius | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
John Urschel PhD ’21, the Class of 1956 Career Development Assistant Professor in the MIT Department of Mathematics, is no stranger to building muscle: Before earning his PhD at MIT, Urschel strengthened his offensive muscles as a lineman for the Baltimore Ravens. He remains committed to helping his students exercise, but now his focus is on critical thinking skills. In the classroom, Urschel shares with his students his lifelong love for solving puzzles, while honing their abilities to be strong quantitative thinkers — skills he argues will be essential in an artificial intelligence-enabled world. 

Urschel recently published two preprints on arXiv, one on the growth factor of random matrices, the other on worst-case behavior in Gaussian elimination, in which he used a combination of human insight and AI tools to solve problems that had stumped mathematicians for decades. That experience provided Urschel with new insights into the future of mathematics and higher education, and the enduring importance of the in-person, residential education offered on college campuses, where students can experience the importance of struggle, problem solving, and human connection. Urschel recently chatted with MIT News about education, AI, and mathematics; excerpts from the conversation follow. 

Q: What is it about studying math that you hope to share with your students?

A: When I was very little, I loved solving puzzles, whether that’s Sudoku puzzles or Martin Gardner math puzzles or crossword puzzles. I think there’s something really enjoyable about being faced with some problem that you don’t quite understand, trying to get your bearings, trying to make your way through it, and finally gleaning some sort of understanding from it. That’s a process that I’ve enjoyed for as long as I can remember, and that’s the thing that I’ve really enjoyed most about math.

When it comes to teaching, first, I want to help our students train themselves and hone their ability to solve problems and their ability to be strong quantitative thinkers.

The second part, which is more specific to whichever course I’m teaching, is to help them assimilate the big ideas or tools or techniques or themes that help them become better problem solvers in that specific discipline. If they’re taking a course on a specific subject, the idea is for me to try to convey important fundamentals so that they can use that learned expertise to become better problem solvers out in the world.

Q: You recently used AI to assist in solving two proofs. Can you talk a bit about the experience?

A: These are the first two papers where I’ve ever touched the machine, and it does feel different. It’s not unlike having a collaborator, but it’s a collaborator who has access to unlimited resources, seemingly, and does certain things much, much faster than I ever could. 

In the same way that computers can do calculations much faster than any of us can, I think at this point it’s very clear that artificial intelligence systems can do certain types of mathematics much, much more efficiently than any of us can. 

Q: What was it like using AI to solve math problems? Was it just as rewarding?

A: For me, personally, I would say that the feeling that I talked about of problem solving, of thinking your way through a problem, I find that that’s most joyful for me when I do that by myself, without AI. 

One thing that I think is really important is to have an independent sense of problem-solving ability, a sense of curiosity — this idea of building those mathematics muscles, which I think are important, even in the era of AI.

Especially when you are talking with a machine, asking the machine for things, I think it’s very important to elevate the idea of understanding. If you’re talking to a machine, let’s say, and it gives you a proof of some mathematical fact, I think the true value in that proof comes from a human understanding and assimilating the way in which the machine combines certain mathematical ideas, and then internalizing that and communicating that knowledge to others.

Understanding is the big thing that I stress to my students who use AI systems. And then for the students who do not use AI systems, I focus on building their problem-solving abilities, which is what we’ve done for centuries in mathematics. 

I think in the age of modern AI machines, as long as there is a role for humans to think and try to solve problems, which I believe there is, then building these skills remains important.

Q: The recent report from MIT’s Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning and Research Training stressed the importance of experiencing the necessary and productive struggle of learning, along with the collaborative aspect of learning. I’m curious what you think about the role of AI in math education going forward. 

A: On one hand, the development of AI technologies should be viewed as a giant win for education, a giant win for leveling playing fields when you have technology that’s easily accessible, that gives you access to vast amounts of knowledge. 

Neither of my parents are professors; I remember when I was a kid, I didn’t know what a mathematician was until I got to college. And the way I learned about advanced mathematical concepts in high school, but also when I got to college, was with a laptop, and with Google. I was able to Google some topic I want to learn about, and it was amazing that I could find papers written by some of the world’s leading experts, just freely available online at my fingertips to learn from. That was really important for me and so helpful for my education.

But I think we’re at a point where modern technology is a bit of a double-edged sword. Because on one hand, with AI systems you can learn something faster than ever, and the resources I had when I was a kid would seem like small potatoes compared to the sorts of things you can do to help yourself learn nowadays. 

But the issue is that this also can take away your ability to think and learn for yourself. I think it’s hard if you’re a high school student or you’re a college student. You have a lot going on, you’re tired, and thanks to AI, you can just finish your homework with the push of a button. You can write your 10-page essay with the push of a button. Also, you can get the false impression that you more or less understand what’s going on when you really don’t. I think that’s one of the big dangers when you don’t try to learn things for yourself. 

People don’t like the word “struggle.” But when you don’t struggle with a certain material on your own, I think you can get the impression of learning without actually learning. Connecting with the material and really pushing yourself, that’s quite an important skill. 

Certainly, there’s work to do from the faculty and instructor side: to make sure that our recitations are maximally useful; to make sure that our office hours are serving students in the best way possible; to encourage the students and try to remind them that they have some responsibility for their education, and that the best way is to come and show up and interact with the material. But we should also recognize our responsibility to the students to deliver them the best learning experience possible and to give them an educational system that challenges them but also is a quality product they want to come and take part in.

Q: Why would you still encourage students to pursue studies in mathematics given the advances AI technologies have made? Do you still see the future of mathematics as exciting?

A: Yes, for a multitude of reasons. The act of learning how to think is going to be more important than ever. This idea of being an expert, of knowing all these things, which are easily available and at your fingertips, is perhaps a little less important when you have a machine that has all these resources. I think something that may become even more important is the ability to think for yourself. Because with the existence of these machines, I think a natural fear is that that skill set is going to lessen in the general population as generations move on and on, and so I think that ability will be at a premium. I think training in mathematics and quantitative sciences more generally is quite important for that. 

The second thing is community. I think learning, not by yourself, but with a group of peers, greatly improves the overall experience. It’s an integral part of the experience. I would say those two things are the reason why I think it’s still important to study math, to study quantitative sciences, and also why it’s still important to come and go to class. 

The world is changing fairly rapidly. I think we as an institution have a responsibility to prepare students for that. We’re having lots of conversations about this right now because the ability to think, reason, and solve problems are core skills that our students, I think, will need now more than ever. I also think we need to make sure that we’re preparing our students for the world that they’re about to enter into. The exact way that we teach our students, or prepare our students for the world, absolutely cannot look like what it was 10 years ago. Because this world simply looks quite different.

item.title: Learning the language of machine learning
item.description: By studying the computational foundations of language learning, Associate Professor Jacob Andreas builds intelligent systems that can communicate effectively with humans.
item.dc:creator: Adam Zewe | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
When deploying deep learning models in high-stakes scenarios, researchers would like to understand how they work. Today, this requires unraveling an enormously complex network of internal processing nodes to understand what the model knows and how it will likely behave in practice.

Jacob Andreas would rather have the models explain themselves. 

The newly tenured associate professor develops techniques that enable artificial intelligence models to communicate accurately about what they learned from their training data, in language humans can understand.

“Rather than needing to use all these external tools to try and understand what is going on under the hood, maybe we can train models to talk about themselves in a way that is accurate,” says Andreas, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and a member of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL).

By studying how machines come to understand language, Andreas and his group work toward building intelligent systems that can learn about the world from human guidance and communicate effectively with human collaborators. They develop methods to make the training process more natural and efficient, so AI models learn in a way that is more like human learning.

Ultimately, he and his group want to help people design more accurate and robust deep-learning models that are better suited for their intended application. 

“We used to debug systems just by looking at their parameters and figuring out whether they make sense or not. Now, we need ‘mind-reading tools’ that can take this really complicated neural computation and translate it for us because it is just not in a language that we, as humans, know how to speak,” he says.

A love of language

Andreas’ fascination with language blossomed at a young age. As a child growing up in the San Francisco Bay Area, he was a voracious reader of any book he could get his hands on. 

One such book, passed along to him by a family friend, contained a pivotal scene where the main character hacked into a computer system to save the day.

That piqued his interest in computers. A few years later, his father brought home a simple BASIC Engine that Andreas could run on their home computer, and he started immersing himself in the world of computer programming.

Andreas chose to major in computer science as an undergraduate at Columbia University but wasn’t sure if he wanted to pursue a career as a researcher, as a software engineer, or at a startup.

His friends signed up for research projects in faculty labs, so Andreas figured he would try that, too.

“I just blast emailed everyone in the computer science department who was working on anything vaguely AI-related, and the natural language processing faculty got back to me first. That is how I wound up in the field where I am now,” he says.

Working in the lab of Michael Collins, the Vikram S. Pandit Professor of Computer Science at Columbia University, Andreas completed an undergraduate thesis project on machine translation. His project involved adapting existing statistical techniques for representing the meaning of language into more powerful AI systems that could translate passages of text.

“I always felt like these deeper questions about how thought works or how to model the world were closer to the surface in language processing problems than in the other tasks that AI people were working on at the time,” he recalls.

A seismic shift

He wanted to keep exploring deep questions, so Andreas enrolled in graduate school at the University of California at Berkeley to pursue a career as an academic researcher. 

Before starting his PhD studies, he spent a year earning a master’s degree at Cambridge University in England. In that historic environment, he was inspired to contemplate the nature of language learning as he worked on computational translation problems.

Those studies fueled his research when he joined the lab of Berkeley professor of computer science Dan Klein. 

Andreas began his studies at the time when neural networks were starting to take off. The field of natural language processing was making a seismic shift from statistical methods to this new world of deep learning. 

Statistical methods utilize transparent, mathematical formulas to analyze text, while deep learning techniques use opaque algorithms to automatically learn complex meanings from massive amounts of text data.

“It was fun to be there as we made this transition to the modern toolkit, and learning and inventing all of that stuff when it was still new,” Andreas says.

He began collaborating with scientists in computer vision labs to tackle increasingly complex questions about language learning. Together, they designed AI systems that excelled at generating natural language by teaching those systems to “see” and understand the world around them. 

“This was all super-exciting because there really hadn’t been a common set of tools for working with both language and vision data. Then, all of a sudden, neural networks gave us this common language,” he recalls.

He completed a thesis project on the use of neural module networks, which are small fragments of neural networks that perform specific tasks, like localizing objects or logical reasoning, in a larger AI system. But it was the more speculative projects he tackled alongside his thesis, like interpretability and creating natural language descriptions of an AI model’s internal states, that would drive the focus of his group at MIT.

Faculty focus

After spending a year at the startup Semantic Machines (which spun out of his lab at Berkeley), Andreas joined the MIT faculty in 2019.

“It felt like this was a fantastic opportunity to be in the homeland of AI research and collaborate with all these amazing, established people, but also do something new and figure out what the modern era in machine learning was going to look like,” he says.

His group focuses on two main areas. First, they are studying the science of large language models to understand the algorithms these models deploy as they learn and process information. 

The tools they develop help scientists and researchers better predict how a trained model will behave in the real world. For instance, one family of techniques they developed trains large language models to explain what is going on inside other neural networks using language a human could understand. 

These techniques can assign a natural language description to every information-processing node in a massive neural network. For example, one such description might represent an individual node that identifies “patches of grass near animals” in input images. 

“That work serves as a jumping off point for a bunch of higher-level questions we ask about how these models represent meaning,” he says.

On the other side, his team designs new algorithms for training machine-learning models, and for predicting how specific datasets or examples will affect different aspects of model behavior. 

“We don’t have a good scientific theory of what is going to happen when you train a model on a particular dataset. This is a big challenge for the field right now,” he says.

A changing environment

The speed of AI advancement presents one of the biggest challenges his lab faces. The field seems to completely change every three to five years, Andreas says, forcing him to stay nimble and ready to learn something new.

That same dilemma carries over into the courses 6.461 and 6.861 (undergraduate and graduate Natural Language Processing), which Andreas co-teaches. He and his fellow instructors must redesign the course each year to keep up with the newest developments.

It’s also challenging to teach the technical pieces of machine learning in an era where every assignment could be completed by a large language model rather than a human pupil.

“I try to impress upon the students that having a really deep foundation in how all this technology works under the hood is the only way they are going to understand it, and will differentiate them in a world where everyone has access to a coding agent,” he says.

With so much change, it is difficult to predict where the field is headed next, Andreas says. He foresees that his group’s work on interpretability will become even more important for making advanced systems like AI agents safe enough to deploy in high-stakes situations.

This will be especially true as researchers design deep-learning models that can aid in scientific discovery. These models will be trained on troves of raw data from research labs that may not be well-understood by scientists yet. 

“Figuring out how to enable these models to verbalize all of this hidden knowledge they have about things people have never written about explicitly will be a huge challenge and opportunity for people who work in machine learning,” he says.

In addition to tackling challenges in the lab, Andreas enjoys pushing himself as a hiker and backpacker. He has loved spending time in the outdoors since his childhood in California and goes on at least one or two backpacking trips each summer.

He and a colleague in the Department of Mathematics are working their way across all the 4,000-foot peaks in the White Mountains of New Hampshire, making slow but steady progress.

And now that he has earned tenure, Andreas is looking forward to getting back into an old hobby — singing in a chamber choir. He’s always enjoyed music and became enamored with chapel choirs and bell ringing during his time at Cambridge University.

item.title: Pipilotti Rist receives the 2027 Eugene McDermott Award in the Arts at MIT
item.description: The pioneer of spatial video, whose work explores deep connections between the human body, nature, technology, and sensory perception, will be an artist-in-residence at MIT in the spring.
item.dc:creator: Leah Talatinian | Council for the Arts at MIT
item.content:encoded:
Artist Pipilotti Rist is the recipient of the 2027 Eugene McDermott Award in the Arts at MIT, which will be awarded at her MIT public presentation on April 8, 2027, and includes an artist residency at MIT in spring 2027. 

Rist is a pioneer of spatial video art whose work explores the deep connections between the human body, nature, technology, and sensory perception using immersive video and light installations.

Rist said upon receiving the award, “I am kissing your Institute and your feet. I am immensely touched and grateful to have this trust and investment in ideas I’ve yet to conceive. I’m honored to receive an award that has been granted to so many of my heroes, and look forward to collaborating closely with the brilliant minds at MIT.”

The Eugene McDermott Award in the Arts at MIT recognizes innovative artists working in any field or cross-disciplinary activity. The prize represents an investment in the recipient’s future creative work, rather than a particular project or lifetime of achievement. 

The official announcement was made at the Council for the Arts at MIT’s 52nd annual meeting at MIT in October. Past recipients include Santiago Calatrava, Es Devlin, Gustavo Dudamel, Olafur Eliasson, Robert Lepage, Audra McDonald, Suzan-Lori Parks, Bill Viola, and Pamela Z, among others.

MIT Vice Provost for the Arts Keeril Makan says, “Pipilotti Rist has spent four decades using digital tools to dissolve the line between screen, body, building, and landscape. Her immersive multimedia installations slow us down, return us to our bodies and the spaces we occupy, and gather us into shared experience, rather than fragmenting our attention. We look forward to presenting Pipilotti Rist with MIT’s highest award in the arts, and it comes at an exciting moment as we gather our students and faculty to activate our new building for the School of Architecture and Planning, the MET Warehouse.”

A distinctive feature of the award is a short residency at MIT, which includes a public presentation of the artist’s work, as well as substantial interaction with students and faculty. The goal of the residency is to provide the recipient with unparalleled access to the creative energy and cutting-edge research at the Institute and to develop mutually enlightening relationships in the MIT community. 

The Eugene McDermott Award in the Arts at MIT was established in 1974 by Margaret McDermott (1912–2018) in honor of her husband, Eugene McDermott (1899–1973), a co-founder of Texas Instruments and long-time friend and benefactor of MIT. The award is presented by the Council for the Arts at MIT, a volunteer group of alumni and friends, fulfilling their mission “to foster the arts at MIT and to act as a catalyst for the development of a broadly based, highly participatory program in the arts.”

The award is bestowed upon individuals whose artistic trajectory and body of work have achieved the highest distinction in their field and indicate they will remain leaders for years to come. The award recognizes innovative talents in any arts discipline, and, thanks to the McDermott family gift, offers its recipient a $100,000 cash prize and a campus residency. The McDermott Award reflects MIT’s commitment to risk-taking, problem-solving, and connecting creative minds across disciplines. Since it was established in 1974, the award has been bestowed upon 40 individuals who work in performing, visual, literary, and media arts.

Pipilotti Rist, a pioneer of spatial video art, was born 1962 in Grabs in the Swiss Rhine Valley on the Austrian border and has been a central figure within the international art scene since the mid-1980s. Astounding the art world with the energetic exorcistic statement of her now-famous single-channel videos, such as “I’m Not The Girl Who Misses Much” (1986) and “Pickelporno” (1992), her artistic work has co-developed with technical advancements and in playful exploration of its new possibilities to propose footage resembling a collective brain. Through large video projections and digital manipulation, she has developed immersive installations that draw life from slow caressing showers of vivid color tones, like her works “Sip My Ocean” (1996) or “Worry Will Vanish” (2014).

For Rist, showing vulnerability is a sign of strength on which she draws for inspiration. With her curious and lavish recordings of nature (to which humans belong as an animal), and her investigative editing, Rist seeks to justify the privileged position we are born with, simply by being human. Her installations and exhibition concepts are expansive, finding within the mind, senses, and body the possibility for endless discovery and poetical invention. “Pixel Forest” (2016), made from 3,000 LEDs hung on strings, resembles a movie screen that has exploded into the room, allowing viewers an immersive walk through three-dimensional video. As she herself puts it, “beside the energy-intensive exploration of the geographical world, pictures, films and sounds have been and are the spaces into which we can escape ... The projector is the flamethrower, the space is the vortex, and you are the pearl within.”

Since 1984, Rist has had countless solo and group exhibitions, and video screenings worldwide. Her recent solo exhibitions are “Your Palm is My Universe” at UCCA Beijing (2025), “Electric Idyll” at the Fire Station Doha (2024), “Prickling Goosebumps & A Humming Horizon” at Hauser & Wirth New York and Luhring Augustine Chelsea (2023-24), “Behind Your Eyelid” at Tai Kwun Hong Kong (2022), “Big Heartedness, Be My Neighbor” at The Geffen Contemporary, MOCA, Museum of Contemporary Art Los Angeles (2021–22), and “Your Eye Is My Island” at MoMAK, The National Museum of Modern Art Kyoto and ART TOWER MITO (2021). “Åbn min Lysning. Open my Glade” at Louisiana Museum of Modern Art Humlebæk Denmark (2019), “Sip My Ocean” at the Museum of Contemporary Art Sydney (2017–18), “Pixel Forest” at New Museum New York (2016–17), and “Your Saliva is My Diving Suit of the Ocean of Pain” at Kunsthaus Zürich (2016) all resulted in record-breaking attendance for each institution.

item.title: Arianna Doss named a 2027 Rhodes Scholar
item.description: A double major in biological engineering and political science, Doss will begin postgraduate studies at Oxford University next fall.
item.dc:creator: Julia Mongo | Distinguished Fellowships
item.content:encoded:
MIT senior Arianna Doss has been selected as a 2027 Rhodes Scholar and will begin fully funded postgraduate studies at Oxford University in the U.K. next fall. 

Doss, who is from Houston, is double-majoring in biological engineering and political science. At Oxford, she plans to pursue a master’s degree in comparative social policy, followed by a master’s in global health science and epidemiology.

She aspires to become a physician and health policy leader who advances health equity, particularly to improve maternal health and chronic disease outcomes among marginalized groups.

Doss was supported by Associate Dean Kim Benard and the Distinguished Fellowships team in Career Advising and Professional Development. She received additional mentorship and guidance from the Presidential Committee on Distinguished Fellowships.

“No two applicants have the same story, and MIT students never fail to surprise us with their ingenuity,” says Professor Taylor Perron, who co-chairs the committee along with Professor Nancy Kanwisher. “Seeing Arianna earn this recognition and opportunity is exhilarating. We don’t know what lies ahead, but I’m confident the world will be better as the result of her work.”

At MIT, Doss worked in the Bryson Lab for more than two years, studying protein degradation within the phagosomes of mammalian macrophages. At Rice University’s Segatori Lab, she investigated gene circuits in retinal pigment epithelial cells to reduce chemotherapy toxicity. She has also researched rural-urban disparities in maternal mortality and analyzed the effects of abortion clinic closures on maternal health.

Doss’s policy and clinical experiences include serving as a maternal health intern for Representative Lauren Underwood, supporting the Black Maternal Health Caucus, and interning at Northwestern Medicine’s Bronzeville Outpatient Center, where she shadowed in family medicine and studied medication hesitancy among hypertensive patients. As a patient navigator with Link Health, she connects patients in East Boston with public benefits. 

Doss is the founding president of the MIT Alliance for the Advancement of Black Athletes, and previously served as attorney general of MIT’s Black Students’ Union. She is also a three-year starter for MIT’s nationally ranked women’s soccer team. Her honors include NCAA Scholar All-American, First Team All-Region, the Princeton Prize in Race Relations Certificate, and Scholastic writing awards.

item.title: Waves that clear waste from the brain during sleep are impaired in older adults
item.description: Researchers now hope to investigate whether increasing the flow of cerebrospinal fluid during sleep could improve brain health.
item.dc:creator: Anne Trafton | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
As people age, they may sleep for shorter periods and wake up more frequently during the night. In addition to those disruptions, MIT researchers have now discovered that a process responsible for flushing waste from the brain during sleep is commonly impaired in older people.

The researchers found that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help remove debris from the brain, are significantly reduced in older adults. This impairment is linked to a decrease in the slow brain waves that normally occur during deep sleep, the researchers found, and is not just a result of getting less sleep.

The researchers now hope to explore whether the disruption of CSF flow increases the risk of neurodegenerative disorders, and if any of the sleep patterns they observed might offer a way to predict an individual’s risk.

“We know that people age really differently. Some people age very successfully with great cognitive outcomes, and other people develop cognitive decline. If we can figure out who has great trajectories of aging and what are the factors that are associated with that, we might be able to use that to predict future outcomes,” says Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT’s Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Her lab also plans to investigate whether there might be any interventions that could improve CSF flow in older adults.

Lewis is the senior author of the study, which appears today in Nature Aging. Sydney Bailes, a postdoc in the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, and Stephanie Williams, a former visiting student at MIT who earned her PhD from Boston University in 2026, are the lead authors of the paper.

Smaller waves

During the deepest stages of sleep, also called non-REM sleep, high-amplitude, low-frequency waves contribute to physical recovery, memory consolidation, and many other functions. In a 2019 study, Lewis found that these slow waves are also critical for generating waves of CSF that help flush waste from the brain.

That finding led her to wonder whether reductions in slow waves in older people might also reduce CSF flow. Previous studies of aging have yielded conflicting evidence; some found that CSF flow goes down in older adults, while others found it goes up, but these studies did not monitor flow during sleep.

In the latest study, the researchers recruited volunteers in two age groups: 18 to 39 and 60 to 84. The tests lasted for about two hours and began late at night, so that participants would be sleepy. 

The researchers used traditional fMRI to measure participants’ blood flow in the brain, along with a modified MRI technique, developed by Lewis, that measures CSF flow. While the subjects were in the scanner, the researchers also measured their brain waves using EEG. 

Many of the participants fell asleep in the scanner, allowing the researchers to compare their brain activity while awake and while sleeping. 

As they had seen in earlier work, the researchers found that when the younger adults fell into non-REM sleep, their EEG slow waves became stronger, and their CSF waves became larger. However, in the older group, the average CSF waves were significantly smaller than those seen in the younger group. 

Impaired flow

In additional experiments done while subjects were fully awake, the researchers tried to figure out what was causing the age-related declines in CSF flow.

First, they explored the possibility that changes in a phenomenon known as neurovascular coupling might play a role. When localized brain activity increases the demand for oxygen, nearby blood vessels dilate and deliver more oxygen and nutrients. That increase in blood flow can be measured with fMRI.

The researchers tested each subject’s neurovascular coupling by measuring blood flow while the subjects looked at a flickering checkerboard image — a task that typically drives an increase in neural activity, along with an increase in blood volume.

In many of the older subjects, while their neural activity did go up, the blood flow didn’t increase much, suggesting that the blood vessels’ ability to respond to increased oxygen demand has diminished.

During another task, the researchers tested whether the brain’s vascular system might be impaired in the older subjects. They asked the subjects to hold their breath, then measured what happened inside the brain. Normally, this leads to an increase in carbon dioxide levels in the blood, which triggers an increase in cerebral blood flow. However, in the older participants, the average blood flow increase was smaller than the increase seen in the younger subjects.

These two factors — reduced neurovascular coupling and diminished blood flow — accounted for much of the decline in CSF flow but could not explain all of it, according to a statistical model developed by the researchers. This suggests that there may be other age-related factors that contribute to the reduction in CSF flow, they say.

“Aging is so complex, and so many different things change, that it’s really hard to disentangle the individual factors,” Bailes says. “We try to account for some of the mechanisms, but there definitely are a lot of other factors related to vascular health and lifestyle. If you were able to measure all of them, you might be able to break it apart into different explanations for why an individual’s CSF flow might be more or less impaired.” 

Enhancing CSF flow

Previous studies have found that sleep disturbances are linked to a greater risk of neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s and other forms of dementia.

None of the subjects in this study had been diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder, but the researchers found that some of the older adults showed signs of gray matter atrophy, which was correlated with a greater decrease in CSF flow. They hope to continue studying some of the participants in hopes of discovering whether changes to CSF flow are associated with a higher risk of developing a neurodegenerative disorder.

They also hope to test possible interventions that might help increase CSF flow. In a recent study, Lewis’ lab found that short bursts of “pink noise” during sleep could increase CSF flow in younger adults, but they have not yet tested that intervention in older adults. 

In other work, they plan to study why some older adults don’t experience a dropoff in CSF flow. In this study, the researchers found that while as a group, older adults showed weaker CSF waves during sleep, some individuals in the group maintained normal CSF waves.

“It’s really intriguing that for some of these older adults, their CSF fell right in the range of the healthy young adults,” Lewis says. “We are really interested in what’s different in those people and how that might be related to future health outcomes.”

The research was funded by the National Institutes of Health, the Simons Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, a McKnight Scholar Award, a Pew Biomedical Scholar Award, an MIT EECS Transformative Research Award, the Picower Institute Neurological Disorder Discovery Research Fund, a Sloan Fellowship, and the Department of Defense National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate Fellowship Program.

item.title: New AI “copilot” helps engineers design better structures
item.description: The system asks humans for feedback to increase trust in machine-generated designs for buildings and bridges.
item.dc:creator: Zach Winn | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
The use of algorithms to design structures has led to new parts optimized for ultralight aircraft, high-bandwidth antennas, and F1 racing cars.

But the best algorithmic design techniques still require lots of computation and time: Users only see the final design after it’s complete, after which they often must start the design process all over again to make changes. That process also makes it harder to trust that the final designs are structurally sound.

MIT researchers are making algorithmic designs more collaborative with a system that acts like an AI copilot. As the algorithm is generating the structure, it presents regions to the human designer for feedback.

In an open-access Communications Engineering paper describing the system, the researchers showed it led to more easily manufacturable structures with higher buckling loads while adding only 15 seconds to the total design time compared to all-algorithmic approaches.

The researchers believe the approach, which uses a design technique known as topology optimization, could make algorithmic design more accessible and manufacturable for a broader class of design engineers.

“Right now, the human doesn’t have any agency or control over the design process as it’s playing out,” explains lead author Dat Ha PhD ’26, a recent MIT civil and environmental engineering doctoral student who is now a structural designer at LeMessurier. “For these really complex designs, we wanted to also tap into our brain, which is the most complex machine there is, to solve these design problems in a way that’s more practical to industry.”

Joining Ha on the paper are Ferdous Alam, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Georgia Tech; Markus Buehler, the MIT Jerry McAfee (1940) Professor of Engineering; Faez Ahmed, MIT associate professor of mechanical engineering; and senior author Josephine Carstensen, MIT associate professor of civil and environmental engineering.

Bringing a human in the loop

Topology optimization is one of the most advanced and promising algorithmic design techniques. It uses formal optimization techniques to iteratively fill in the space given for a design in a way that maximally achieves the stated goals. For most applications, the process requires a lot of computation and time. When it’s finally done, the designs can be impractical to build or have other issues the engineer didn’t consider. For instance, some designs might have eight or more beam connections at a single point, which would be difficult to make in the real world.

“Engineers are always very skeptical of computer programs, especially if they give you very weird-looking or unexpected designs,” Ha says. “On paper, topology optimization is really powerful and can achieve great, high-performing designs, but its black box nature has made it less widely adopted in industry.”

Topology optimization has gotten traction in the automotive and aerospace industries, but it’s been used less to design buildings or bridges, partly because design engineers need to know they can trust the output.

“A big limiting factor has been that the design engineer has very little influence over how the design evolves and therefore can’t control undesirable features,” Carstensen explains. “The lack of control and lack of ownership also inhibits its use.”

To address those problems, the researchers made topology optimization more collaborative in an approach that Carstensen compares to having a design copilot.

Prior attempts at adding human judgment slowed things down dramatically. The researchers’ new system uses machine learning to quickly identify the most likely regions of an algorithmic design that a human would want to change. To train the machine-learning model, the researchers created a synthetic dataset of probable human feedback to thousands of designs that critiqued things like aesthetics, performance criteria, and manufacturability.

“We thought if we could create a record of where humans have made changes to these programs, then perhaps there’s a pattern to those choices, which is not very different from other types of machine-learning approaches,” Ha says.

Carstensen sees the system as bringing together the best of algorithmic and human design approaches.

“The idea is to tap into the brains of the designers and get them to infuse their domain knowledge as the design evolves,” Carstensen says.

In demonstrations, the researchers showed their human-in-the-loop approach improved manufacturability and linear buckling load by 39 percent while only modestly increasing the total design time.

Right now, the approach only allows users to make structures within identified regions thicker or thinner, but they hope to add other options for modification in future versions.

“The hope is that by addressing these hurdles, we open up topology optimization to a much wider audience, not only in industry but also to researchers and students in academia,” Carstensen says.

From designs to structures

The researchers see their approach complementing AI only-approaches to design.

“We are arguing there’s room for both,” Carstensen says. “If you are in a discipline that has a lot of computational resources, you can use the other approach. But if you really need the human input, you can use this collaborative approach.”

Adding human input also serves to increase trust.

“In some settings, the humans need to make the final decisions before advancing the final design,” Carstensen says. “By involving humans, we can get higher-performing designs to the real world to create higher-performing structures. Because it’s not just about designing good artifacts; it’s about creating good artifacts that humans will actually accept and make.”

The work was supported, in part, by the MathWorks Engineering Fellowship Fund, TATA Steel, and the MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium.

item.title: Helping robots fit into the human workplace
item.description: Founded by Anthony Jules ’92, SM ’92 and Professor Emeritus Rodney Brooks, Robust AI’s robots are designed to collaborate with humans in factories and warehouses.
item.dc:creator: Zach Winn | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
Despite fears about robots replacing humans at work, there are still plenty of things humans can do far better than machines. That’s fine with Robust AI, a startup building robots designed to complement what humans do best.

The company’s mobile robot, named Carter, resembles a utility cart on wheels and is designed to fit seamlessly alongside humans in fast-changing warehouse and factory environments. Carter features a force-sensitive handlebar for easy guidance, an AI-powered vision system, and holonomic wheels for instant movement in any direction.

As a result, humans can cut Carter off, push and pull it in any direction with one hand, and direct it with gestures or the onboard touch screen.

The company’s robots are currently deployed in logistics warehouses and on factory floors, where they help humans while picking or stocking shelves and moving items across facilities autonomously.

“In these environments, what really determines success is how the overall system performs,” explains Anthony Jules ’92, SM ’92, who co-founded the company with MIT Professor Emeritus Rodney Brooks. “The robot does some of the work, the people do some of the work, and the backend systems do some of the work. It’s that combination that determines how well your system performs. We believe it’s really important that people have an appropriate level of agency and input so that they’re always moving the system forward.”

Collaborative robots

Brooks was a faculty member at MIT from 1984 until 2010 and served as the director of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) from 1997 until 2007. While at MIT, he co-founded iRobot, which invented the popular Roomba vacuum and went public in 2005. Later, he co-founded the company Rethink Robotics, which also designed collaborative robots.

Jules met Brooks as a graduate student at CSAIL in the 1990s. The two never worked together, but their labs were on the same floor. The pair kept in touch after Jules graduated and co-founded the company Sapient, which went public before being acquired by Publicis in 2015.

In 2019, Brooks bumped into Jules at a robotics conference. He told Jules he was thinking of starting a robotics software company, which he compared to a video game engine for training robots. Robust AI was founded later that year.

The Covid-19 pandemic caused the founders to shift to creating robots that could autonomously disinfect surfaces, but when it was discovered that Covid-19 was not transmitted via surfaces, they had to pivot again.

“That forced us to decide how to use this technology we had been building, which was really about helping robots understand the world more fully,” Jules recalls. “Long story short, I said to Rodney, ‘I have an idea. You’re going to love it and you’re going to hate it. You’re going to love it because it’s solving problems for customers that we’ve been hearing about, and you’re going to hate it because we have to build hardware.”

The founders had been interviewing potential customers for years through Robust AI’s early pivots. They finally decided on logistics and manufacturing as the industries to target early on.

“When people think about automation in factories, they think about pictures of the 5 percent that are fully automated with $50 to $200 million dollar systems,” says Jules, who now serves as Robust AI’s chief innovation officer. “They don’t think about the vast majority of factories that aren’t automated at all. These factories don’t even have a conveyor belt. They are not going to tear everything out and replace it with a $200 million system.”

Robust AI’s robots can be phased into operations as needed and offer several workflows for customers. In one workflow, the robot can guide human workers to specific spaces to retrieve items. In another it can follow humans to important spots for loading. The primary workflows involve Carter robots moving things from one place to another, often in large warehouses or factories, where they say human workers can walk on average 30,000 steps a day.

“These are huge spaces, so a person might load the robot with things and then need to bring them to another station, but that could be 400 feet away,” says, Brooks, Robust AI’s chief technology officer. “Now the person can just say ‘done’ and the robot brings it instead. How the robots are integrated into the workspace is entirely up to the customer.”

Getting work done

Leila Takayama, Robust AI’s vice president of human robot interaction, recently discovered a peer-reviewed study of robots in hospitals, which were used to do things like gather dishes, move sheets, and transport other equipment. The researchers discovered that, in many hospitals, a large number of robots were turned off and against the walls. The nurses said they broke.

“What really happened was the nurses were rushing with a patient on a gurney, and the robot sees them in the hallway and stops dead, and they couldn’t get the gurney around them,” Brooks says. “The robots were getting in the way of nurses’ primary tasks.”

Robust AI’s approach to technology development is to understand workers’ primary tasks deeply and build features that accelerate those tasks, whether a human or a robot is doing them.

“We let humans do what humans are good at in the physical world, which we’ve had millions of years of evolution to get good at, and have the digital system respond to that and provide us with all the things that it is good at,” Brooks explains.

item.title: New research could lead to faster, trustworthy AI models for climate prediction
item.description: MIT scientists developed a training method to generate models that simulate the effects of human activities on climate much more quickly than other approaches.
item.dc:creator: Adam Zewe | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
Accurate, up-to-date climate projections are essential for planning decisions that enhance the resilience of power grids, protect public health, maximize agricultural yields, and more.

Now, MIT researchers have developed a technique that streamlines the production of fast, trustworthy, and adaptable artificial intelligence models for climate prediction.

These specialized AI models, known as climate emulators, can rapidly simulate the effects of human activities onto a future climate, predicting impacts on temperatures or sea level, for example. 

Because emulators run in a matter of seconds, scientists use them to efficiently test thousands of varied climate scenarios. This provides more reliable estimates and can identify unexpected outcomes of regional interventions.

The MIT researchers developed a training technique that boosts the performance and adaptability of a climate emulator while using only a fraction of the data typically required. This significantly cuts production time for these practical scientific tools.

They show that an emulator trained with a much smaller amount of carefully selected synthetic data accurately predicts outcomes of scenarios it did not see during training, while traditional emulators failed to adapt to new situations.

“Climate emulators are especially well-suited for modeling policy-relevant scenarios. By using our method to generate optimized training data for an emulator, we can speed up the production of much more reliable emulators, so we can better trust their outputs for making policy decisions,” says Christopher Womack ’22, SM ’24, PhD ’26, who is now a postdoc at ETH Zurich and lead author of a paper on this technique.

He is joined on the paper by Shahine Bouabid, a postdoc in the MIT Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS); Andrei Sokolov, a research scientist in MIT’s Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy (CS3); Popat Salunke, a postdoc in CS3; Glenn Flierl, a professor of oceanography in EAPS; Sebastian D. Eastham, an associate professor at Imperial College London; and senior author Noelle E. Selin, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and EAPS, and director of CS3. The research appears this week in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 

Speedier surrogates

Climate scientists typically use earth system models (ESMs) to make long-term projections about how global temperature or precipitation could change in response to varying greenhouse gas emissions.

These enormous, physics-based models capture the major components and interactions of the earth’s climate in extreme detail. While powerful, ESMs can take months to run on a cluster of supercomputers — and that’s only to project one possible future climate scenario. 

Selin and her collaborators design climate emulators, which are fast AI surrogate models that mimic the behavior of full-scale ESMs. Emulators help scientists test many scenarios, make more accurate forecasts, and explore specific pollutants and regional effects.

“Climate emulators can run in just a few seconds, so it really expands what we can do in terms of exploring these future climate scenarios,” Womack says.

When scientists design a climate emulator, they often train the AI model using a set of six to eight future scenarios based on realistic future trajectories of emissions. They must run each scenario through a full-scale ESM, making these datasets costly and time-consuming to generate. 

The MIT researchers recently found that using realistic future scenarios as training data can lead to underperforming emulators that fail to predict unfamiliar or novel scenarios. 

In this work, they developed an algorithm that generates a synthetic dataset of optimized climate scenarios tailored to boost one emulator’s predictive performance.

“Our algorithm might generate some weird scenarios which look nothing like a realistic future, but we don’t care so much if the training scenarios are realistic. We are just trying to make the best possible dataset to train an emulator,” Womack says.

Importantly, rather than needing to run a full ESM six or eight times to generate training data, a user would only need to run that model once.

Tuning the training data 

The researchers begin by generating an arbitrary climate scenario using a fast and simple climate model. They test how well their emulator can reproduce the results of that ESM, which gives them a measure of error.

Because of the programming technique they used to build the training pipeline, they can iteratively update the training data to increase the emulator’s predictive skill. For instance, the algorithm could increase CO2 emissions dramatically in the year 2050 or rapidly decrease methane emissions in 2037.

Then the optimization updates the training data until the emulator’s error level reaches a certain threshold.

In the end, rather than resembling realistic scenarios in which emissions follow smooth trajectories, the synthetic data contain rapid variations.

“By introducing these high-frequency wiggles and oscillations, our data enable the emulator to extract a lot more information about the overall system,” Womack explains.

Their training algorithm outputs these emissions scenarios, which they can use to train an emulator that is more accurate and adaptable.

“In the future, we are definitely going to see climates and scenarios we haven’t seen before. If we can simulate these different scenarios more robustly, we can provide more reliable information to the stakeholders who need it,” Selin says.

For instance, an emulator trained with their technique can capture the effects of local pollutant control policies that reduce one pollutant while other emissions continue rising. The traditional emulators they evaluated failed this test.  

In the long run, Womack hopes this work improves the usefulness of fast and adaptable climate emulators for policy formulation. 

“This is such an important piece of the pipeline when it comes to creating useful tools that speak to stakeholder needs. Because the process of training an emulator can takes months or even years, the emulators we have are usually out-of-date. By cutting down that production time, I think this technique will be a game-changer in terms of getting updated tools into the hands of researchers and practitioners,” Selin adds.

In the future, the researchers want to test their technique using an emissions scenario generated by a full ESM. They also want to apply it to other types of climate models and explore its effectiveness in broader machine learning and computer vision applications.

This research was part of the Bringing Computation to the Climate Challenge (BC3) project and supported by Schmidt Sciences through the MIT Grand Challenges.

item.title: Inspired by networks found in nature, engineers design stronger, more resilient “metamaterials”
item.description: The new design approach could improve impact absorption for helmets, packaging, and armor.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Chu | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
Order has long been the rule in the design of synthetic “metamaterials,” which have internal structures that give the whole material exceptional properties not found in nature.

When scientists engineer a metamaterial, they design from a single building block, or “unit cell,” that is then copied and pasted many times over. The result is a precise, periodic microstructure that results in improved material performance. 

Now, a team from MIT and Northeastern University has found that engineering a little disorder into a material can further enhance its “meta” features. 

In an open-access study appearing today in the journal Nature, the researchers introduce a new way to design metamaterials, inspired by the types of networks that appear in a leaf’s vasculature, the veins in a dragonfly’s wings, and the virtual connections in a social network. These new metamaterials — termed “scale-rich metamaterials” — exhibit structures of varying sizes, which sprawl and connect to form a physical network.

For decades, networks have been used as theoretical constructs to describe everything from cities to the internet to connections between neurons. The team has now applied such network designs to physical materials. They designed metamaterials made not from repeating unit cells, but from tiny support beams of varying sizes, similar to a network’s dense, web-like patterns. 

When subjected to physical tests, the new materials attained a widely controllable range of stiffness and held up against sudden impacts better than conventional, ordered metamaterials. They also were able to cushion and protect fragile objects embedded within the materials.

The team designed their materials using an algorithm which generates an optimal network of microstructures for a desired material property. The procedure can be used to design resilient, impact-absorbing materials such as helmets and armor, as well as acoustic lenses — materials whose microstructure efficiently focuses sound or vibrations.

“This is a completely new way of thinking for metamaterials,” says study author Carlos Portela, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT. “Unlocking this network design for materials really frees us to think of new microstructures and mechanical benefits that haven’t been possible before.” 

The study’s MIT co-authors include Andrew Yen-Jong Chen, Mohammad Charara, and Jayna Wadhwa, along with Csaba Both, Ting-Ting Gao, and Albert-László Barabási of Northeastern University, and Niek Mooij of Utrecht University in the Netherlands.

Looking beyond order

Network science is a field of research that studies complex networks, the nodes and connections within a network, and how these elements relate to each other and to the network as a whole. Network science has been used to map and characterize a wide range of systems, from networks in nature, such as food webs, evolutionary trees, and neural connections, to financial markets, cellular and social networks, and the internet. 

Albert-László Barabási, a co-author of the new study, has been at the forefront of network science. A professor of physics at Northeastern University, Barabási explores the structure of complex networks across many disciplines, studying where a network may exhibit vulnerabilities and how it could be made more robust.

Most of Barabási’s work has involved conceptual networks, or networks that are mapped onto existing systems. Recently, he wondered: Could network science be applied to build a physical material with certain desired properties that are not possible in nature? 

For this, Barabási joined efforts with Portela, whose group at MIT specializes in metamaterials. The researchers engineer materials from the ground up, with precisely patterned microstructures that enhance the material’s performance overall. Like others in the field, Portela has built metamaterials from a single unit cell, repeating this building block in patterns such as square lattice structures and honeycomb architectures.

In many cases, Portela has found that such ordered patterns do improve a material’s strength and resilience. But if these materials are punctured or cracked, the rest quickly buckles and fails. He says that’s because the internal structure is all the same; if one region of the material is deformed, the surrounding, similar unit cells will respond and deform in kind.

“We’ve spent years looking at periodic and ordered microstructures, and we’ve learned there are a lot of limitations and non-ideal responses, such as this localization effect,” Portela says. “We wanted to break free of that notion and use network science to design these materials.”

Line by line

The team developed an algorithm to virtually generate a network of beams with the constraints of a physical material. When applying network science to something like the internet, researchers haven’t had to consider physical constraints, such as limiting the number, density, or intersection of connections. In a physical material, the number and thickness of beams, and the space between them, start to matter. 

To design a physical network, the team’s algorithm starts by drawing a point at a random coordinate in a domain representing the size of the final material. The program draws a line at a random angle, which stretches through the point and crosses the entire space. The program then repeats the process with a second point, at a second random coordinate, and a line drawn through the point at another random angle, until that second line reaches a boundary, of either the whole domain, or the first drawn line. The process then repeats, again and again, drawing progressively shorter, thinner lines. The resulting material represents a dense network of intersecting beams of many varying sizes. 

Scientists can vary the type of network that the program generates, by varying the thickness of the starting line and how fast that thickness decreases with each successive line drawn. By simply tuning these two parameters, the team found they could generate a huge range of networks. They then carried out simulations to predict how tuning one or the other, or both, by varying degrees, would change a material’s stiffness and other physical properties. 

“We see we can really tune the stiffness of a material just by changing these two parameters, which dictate how these network patterns get generated,” Portela says. 

The team then fabricated physical materials with microstructures that were patterned after the networks they virtually generated. They used 3D-printing methods to deposit polymer into patterns of tiny, interconnecting beams. Each resulting sample was a large square, about the size of a credit card, with internal beams that ranged from microns to centimeters in scale. 

They put the samples through various physical tests, such as dropping a large weight onto them and squeezing them with increasing force. They recorded the materials’ response, along with samples of conventional lattice and honeycomb metamaterials. The network-inspired samples, they found, were more resilient to compression and impacts. 

“Because there is such a richness of length scales in these networked materials, if one part fails, there is a strong web of structures around it that keeps the entire material from failing catastrophically,” Portela says. “It’s more efficient at distributing damage and absorbing energy.”

As another demonstration, the researchers designed a material inspired by the density-graded microstructure of a pomelo’s thick rind. They designed the material with edges made from a denser network of beams, and showed it could cushion and protect a fragile object that was embedded at the center of the network.

“This work provides a design framework for materials whose features vary over a very wide range,” says materials expert Tian “Tim” Chen, associate professor in the Department of Aeronautics at Imperial College London, who was not involved with the study. “That may lead to a next generation of materials with unprecedented physical behavior, for any structure that must carry load, absorb energy or control vibration.”

This work was supported, in part, by the U.S. National Science Foundation’s Designing Materials to Revolutionize and Engineer our Future (DMREF) program.

item.title: MIT student leaders: Q&A with men’s football co-captain Dominic Hess
item.description: An Academic All-American defensive back and co-captain for the Engineers, Dominic Hess says football keeps him grounded — and inspired.
item.dc:creator: Chad Galts | Division of Student Life
item.content:encoded:
A senior studying mechanical engineering and finance, Dominic Hess is an Academic All-American with a packed study schedule. But he and his teammates still make room for about 20 hours a week of football during the regular season. (“It’s a little less in the spring,” he notes.) All this time practicing, working out, and playing in games, he says, doesn’t take away from his academic experience at MIT — it amplifies and improves it. In this interview, Hess discusses his experiences on and off the field at the Institute, as well as plans for the future.

Q: How would you compare your high school football experience to your MIT one? 

A: I'm originally from a small town, Damascus, in Maryland. On my way to high school, I would drive past seven farms and a lot of cornfields. 

Football was big there, and the town was historically really good; I think we’ve won 12 state championships. I grew up playing several sports and decided to stick with football going into high school. Being in a super-competitive environment was a great experience. In my freshman year, the No. 1 player in the nation was on my team. And as a 5'10", 135-pound kid playing with a guy who was 6'6" and 280 pounds, it was crazy — a very high level of football. 

I took my academics very seriously and decided I wanted to keep playing in college, but I knew I wasn’t good enough to play at a Division I school. Luckily, I ended up here — and it has been the most impactful four years of my life.

I’ll say, coming to MIT, it was different. I tell people that I play football here, and they're like — “MIT has a football team?” 

Q: How do you strike a balance between academics and football? 

A: It definitely took some getting used to, especially during freshman year. 

Football actually helped a lot. We come to campus in August, a few weeks before classes start. As a freshman, I had no idea about what classes to take, what the numbers all mean, what the names of things are — all that stuff. But I had all this time where I could talk to my teammates about careers, different majors, and what classes to take. I learned a lot. 

Once school starts, you're taking classes that are harder than anything you've ever taken in high school, and the workload is way more than you’ve had before. It's a huge adjustment, and the balance is not easy — but you get to do it with other people. The community in an athletics team, having built-in friends who can support you, really benefits you on the academic side. 

Also, to me, it’s a grounding thing. I have all this other stuff going on — academics, clubs, my fraternity, whatever. When I walk onto the practice field, I say: “I'm just going to focus on football right now.” Those two hours are the one time of my day when I don't have to worry about anything else. It's a blessing to be there.

Q: What was it like when you became a captain of the team? 

A: I was captain of my high school team, but coming into MIT was a reset. You're back to being a freshman, back to the bottom of the lineup, just trying to earn your stripes. You need to do the work to become a good player and a good teammate. Over my first three years, I was able to improve a lot. I guess my teammates and my coaches recognized that, and I ended up getting selected. 

I think a key thing about being a leader, especially on a sports team, is asking your teammates, What are your goals? And then, just as important, What steps are you going to take to get there? I really want to win a NEWMAC [New England Women's and Men's Athletic Conference] championship, and, obviously, the guys on the team want the same thing. Taking the steps to get there is what's important. You're not going to win a championship in a random way in December, but you can do something today and keep stacking it and getting better and better. 

Being a captain on the field is a little different. It's really about keeping players motivated. I've been watching this documentary about Nick Saban, the Alabama football coach. He talks about each play being six seconds — and all you have to do is focus on this play and go all-out for six seconds. 

Q: What motivates you, on and off the field?

A: I'd say, especially at MIT, the community really motivates me. I grew up with three brothers and was very close to my parents. My dad’s in tech consulting and worked at home, so I got to spend a lot of time with him growing up. My mom quit her job to raise us. Four boys is a lot of work. (They've made it to every game this season; my mom always jokes how this season will be the end of her “sports-mom” era.)

And so, coming here, I guess I was looking for a new family — and I was fortunate to find it in football. You hear a lot of things about MIT, like how hard it is and how students can feel alone. It can obviously be hard here, so I wanted to find that community. 

I've been with the same roommate all four years; we’ve gotten very close. I’m also in a fraternity, DKE [Delta Kappa Epsilon]. Also, being a part of the Catholic community has been really important. It turns out a lot of the guys on the team are also Catholic. I didn't know I'd find that here.

Q: What’s after MIT for you?

A: I interned in New York City the past three summers and am fortunate to have a job lined up for next year. My two older brothers already live and work there, so I'm planning to move in with them. Both my parents are actually from New York, so unfortunately that means I'm also a Jets fan, and unfortunately, now, I can say it means being a Yankees fan. But the Knicks….

item.title: Professor Emeritus Jeffrey Goldstone, highly influential theoretical physicist, dies at 93
item.description: An MIT faculty member for nearly half a century, Goldstone was a “theoretical physicist of rare talent and impact” who made fundamental contributions to multiple disciplines.
item.dc:creator: Scott Morley | Laboratory for Nuclear Science
item.content:encoded:
Eminent theoretical physicist Jeffrey Goldstone, an MIT professor emeritus, Dirac Medalist, and holder of the Department of Physics’ Cecil and Ida Green chair, died Oct. 12 at age 93. 

A member of the MIT physics community for 49 years, Goldstone was especially known for his influential work in quantum field theory as well as contributions to quantum optimization algorithms. Notably, he is the namesake of the Goldstone boson and the related Goldstone theorem.

“Jeffrey was a giant of theoretical physics who will be long remembered and very much missed,” says Tracy Slatyer, director of the MIT Center for Theoretical Physics – a Leinweber Institute (CTP-LI) and professor of physics. “He contributed greatly to the CTP-LI over the years, and it was an honor to have him as a colleague.”

“Goldstone was a brilliant theoretical physicist and a charming, yet diffident and remarkably humble human being,” says Frank Wilczek, a CTP-LI colleague who is the Herman Feshbach Professor of Physics, Emeritus, and a 2004 Nobel laureate. “He made renowned, fundamental contributions to diverse areas of physics, ranging from condensed matter and quantum computing to string theory. Throughout, you can perceive a consistent style: enormous mathematical talent brought to bear on important, concrete, sharply posed physical problems.”

Goldstone is renowned for his remarkable range of groundbreaking discoveries. He began his career as a nuclear theorist. In his early work on nuclear matter with Hans Bethe, he developed the use of Feynman diagrams for non-relativistic many-fermion systems.  

He later turned to particle physics, investigating relativistic field theories with spontaneously broken symmetries. Building on ideas inspired by superconductivity, he demonstrated that spontaneously broken continuous symmetries must be accompanied by massless, spinless particles — now widely known as Goldstone bosons (or Nambu-Goldstone bosons, in recognition of Yoichiro Nambu’s earlier related insights). 

In subsequent work with Abdus Salam and Steven Weinberg, Goldstone formalized and generalized this result, which became known as the Goldstone theorem. With Claudio Rebbi, Charles Thorn, and Peter Goddard, he worked out the light-cone quantization of relativistic strings, a foundational result in string theory. Goldstone also worked with Roman Jackiw and Frank Wilczek on solitons in quantum field theory.  

Goldstone was born in 1933 in Manchester, England. He earned his PhD from Trinity College at the University of Cambridge in 1958 and completed postdoctoral work at Cambridge, Harvard University, CERN, and Copenhagen University. After shifting his focus to particle theory, he joined the faculty at Cambridge in 1962. He moved to MIT as a professor of physics in 1977 and as a researcher in the Laboratory for Nuclear Science, and was appointed the Cecil and Ida Green Professor of Physics in 1983. Goldstone served as director of the Center for Theoretical Physics (now known as the CTP-LI) from 1983 to 1989.  

“Goldstone’s name will always be associated with spontaneous symmetry breaking, where 'Goldstone’s theorem' and 'Goldstone bosons' feature prominently,” Wilczek notes. “His early, seminal papers relating the mathematical concept to physical phenomena gave firm foundations upon which people built fruitful theories of magnetism, meson physics, and eventually the Standard Model and early universe cosmology.

“Jeffrey Goldstone’s ideas are so deeply woven into physics that it takes an occasion like his passing to remind us how much we owe him. I had the pleasure to work with Jeffrey in the early days of fractional charge. The short paper we wrote together is one that I’m especially proud of. It contains the seeds of many later developments. Thank you, Jeffrey, for that fond memory.”

Alan Guth ’69, PhD ’72, MIT’s Victor F. Weisskopf Professor of Physics, Post-Tenure, says, “Jeffrey was a wonderful friend and colleague, and a towering figure in theoretical physics. When I was trying to arrange to come back to MIT after being a postdoc for nine years at other places, it was Jeffrey who I contacted to try to make this happen. When I first learned in 1981 that Andrei Linde had figured out how to make cosmic inflation work, in the form known as 'new inflation,’ I remember that I ran into Jeffrey's office to share my excitement. I have learned a great deal from Jeffrey over the years, and will forever have warm memories of our friendship.”

“Jeffrey Goldstone was a theoretical physicist of rare talent and impact,” says David Kaiser, MIT professor of physics and the Germeshausen Professor of the History of Science. “His landmark article, 'Field theories with superconductor solutions,' published in 1961, helped to launch the modern era of symmetry breaking in high-energy physics. Building on insights from neighboring fields such as condensed-matter physics, Goldstone demonstrated that for any model in which a continuous symmetry is spontaneously broken, there will emerge zero-mass, zero-spin particles now known as 'Goldstone bosons.' His watershed study, and several influential follow-up articles, have become central to our Standard Model of particle physics, with further application as far afield as early-universe cosmology to spin waves in magnetic materials and quantized vibrations in excited fluids. Later in his career, Goldstone turned his attention to quantum information science, helping to construct several novel algorithms for quantum computation. 

“Typically reserved, his close friends admired his droll humor. Writing to Harvard physicist Sidney Coleman in November 1976, for example, Goldstone declined Coleman’s invitation to attend an upcoming physics workshop. 'I expect to be in total confusion during January [1977] and wish to simplify my life,’ Goldstone replied. 'Forty-three years in the womb’ — including decades at his alma mater, the University of Cambridge — 'have unfitted me for coping with normal trivial details of survival. It’s probably a good thing I’m coming out, but the birth pangs are hell.’ 

“The birthing event to which Goldstone referred was his move to MIT to join the Physics Department faculty in 1977. Thank goodness he braved the move. Over nearly 50 years, Jeffrey Goldstone enriched our Department of Physics at MIT, and especially our Center for Theoretical Physics – A Leinweber Institute, with his deep insights and gentle manner.”

Even after retiring from MIT, he remained active in research for the next two decades, working in quantum computation. 

Edward Farhi, professor emeritus of physics and a frequent collaborator for over 20 years, describes Goldstone’s contribution to the field from its early stages as “very significant.”

“FFG [Farhi, Goldstone, and Samuel Gutmann] teamed up with Donner Professor of Mathematics Michael Sipser and showed that there was a problem which could not be sped up with a quantum computer, learning parity in the oracle setting,” Farhi says. “This was the first demonstration of this kind of limitation, although the same week another group proved the same thing by a different method. In 2000 FGG, along with Sipser, introduced the concept of Quantum Computation by Adiabatic Evolution. This is an all-purpose approach to optimization and was later shown to be universal, which means that any quantum computation can be encoded as quantum adiabatic. Furthermore, the company D-wave was founded to run this algorithm. D-wave is the progenitor of all of the superconducting hardware efforts such at the ones at Google and IBM. We later showed that using scattering theory a quantum computer could determine who wins a game provably faster than the best classical algorithm for this task.

“FGG introduced the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm. This was the first time a general purpose quantum optimizer could provide worst-case performance guarantees for combinatorial optimization problems. These guarantees as of now (with one exception) do not beat the best classical. Still, this paper has over 6,000 citations, making QAOA one the most-studied quantum algorithms.

“In 2019, FGG and Leo Zhou applied the QAOA to the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. We showed how to analyze performance in the infinite size limit at any depth. Our work and others indicated that as depth increases with optimal parameters, the QAOA would approach the celebrated Parisi value. Recently the Open AI math dump, the conjecture that the QAOA would hit Parisi, was proven by the AI. I bet Jeffrey would have been surprised and impressed!”

Jeffrey Goldstone was a fellow of the American Physical Society Fellow, the Royal Society, and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and he was an honorary fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge. 

His honors included the Guthrie Medal of the Institute of Physics, the Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics of the APS, and with Stanley Mandelstam the Dirac Medal (1991) of the Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics, awarded for “his fundamental clarification of the phenomenon of spontaneous symmetry violation in relativistic field theory.”

He is survived by his son Andrew Goldstone, associate professor of English at Rutgers University’s New Brunswick campus; his daughter-in-law Anne Dewitt, a clinical associate professor at New York University’s Gallatin School of Individualized Study; and his granddaughter, Helen. His family is planning a memorial in 2027.
