item.title: MIT-led team receives funding to develop next-generation alternatives to modern weed killers
item.description: With up to $53 million from ARPA-H, the researchers will use AI to generate safer herbicides that reduce dependence on imports and improve the security of the U.S. food supply.
item.dc:creator: Anne Trafton | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
MIT researchers will lead an up to $53 million effort, awarded by the U.S. Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) as part of its STREAM (Systems for Tracking and Resilience in Efficient Agricultural-input Management) program, to develop next-generation weed killers that help farmers and protect human health. 

More than 1 billion pounds of herbicide are used in the United States every year. Herbicides help farmers by preventing significant crop loss due to weeds, and they enable regenerative farming practices that protect the soil, but some weeds are becoming resistant to the most common herbicides. 

Exposure to herbicides may contribute to increased risk of cancer, metabolic and endocrine disorders, and other adverse health outcomes. Farm workers can be exposed from frequent herbicide use, but many U.S. residents are also exposed to these chemicals in small amounts through food and drinking water. 

The MIT-led research team will develop new generative artificial intelligence tools to help them discover herbicide alternatives that are more effective and developed with human health in mind. Such alternatives could also help to reduce U.S. dependency on imported phosphorus, which is a critical ingredient in a major herbicide, glyphosate.

“With herbicides like glyphosate and atrazine, there’s a real crisis because of resistance mutations that are coming,” says Christopher Voigt, head of MIT’s Department of Biological Engineering. “And if you combine the resistance mutations with issues around national security of the supply chain of the precursors to herbicides, we could find ourselves without these core agrochemicals that are absolutely essential for getting the high crop yields and economical prices that the United States now sees.”

Voigt is the principal investigator for the project, known as Precision Learning for On-target Weed control (PLOW). The team is also expected to include researchers from the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, the University of Tennessee at Knoxville, the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, and Robigo.

The researchers are grouped into three teams that will tackle different aspects of the project, aligned with the STREAM Technical Areas. The generative AI group will develop models that can predict molecules — either chemical compounds or small interfering RNA (siRNA) — that disrupt the same plant enzymes targeted by glyphosate and other herbicides.

Glyphosate kills weeds by interfering with an enzyme called EPSP synthase, which plants need to produce several critical amino acids. After many years of herbicide use, some weeds have begun to acquire genetic mutations that allow them to become resistant to those herbicides, which makes them less effective and poses a significant threat to crop yields.

“There’s a real need for new herbicides because of resistance mutations that have been arising,” Voigt says. “There are also concerns about herbicides’ possible impacts on the environment and on humans, so it’s important to identify alternative ways of making herbicides, which as a general class of molecule are really critical to agriculture.”

The MIT-led team plans to design generative AI models that will be able to predict molecules that can help prevent resistance from arising. The models will also optimize for other features such as low cost of synthesis, low risk of inducing resistance, and low risk of harming humans or causing ecological damage. 

The group developing these AI models is led by Connor Coley, the Warren K. Lewis Associate Professor of Chemical Engineering at MIT; Regina Barzilay, the School of Engineering Distinguished Professor for AI and Health at MIT; and Alexander Tropsha, the K.H. Lee Distinguished Professor in the UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy.

The models are expected to generate billions of possible candidates, which will then be tested by a second research team. This high-throughput screening group will be led by Angela Koehler, the Charles W. and Jennifer C. Johnson Professor of Biological Engineering at MIT, and Jaime Cheah, the associate director of scientific outreach and collaborative screening in the Center for the Development of Therapeutics at the Broad Institute.

“Those libraries will be screened both to identify those molecules that hit their target, but also to then provide all of that screening data back to the computational approach in order to improve it,” Voigt says.

Once the candidate pools are narrowed down, researchers on a third team will begin greenhouse studies to evaluate how each molecule performs under different agricultural conditions. That team will be led by Neal Stewart and Scott Lenaghan, co-directors of the Center for Agricultural Synthetic Biology at UTK; Patrick Tranel, the Tom and Peggy Ainsworth Professor of Crop Sciences at the University of Illinois; Tim Willson, the Harold Kohn Distinguished Professor at the UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy; and Andee Wallace PhD ’20, CEO and founder of Robigo. 

The first greenhouse tests of initial RNAi candidates are expected to be complete by the end of the first year of the program.

As part of this project, the research team will also develop living microbial systems that degrade agrochemicals before they reach food, soil, or waterways. Engineered bacteria, fungi, and srRNA will convert chemicals and formulation ingredients into biomass, providing a scalable strategy to reduce environmental and human exposure.

This research is funded by the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) under agreement number 140D042690030. The views and conclusions contained in this article are those of the authors and should not be interpreted as representing the official policies, either expressed or implied, of the United States government.

item.title: Streamlining metal parts production to revitalize American industry
item.description: Founded by MIT alumni, Fabri uses 3D printing and software to eliminate many of the steps that slow down traditional metal casting.
item.dc:creator: Zach Winn | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
The United States used to be the world leader in metal casting, a process where liquid hot metal is poured into a mold to solidify into a desired shape. But more than 70 percent of American metal casting facilities have closed since the industry’s peak in the 1950s. Today, China and India dominate global metal casting production, which is critical for making the components of jet engines, nuclear and gas turbines, medical devices, and more.

Fabri is trying to revitalize American metal casting. The company, founded by Steven Davis ’24; Thomas Cole ’91, MBA ’13; and Pieter Coulier, is building a new kind of metal casting foundry that uses additive manufacturing, software, and vertical integration to eliminate many of the most labor-intensive steps associated with traditional metal casting. 

Fabri is already producing parts for a growing list of customers at its 16,000-square-foot plant in Billerica, Massachusetts, where it is applying its approach to one of the most multidisciplinary and challenging types of metal casting, known as investment casting. The company is working with Raytheon, Lockheed Martin, and Sikorsky Aircraft, among others, and is moving through qualification to make parts for the most critical aerospace and defense applications.

Fabri’s first foundry was designed to be quickly replicated. Even as it significantly expands capacity at its current plant, demand from customers is driving the company to build a far larger facility in 2027 that will produce bigger parts at higher volume as customer programs move into production.

“Metal casting is one of the oldest and most prevalent manufacturing methods in the world,” Davis says. “It’s a uniquely difficult process because there are so many different steps. There’s so much domain knowledge and experience you need to understand it. If we get cut off from the world’s casting capacity, that means no more pots and pans, no more storm drains and other basic things, but also no more aircraft. Lots of medical devices, like titanium hip implants, are cast. Power generation also depends on metal parts. These are very critical industries that we need to continue to produce.”

Faster metal production

Davis grew up competing in robotics competitions like BattleBots. The biggest challenge for his small, underfunded teams was getting the parts to make the robots.

Davis arrived at MIT in 2020, where he majored in mechanical engineering. As part of a summer internship after his sophomore year, he worked at Relativity Space, which builds reusable rockets. There he saw multi-million-dollar projects being delayed by the same hurdles he faced in robotics competitions. His team would wait weeks for expensive machines to make parts.

“I realized the problem was scale,” Davis says. “These production processes couldn’t even scale to aerospace, so they weren’t going to scale to far larger industries.”

When Davis returned to MIT that fall, he worked on adapting the precision and flexibility of 3D printing to producing metal parts. Davis also took several classes taught by John Hart, MIT’s Class of 1922 Professor and head of the Department of Mechanical Engineering. Hart co-founded several additive manufacturing companies including VulcanForms and Desktop Metal. He continues to advise Fabri.

“I was very interested in finding the best uses of additive manufacturing,” Davis recalls. “A lot of the most successful companies weren’t making end parts; they were making tools. My favorite example is Invisalign. They’re not printing the dental liners: They are printing the molds that make the aligners.”

Davis began thinking about starting a company roughly midway through his bachelor’s degree at MIT. He met Cole through his MIT network. Cole had founded a fully automated CNC machining company making dental implants that was acquired by AstraZeneca. Pieter Coulier, Fabri’s third co-founder, previously developed the simulation and metal 3D-printing algorithms at Velo3D that enabled SpaceX’s Raptor engines to be printable.

Davis also began visiting foundries, where he repeatedly heard their biggest bottleneck was labor.

“They all have huge ‘Help Wanted’ signs out front,” Davis says. “Capacity is going down. That’s why we realized automation had to be a core part of our thesis. According to the American Foundry Society, these workers are retiring at a rate of 3-to-1. It’s really hard to find these foundry engineers who understand what goes into the process and can design these molds. We have customers tell us they had an engineer retire and now they can’t make certain parts anymore. We want everything we learn to be encoded into our software forever.”

Investment casting is a complex, multistep process.

“Traditional investment casting starts by cutting a hard tool out of steel,” Davis explains. “Then you injection mold wax patterns into it. Those wax parts get glued together into what’s known as a tree. Then you dip the tree into liquid loaded with ceramic powder, you stucco it with sand, dry it, and repeat the process seven or eight times. That’s how you get the ceramic mold to pour your steel into to make the part.”

Fabri’s process starts with the part’s computer-aided design (CAD) file. The company’s proprietary software, FoundryOS, designs a pattern for each part, which Fabri prints in resin using established techniques including digital light processing (DLP) and stereolithography. The printed pattern is dipped in ceramic slurry to build the shell that molten metal is poured into. FoundryOS incorporates data from every step and uses machine learning models to improve the process and the parts with each casting.

“By printing that mold right off the bat, we remove the need for all those early steps,” Davis explains. “We fully automate the creation of the [complex patterns and channels] needed for making that tree. Instead, we print it all in one piece and consolidate a lot of that work.”

Davis says traditional tooling can cost upward of $1 million for complex enough designs and take many months to make — a big reason companies have to wait so long for parts.

Davis built the first prototype of Fabri’s printer in the basement of his MIT fraternity using funds from the MIT Sandbox Innovation Fund. After subleasing a space in Ashland, Massachusetts, Fabri was pouring metal within six months. Today, he says Fabri’s approach also cuts post processing and benefits from the increased flexibility of 3D printing, which allows Fabri to iterate on parts in days.

“What really hurts traditional foundries is they put a design into production, they tool up, they cut a tool, and when they get their first part, they realize something’s wrong,” Davis says. “Then they have to rework it or fix it. They’d like to fix the tooling in the process, but they can’t because they spent so much on the tool and waited six to nine months for it.”

Reinvigorating an industry

Fabri opened its first foundry in Ashland in 2025 and moved production to Billerica in spring of 2026. Davis says the company can go from receiving a design to producing a finished part in as little as a week. Fabri is making parts out of aluminum, copper alloys, and stainless steel, primarily for munitions, aviation, and naval applications. In early 2027, the company plans to begin casting nickel superalloys, the metals used in the turbine blades that can currently have four-year wait times.

The company’s process also enables complex geometries and organic topologies that hard tooling can’t produce.

“We’re building the software that can make these parts more intelligently and faster,” Davis says. “Qualifying for aerospace production with a company like Raytheon is a really big deal. Most startups and 3D-printing companies we know haven’t done it. The ability for us to go from opening our first facility in 2025 to now going into production with some of the nation’s most critical platforms is a huge milestone. We are going to be making parts that are going to fly in the systems and go into the munitions platforms that the country needs.”

item.title: “Somebody’s got to do it. Why not me?”
item.description: Through leadership roles in ROTC and Camp Kesem, plus navigating an academic pivot, senior Andrew Voelsing has learned to face new challenges with enthusiasm.
item.dc:creator: Gitana Savage | MIT News correspondent
item.content:encoded:
When Andrew Voelsing was 8 years old, he decided he was going to MIT.

He was fascinated by space and dreamed of building spaceships. The Institute, and its well-known aerospace engineering program, seemed like the obvious destination. 

Years later, as a senior studying climate system science and engineering, Voelsing is preparing for a different kind of career: serving as a Navy officer, using his technical training to help the armed forces understand the ocean and atmosphere. 

Even during childhood, military service was never far from his mind. His mother attended the U.S. Naval Academy, and his father participated in the Reserve Officers’ Training Corps (ROTC) at the University of Notre Dame. The two met while serving in the Navy in Japan. Growing up, Voelsing heard their stories about military life and saw how their experiences as naval officers shaped their lives.

Voelsing was eventually accepted to the Naval Academy himself. But he chose MIT for the variety of faculty and activities he could pursue while also earning his commission as a Navy officer through the NROTC program. He will soon assume the highest-ranking student role of Battalion Commander, responsible for NROTC across Greater Boston.

But the path from an 8-year-old’s dream to his senior year in Cambridge, Massachusetts, was not quite as straightforward as he had imagined. After arriving at MIT, Voelsing struggled to find his footing academically.

“I thought I was smart in high school. I thought I was at the top of my class, and then I got here and I was failing midterms,” he says. “All my friends seemed to be getting things faster than I was, and I just felt really out of place.”

During the winter break of his first year, he talked with his father about how he was feeling. His father encouraged him to find something that combined what he was good at, what fulfilled him, and what the world needed.

The conversation helped Voelsing reconsider his academic path. He switched from aerospace engineering to climate system science and engineering (Course 1-12), a then-new major offered jointly by the departments of Civil and Environmental Engineering and of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, and returned to campus feeling energized by his studies. 

The change also helped him see how his education could serve a purpose beyond earning a degree. As he continued his ROTC training, he began to consider how technical knowledge about the environment could inform decisions with real-world significance.

The change, he says, was like night and day.

“I really figured out how to study,” he says. “Finding out my own vision of self and academic fulfillment helped me propel myself forward.”

A course in environmental history with Professor Susan Solomon, an atmospheric chemist who helped discover the cause of the Antarctic ozone hole, further shaped his interests. Each week, the class examined a different environmental issue, encouraging students to investigate primary sources and identify questions that had received less attention.

For his final paper, Voelsing researched an agroforestry project in Uganda. The project sparked a deeper interest in global agricultural and food systems, an area he hopes to explore in graduate school.

“There’s not going to be this one technology that comes along, and suddenly climate change isn’t an issue,” he says. “It will be a combination of 100 things making it 1 percent better for us to get across that finish line.”

Outside the classroom, one of Voelsing’s most formative experiences has come through Camp Kesem, a student-run nonprofit that provides free summer camps for children whose parents have been affected by cancer.

He joined MIT’s chapter as a first-year student. The chapter serves more than 200 campers, ages 5 to 18, giving them a week of sleepaway camp filled with activities such as ziplining, swimming, and games.

Over the years, he has taken on several leadership roles. He started as a counselor, then became operations coordinator, helping plan and run the camp. Later, he led alumni relations and organized a fundraising gala. As a senior, he returned to counseling, realizing that the part of the experience he valued most was spending time with the children.

“The thing I enjoy most isn’t all the planning; it’s not all the coordinating,” he says. “The thing I enjoy most is just spending time with kids.”

Camp Kesem also changed how he understands empathy. Before joining, he says, he was uncomfortable when other people cried. Through conversations with campers and fellow counselors, he learned the importance of sitting with someone through difficult emotions instead of trying to make those feelings go away.

“Being able to sit with a person as they grieve and experience that grief with them really changes your views on empathy and changes your views on what is actually important,” he says.

Voelsing has tried to bring that openness to his friendships on campus, too. He values conversations that allow people to understand how different experiences have shaped their perspectives, and he makes an effort to connect people who might not otherwise meet.

“I would give up a good night’s sleep seven nights a week for a good conversation or staying up talking to a friend,” he says. “And I often do.”

That same willingness to learn from others has informed his experience in ROTC. Through the program’s training and relationships with fellow midshipmen, Voelsing has gained a perspective on military service that extends beyond the family stories he grew up hearing.

He recently received his service assignment as a meteorology and oceanography officer, a specialty that will allow him to draw on his scientific background. 

Before beginning his service, however, Voelsing hopes to attend graduate school. He wants to deepen his expertise before joining the Navy full time, believing that further study will allow him to contribute more once he begins his career.

Balancing his academic work, ROTC commitments, and extracurricular activities requires him to be deliberate about how he spends his time. Rather than getting overwhelmed by everything on his plate, Voelsing tries to focus on the responsibility in front of him.   

“I’m trying to tackle it with enthusiasm, and trying to be where my feet are and do the thing well,” he says.

Looking back on his four years at MIT, Voelsing says the most important influence on him has not been a particular class or professor, but the community he has found among his friends. He values the way MIT brings together people with different interests, backgrounds, and ways of thinking, and he hopes to be someone who helps those people connect.

That sense of responsibility also informs how he thinks about the future. Whether in climate science or the military, he wants to approach difficult decisions with an awareness of their consequences and a willingness to take on challenges others might find daunting.

“Somebody’s got to do it. Why not me?” he says. “I think that is really the through line of what I want to do academically and the kind of life I want to lead.”

item.title: In postcolonial Ghana, a fresh start but not a blank slate
item.description: A new study of the country’s bureaucracy shows the challenges of state-building at the moment of independence.
item.dc:creator: Peter Dizikes | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
It was a landmark in history: In 1957, Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African state to achieve independence from colonial rule, having previously been under the control of Great Britain. 

But gaining political independence does not mean the past is left behind, and there has long been public debate about the many long-term effects of the colonial period on state and society in subsequent decades.  

Now, an empirically rich study explores one aspect of the Ghanaian state, the composition of its bureaucracy, during and after British rule. The study finds that two ethnic groups, the Ga and the Fante, which made up 14 percent of the population combined, held over 70 percent of public-sector positions in the 1950s, suggesting goods such as desirable jobs had been heavily distributed along group lines. 

“At the moment of independence, you have a state that is not meritocratic, and is highly captured by certain ethnic groups,” says MIT scholar Noah Nathan, co-author of a newly published paper detailing the study’s findings. As a result, he adds, “You can imagine the politics that creates, which are demands to equalize access to state power and state authority. And things start off on this foot of ethnic political competition over the state. That is in part a legacy of colonial state-building.”

At least in this case, “Independence in Africa wasn’t this hard break from the past,” suggests Nathan, a Ford International Professor of Political Science in MIT’s Department of Political Science. “Africans became the leaders of their countries, but the state institutions that they inherited weren’t born fresh at independence. They were carried over from the colonial period.”

The paper, “The Seeds of State Capture: Merit and Patrimonialism in the Colonial Bureaucracy,” is published in advance online form in the American Political Science Review. Nathan’s co-authors are Sarah Brierley, an associate professor at the London School of Economics and Political Science; George Kwaku Ofosu, an associate professor at the London School of Economics and Political Science; and Tingxuan Zhu PhD ’26, a recent graduate of MIT’s doctoral program in political science at MIT. 

Analyzing names

To conduct the study, the scholars dug into records from the period of British rule in Ghana, which extended from the 19th century until 1957. Using documents from the British National Archives, they examined individual-level employment records for 11,702 bureaucrats from the colonial-era civil service, building a dataset spanning from 1897 to 1955. The records included 6,879 Ghanaian civil servants and 4,805 European civil servants. The scholars’ aim was to shed light on the dynamics of civil service hiring and politics. 

British leaders at the time, and some commentators subsequently, have cast the colonial state as one built on rational, merit-based principles — what scholars call a “Weberian” bureaucracy, named after the famous German sociologist Max Weber. Scholars say that other types of bureaucracies, in contrast, display “patrimonialism,” with jobs being assigned not on merit but through patronage.

To analyze this question further, the scholars looked at 13.8 million names of registered voters from contemporary Ghana, along with localized ethnicity data from the 2010 national census. They used this to establish a baseline of the relationship between names and ethnicity in the country. Then, the scholars went back to the historical archives, and, using the names there, determined the ethnicities of past Ghanaian civil servants, from 1897 to 1955. 

Ultimately this approach showed that on the eve of independence, the Ga and Fante had managed to gain a percentage of civil service jobs that was five times greater than the percentage of the population they represented. That strongly suggests that the colonial-era bureaucracy built under British rule was not merit-based, at least in terms of overall composition. 

“Scholars have said this post-1957 independent Ghana brings with it the introduction of patrimonialism into the bureaucracy, and we’re saying this was going on long before,” Nathan explains. “It actually wasn’t meritocratic at all, and Kwame Nkrumah, the first president of Ghana, didn’t inherit some Weberian rational bureaucracy that he then destroyed. He inherited this thing rife with patrimonialism and patronage, that he then adapted. And that’s a very different interpretation of the post-independence period.”

Exams and education

To further examine the question of merit, the scholars even obtained individual-level results from Ghana’s civil service exams, then analyzed those in relation to which applicants got hired — or passed over for jobs. The results indicate little correspondence between exam results and job offers, again suggesting that ethnicity and social ties mattered more in hiring, on aggregate. 

“If you were from the right ethnic group, you were going to get a job, even if you did pretty poorly on the civil service exam,” Nathan says. “And people from disfavored ethnic groups who did much better on the exam were not getting the same positions.”

The study also rules out a seemingly logical explanation for at least part of the ethnic skew in the composition of the Ghanaian civil service — that hiring reflected levels of educational attainment, even if access to schooling itself might have reflected ethnic iniquities. But the data indicate that was not a factor. 

The scholars located every school in the country geographically, dating to the 1890s, and closely measured access to education for all ethnic groups over time. The Ga and Fante groups may have had some initial advantages in this regard, but by the 1930s, many other groups had caught up in educational attainment and still were not procuring the same relative numbers of civil services jobs through the 1950s. 

“At least in this case, that can’t explain why these two groups got favored in the hiring process,” Nathan says. “It wasn’t just a direct outcome of the fact that some parts of society had more education than others.”

As it happens, geographical proximity to civil service jobs is also not an explanatory factor; the scholars also examined the locations of government offices and found they cannot account for the quantity of jobs going to the Ga and Fante. 

Out of sight

Instead, the researchers believe the likeliest scenario is that, once established in the civil service, people from the Ga and Fante managed to use their social connections to get more and more jobs offered to others from their own groups. Moreover, they may have done so not necessarily with explicit British approval, but with something more resembling indifference on the part of the colonial rulers. 

“The mechanics of the hiring process were very decentralized,” Nathan says. “And the British didn’t know very much about the society they were governing. That created an information asymmetry where local bureaucrats could get friends into jobs in a way their superiors were either not aware of or didn’t have very much incentive to stop.”

All told, Nathan observes, “The ministry of finance in Ghana in 1957 isn’t some new thing that’s created from scratch. It’s the colonial ministry of finance that’s been in place for 60 years, and the bureaucrats in it showed up to work the next day in the same jobs. [The new leaders] inherited thousands of employees who had gotten there through this process.”

The study is one of several that Nathan has published using data to answer questions that span both political science and history. Quantifying the issue in a granular way helps illuminate the large-scale political dynamics.

“People have written about this in broad strokes, even the fact that certain ethnic groups in some countries got more access to positions than others, but they haven’t had detailed microdata on exactly who got which job and when,” Nathan says. “That’s the innovation of our paper … we could unpack the nuts and bolts of how this hiring process happened, and in doing so dispel some conventional wisdom about how African states were built in the colonial period.”

The new paper is not the only piece of scholarship taking this kind of data-intensive approach to studying colonial state-building and its legacy. Ada Johnson-Kanu, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Kentucky, has conducted this sort of study of Nigeria’s bureaucracy over time, in work she completed in 2021. 

Nathan, for his part, says he hopes that other scholars can expand upon this kind of data-driven approach to digging into certain historical questions. 

“There is just incredibly rich archival evidence out there in the world for a lot of countries,” Nathan observes. “I think this is a really fun way to do research.”

item.title: A single AI model simulates the behavior of many substances, from sliding sand to folding proteins
item.description: By learning how matter moves, the WorldParticle system could assist with developing soft robots, medicines, and more.
item.dc:creator: Adam Zewe | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
Today, a scientist who wants to simulate a physical process must pick the right tool for that one job, such as a solver built for flowing water or another designed to model the way a protein folds. Each one is hand-coded around the specific equations that dictate how that process behaves.

Researchers at MIT, the University of British Columbia (UBC), and elsewhere have now replaced that patchwork with a single deep-learning system, called WorldParticle, that could help engineers model different physical phenomena, from sliding sand to folding proteins, with one unified artificial intelligence architecture.

Scientists and engineers could use this system to model processes that typically require separate simulators, such as a fluid sloshing against a deformable solid. This could offer a faster, more accurate way to simulate how sloshing oil might impact an elastic valve in a storage tank, for instance. It could also help engineers study where and how granular materials, like sand or soil, could move when a soft robot touches them.

The system represents every material it simulates, from a dune of sand to a protein molecule, as tiny particles and predicts where those particles will move one step at a time. Because it learns the underlying dynamics rather than being programmed with an equation, the model can adapt to materials, forces, and environments it never encountered during training.  

In the long term, the researchers hope this work helps scientists discover new materials and explore physical processes they would be unable to effectively study with existing simulation methods.

“We want to have a GPT moment for simulation,” says Peter Yichen Chen, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at UBC, and is a co-corresponding author of an open-access paper on this technique. “Every time people want to build a simulator for a particular physical phenomenon, they need to code it up from scratch. Our vision is to have a foundation model that works out of the box for any scenario you want to simulate. This is a first step in that direction.”

Chen is joined by co-corresponding and co-lead author Minghao Guo, an MIT postdoc; co-lead authors Caoliwen Wang and Siyuan Chen, UBC graduate students; Wojciech Matusik, an MIT professor of electrical engineering and computer science who leads the Computational Design and Fabrication Group within the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL); and others at UBC, Georgia Tech, Inria, Meta, the University of Pennsylvania, the University of Utah, the University of California at Los Angeles, and the University of Hong Kong. The research will be presented at the ACM SIGGRAPH Conference and Exhibition on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques in Asia.

Unified simulation

For this work, the researchers drew inspiration from world models. These powerful AI systems learn the rules that govern the physical world so they can predict how objects or environments will change over time in response to certain actions or conditions.

The researchers applied these concepts to develop a unified AI architecture that can simulate multiple types of physical phenomena. 

“If you study deformable objects and fluids, you would need two simulators — one for each physical regime. But if you unify them into one model, maybe you could couple the physics of these two processes and gain insights into new problems?” Guo says.

WorldParticle breaks an object into thousands or millions of tiny, three-dimensional dots, or particles, using what is known as a Lagrangian representation. It tracks the movement and velocity of the particles over space and time to simulate the material’s dynamics.

Typically, when scientists model materials and physical processes using Lagrangian particles, they use a governing equation that defines the fundamental laws which control how that material behaves over time and space. They must convert that complex equation into a formula a numerical solver can handle, repeating these steps for each material and process they want to model.

Instead, the researchers designed a neural network that learns to solve governing equations in general, eliminating the need to design a new model and solver to handle each one. 

Once WorldParticle converts an object into particles, a neural network takes the 3D positions and physical properties of the particles as inputs. It outputs their positions and properties for the next frame of the simulation, predicting the material’s motion over time and space in one-second increments. 

“It is a similar architecture to ChatGPT. But instead of predicting one word at a time to write a piece of text, we are predicting how these particles will move, one step at a time,” Chen says.

Before each simulation step, WorldParticle separates the external forces that affect the physical system, like impulse forces that affect an ocean wave when it slams into a seawall. 

After predicting the initial states of the particles, WorldParticle integrates the external forces back into the simulation, correcting its particle predictions based on how those forces affect the object’s behavior. In this way, the system can generalize to unseen materials, changing environmental conditions, and varied forces.

A general, scalable framework

But because a complex object could be broken into millions of particles, the problem quickly becomes too computationally intensive for the model to handle. 

To streamline processing, the researchers employed a merging technique to combine and compress particles while still allowing WorldParticle to capture fine-grained details of their behavior.

“We needed to do a lot of detailed engineering and employ many tweaks to the architecture for it to be truly generalizable and scalable,” Guo says.

They demonstrated WorldParticle by modeling six different physical phenomena, including deformable objects, granular materials, and proteins, with higher accuracy than numerical simulation methods. 

For instance, WorldParticle effectively captured how a granular object would collapse into a pile while some baseline methods left sand particles floating in the air. Their method also modeled how protein structures change over time about 100 times faster than numerical simulators, Guo adds. 

The general-purpose framework could be applied to many materials and processes, including soft robot manipulation tasks, RNA evolution, and astrophysical phenomena like the merging of galaxies, the researchers say.

Moving forward, they want to adapt WorldParticle to simulate these and other physical systems. They also want to build on this work toward the development of a full, general-purpose simulation pipeline for scientific discovery. 

 “We see the unification of computation and science giving us new insights and tools to discover physical phenomena or explain some unexplainable physical phenomena,” Guo says. “With a unified model, we could unlock many discoveries that we can’t even imagine.”

item.title: AI-assisted learning platform helps robots reason beyond literal commands
item.description: The new approach, known as FLEX, could lead to more intuitive, interactive household and assistive robots.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Chu | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
Humans are intuitive by nature. We can sense meaning beyond the literal words that we encounter. Now, a new artificial intelligence-assisted learning platform developed by MIT engineers is enabling robots to read larger meaning into a human’s natural language commands. 

In a study to be presented at the annual Conference on Robot Learning this month, researchers from MIT and New York University introduce FLEX, a flexible feature-editing pipeline for robot motion-planning. 

With FLEX, humans can interact with a robot by giving it instructions in natural, conversational language. The robot can not only follow the instructions literally but also read into the words to draw larger generalizations that help to improve its motion-planning task. 

The team demonstrated FLEX in several simulated scenarios, including one in which a robot serves a cup of coffee. In these virtual scenarios, a person interacts with a robotic arm by typing commands in natural language. As the robot moves the coffee cup over a cluttered table, the person might type “Don’t spill on the laptop!” In response, the robot will reason about why it should avoid the laptop. For this, FLEX incorporates a large language model (LLM) — a type of AI system that is trained on enormous libraries of text, including social media posts, video transcriptions, and web content, which the LLM uses to identify larger trends, patterns, and generalizations. 

“LLMs have seen so many texts from the internet,” says study author Nathan Dennler, a postdoc in MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). “People might have written about, ‘Oh, my phone dropped in the water and now it doesn’t work,’ or ‘I spilled coffee on my computer and now it doesn’t work.’ So LLMs pick up on the idea that liquids plus devices leads to things not working.”

Through the LLM, the robot reasons that it should also avoid bumping into all electronics. In its updated path, the robot adjusts to avoid both the laptop and a nearby phone, without the person having to explicitly spell this out.

“The idea is that there is some higher-level intention behind the words that you say,” Dennler says. “People naturally get this. But you have to carefully explain that to a robot, which takes time and effort. FLEX gives you an interface of communication with a robot to say, ‘When people say this, they mean that.’”

The study was led by Andreea Bobu, assistant professor of aeronautics and astronautics at MIT. Co-authors are Audrey Lee SM ’26 and Ilia Sucholutsky of New York University.

Beyond what we say

At MIT, Bobu heads up the Collaborative Learning and Autonomy Research (CLEAR) Lab, where her group develops autonomous agents that learn to work for, with, and around people. She is focused on developing assistive and household robots that can carry out physical tasks, and reason and adapt in real-time, in response to a person’s natural, conversational commands. 

“Robots use math to do their trajectory planning. But we can’t expect a consumer to learn to do this math in order to tell a robot what to do,” says Dennler, who is a member of the CLEAR Lab. “Instead of having to get people to learn how to use a robot in a specific way, the goal is to interact with the robot through natural language.”

There is a large effort in the robotics community to incorporate natural language into robotic learning pipelines. Various strategies include using language to clarify a task’s goal, redirect a robot’s trajectory, and update its understanding of what is a safe path to take. These existing methods use natural language to tell the robot how to physically perform a task. But a robot could potentially learn much more from what we tell it. 

Bobu and her colleagues are expanding what robots can learn from natural language commands. In their new study, they focused on enabling a robot to interpret a person’s underlying, unspecified preference from limited natural language commands.  

Absorbing common sense

The team’s new robot learning platform, FLEX, is a three-step process that helps a robot read more into a natural language command, beyond what it is explicitly told to do. 

The first step, “Add,” instructs a robot to add a feature to its list of things in its environment that matter for the task at hand, based on a user’s natural language command. For instance, as a robot is moving a bowling ball from one location to another, a person might interject with “Don’t drop it on my mug!” The robot would then add the mug to a list of things to avoid in its path. This first step is how previous methods have worked. Every time a person makes a correction, the robot adds to its features list, and updates its trajectory to avoid those features. 

“The problem happens when your feature list becomes super long, and some features are no longer relevant because your environment may have changed,” says Dennler, who notes that this approach can grow tiresome if a person has to specify every specific feature to avoid. 

The second step, “Generalize,” is the new solution that FLEX provides. This step incorporates an LLM — in this case, GPT-4o — that considers the mug, along with any other features that the person has so far specified to avoid. The LLM automatically searches through its vast cache of data for patterns and connections among these features, to ultimately make a generalization that it should avoid objects that are fragile, even when the person has not explicitly said so. 

“LLMs have seen so many texts from the internet, from all sorts of people and places,” Dennler says. “Because they’ve trained so much on those things, some of that common sense gets absorbed into the LLM.”

In the third step, “Mask,” the robot’s standard computer vision system assesses its environment to determine what objects are no longer present, and then deletes those objects from its features list. This entire three-step process takes about five seconds. 

The team tested FLEX in simulations of a robot arm carrying out three different tasks: serving a cup of coffee, moving a candle, and carrying a bowling ball. In all three scenarios, volunteers interacted with the virtual robot by typing natural language commands, such as “Don’t spill on my laptop,” “Stay away from the stack of paper,” and “Don’t drop on the mug.” With FLEX, the robot followed all three commands literally and also reasoned at a higher level to not spill on electronics, stay away from flammable objects, and not drop its cargo on fragile things. 

“Everyone’s homes are different, and everyone cares about different things, so no robot comes out of the box knowing what matters to you,” Bobu says. “What excites me about FLEX is that it can pick that up from a sentence or two instead of asking you to spell out every rule — and that’s the difference between a robot people put up with and one they actually want in their home.” 

This work was partly supported by the MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium and the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing’s Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing program.

item.title: Fabric molds could bring material-saving concrete beams within reach
item.description: MIT engineers cast a concrete beam using a sewn fabric mold with one-third the amount of concrete and half as much steel as a conventional beam.
item.dc:creator: Stephanie Martinovich | Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering
item.content:encoded:
Topology optimization is a computer design method that can help engineers design beams using reduced amounts of concrete and steel. But those intricate shapes produced from the tool are often too complex or expensive to pour into conventional rigid molds. The few that have been built have mostly relied on specialized equipment, such as concrete 3D printers or machine-carved molds, equipment that is out of reach in regions where new construction is expected to grow.  

Now, MIT engineers have shown that highly efficient beams can be cast in something more accessible: sewn fabric. In a paper published in the Journal of Building Engineering, the team designed and built a 3-meter (about 10-foot) test beam using fabric molds created through an automated pattern-making process. Compared with a conventional beam designed to carry the same weight, the optimized beam used about one-third as much concrete and half as much steel reinforcement. When tested, its measured response was within about 2 percent of what the team's computer model predicted.

Fabric formwork, in which concrete is poured into a mold made of textile, has been explored for years to create beams that vary in depth, rather than in rectangular shapes common in construction. But because fabric deforms under the weight of wet concrete, that flexibility has made the final shape hard to predict.

“The key realization was that this flexibility is not just a limitation to manage; with the right computational pattern design, it can become a way to produce optimized structural forms,” says Josephine Carstensen, the Gilbert W. Winslow (1937) Career Development Professor in Civil Engineering and senior author of the study.

Fabric molds can also be inexpensive, lightweight, and fast compared to wood or steel molds. “You could sew a formwork together off site, pack it into a box, and bring it to a job site very easily,” says Jackson Jewett PhD ’25, co-author of the study. “We joke that we are developing the H&M of the construction industry.” 

Less material, lower carbon

Cement production accounts for roughly 8 percent of human-caused carbon emissions. 

“This work addresses concrete’s climate footprint primarily by reducing material demand,” Carstensen says. “Cement production is highly carbon-intensive, so using less concrete is an important part of decarbonizing construction.”

Where new construction happens matters, too. The world’s number of buildings is expected to nearly double by 2050, with about 85 percent of that growth in developing countries, where access to advanced construction equipment is often limited. That is why, Carstensen says, the team focused on an accessible, cost-conscious fabrication approach.

Designing the beam

Concrete is strong when compressed, but weak when pulled, so it’s reinforced with steel that can handle the pulling forces. The researchers first mapped a path for the steel reinforcement using a method called graphic statics, which can generate structural designs almost instantly. They used it to shape the steel bar so that it carries an equal share of the weight along its entire length to keep the reinforcement simple enough for builders to make. Topology optimization, which works more slowly but can place material freely, was used to determine where concrete was needed and where material could be removed from areas where it contributes little to the structural performance.

“Both methods are good at different things, so we tried to combine the strengths of both into a single methodology,” says Jewett.

The resulting beam has a top section, narrow angled legs, and a thin bottom section for the steel reinforcement. The team’s automated process translated the 3D beam design into flat fabric pieces that can be cut and sewn into a mold, accounting for how the fabric will deform once concrete is poured in. A simple timber frame supported the finished fabric mold.

Watching the beam take shape

For Mark Hellrich SM ’26, the study’s lead author, the main hands-on challenge was getting the concrete mix right. Woven cotton fabric lets water seep through, so a mix that is too runny loses water through the mold. It also presses harder against the fabric, pushing it away from the intended shape.

The team used a moderately wet, sand-rich mix with only small stones, so the concrete could flow through the beam’s narrow, angled legs and thin bottom section without getting stuck. They then packed it in by hand, prodding each layer and tapping and kneading the fabric from the outside.

“This is where the flexibility of the mold becomes an advantage: you can work the concrete through the interconnected passages without a vibrator, which a rigid mold of this shape would need,” says Hellrich. A concrete vibrator is a tool typically used to shake air pockets out of freshly poured concrete in rigid molds. 

Once the concrete was in place, the wet fabric revealed the beam’s final shape. “All three beams were free of wrinkles and creases,” says Hellrich. The top surface stayed close to the design, while the main difference was a downward sag along the bottom, with the angled legs folding slightly inward.

Finding the right fabric mold

To find out how much sewing precision the beam needs, the team built three molds for the same design, made from 36, 56, and 76 fabric pieces. Comparing the 3D scans of the cast beams with the target design, the researchers found that more seams gave finer control over the details, but did not necessarily make the beam’s overall shape more accurate.

“More seams improve local control because they divide the fabric into smaller, more constrained panels. But a more complex pattern also has more pieces to align and more seam length, so small cutting, sewing, and assembly inaccuracies can accumulate across the mold, explains Carstensen.

The 56-piece mold demonstrated the best balance, capturing the important design geometry without the added time, effort, and potential errors associated with the most complex pattern.

The researchers then load-tested one of the beams, gradually stacking 36 water-filled buckets on top of it, up to about 30 percent of its design load to reflect everyday service conditions. Weighted lines hung from the beam’s underside to precise measuring gauges below, tracking how far the beam bent as the load was added and removed. At the beam’s center, the measured deflection — its downward movement under the load — was within about 2 percent of the computer model’s prediction.

Where it fits in the real world

The team also compared the cost of a single fabric-formed beam with a conventional one and found that location makes all the difference. In the Global South, where materials tend to cost more relative to labor, all three fabric versions were cheaper, with savings of about 10 to 20 percent. In the Global North, higher labor costs for sewing reversed that advantage, making the fabric versions about 16 to 55 percent more expensive.

The findings suggest that fabric formwork is most promising for custom-shaped concrete components produced as a one-off or in small batches, such as exposed beams, roof or long-span framing, pedestrian structures, and landscape elements. For the repetitive, rectangular beams found in most buildings, conventional reusable molds remain the more economical choice where labor is expensive.

“To get started, a builder would need the digital pattern for the target component, a sewing machine and suitable fabric, and a simple timber support frame,” Carstensen says. “That is a much lower equipment threshold than robotic fabrication, concrete 3D printing, or CNC-milled molds.”

The researchers describe the 3-meter beam as a proof of concept comparable to a short building span. It is also a big step up from the 1.2-meter beam the team built in a previous project, Jewett notes.  

Building bigger isn’t just a matter of enlarging the design, Carstensen notes. As a beam gets longer, its own weight and the pressure on the fabric mold change, so a larger beam would need a new design. The next step, Carstensen says, is “to test multiple beams to failure.”  

“The nice thing about these optimization methods is they generate structures that look organic,” Jewett says. “Their geometries are clear expressions of how the forces move through the structural system. There is elegance to them. It makes you ask why we don’t design all our structures in this way.”

Joining Carstensen, Jewett, and Hellrich on the paper are co-authors Abhinit Sati, Edward Chien, and Emily Whiting, of Boston University’s Department of Computer Science.

The work was partially supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation.

item.title: How to predict the behavior of molecules from scant data
item.description: A machine-learning approach called CheMeleon provides a practical way to develop new drugs or other molecules with much less detailed, expensive experimentation.
item.dc:creator: David L. Chandler | Department of Chemical Engineering
item.content:encoded:
Discovering new molecules for specific uses is a major driver of progress in a wide variety of industries, whether it’s pharmaceutical companies looking for new drugs, or electronics or energy companies seeking new materials with particular properties. But it’s also largely a trial-and-error process, because there is not yet any way to perfectly predict how a given chemical compound will behave in terms of the myriad different properties and responses materials can exhibit.

Recent progress has been made on using artificial intelligence and machine learning to supplement or speed up laborious calculations based on physical principles that can at least provide some initial guidance on which compounds might be worth synthesizing and testing. Now, a new method developed at MIT shows that when there are few data on some technologically relevant property, such as ligand affinities for a recently discovered cellular target for a potential drug, this approach can outperform other existing methods for winnowing down the field of possible molecules that might be worth looking at.

The findings were reported in the Sept. 14 issue of the Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling, in a paper by MIT graduate student Akshat Shirish Zalte and recent graduate Jackson Burns PhD ’26, Research Scientist Charlles Abreu, Professor William Green, and three researchers from the chemical company BASF. 

An earlier version of the paper has been online since last year, and the open-source model the team developed, called CheMeleon, has already found regular use by several pharmaceutical companies. CheMeleon was built using ChemProp, an open-source machine-learning package also developed and maintained by the Green group at MIT, and anyone can download CheMeleon through ChemProp and fine-tune it for their own purposes.

Earlier this year, there was a contest organized by OpenADMET for trying to predict the properties of a variety of new molecules that had not previously been synthesized, says Green, who is the Hoyt Hottel Professor of Chemical Engineering. “It was a big contest, a lot of people participated,” he says. When the winners were announced, it turned out that nine of the top 20 entries had used CheMeleon in their process. “So then we started getting all kinds of inquiries from the pharma companies about this, but our paper had just been submitted; it wasn’t even peer-reviewed or anything yet.”

While the paper went through that review process, its influence was already spreading. At least one pharma company, Green says, “sent a message to all their people, and said ‘Anytime you’re modeling a property, start with CheMeleon, that’s our new company policy’” when making initial decisions about which molecules to pursue.

The key to CheMeleon was pre-training a machine-learning model with detailed data about a million different molecules, so that it gets to learn correlations between the structure of a given molecule and how it behaves with respect to a catalog of about 1,600 descriptors that have been developed by chemists over decades. CheMeleon can then be fine-tuned to predict well-known properties like solubility and viscosity, to more esoteric properties such as bioactivity or reactivity, with a certain protein or enzyme.

Those million molecules are a minuscule fraction of the innumerable ways that atoms can bond together, but they provide enough examples so that once the AI system has been trained on them, it can work out on its own many underlying patterns and relationships, and then apply those to a new, unknown molecule that’s presented to it.

“Most of today’s deep-learning models require more data than traditional methods,” says Zalte. Some successful models use extensive data from the published literature in chemical journals, he says. “We don’t look at the literature at all. We just calculate a bunch of molecular descriptors like molecular weight or number of oxygens, among others.” Then predicting those descriptors forms the basis for their pre-training task.

CheMeleon is a pre-trained foundation model. Inspired by the well-known foundation models in language such as ChatGPT and Claide, which essentially are developed by feeding them massive amounts of information from the internet, CheMeleon uses molecular descriptors of a million molecules from PubChem, a large, freely available database of chemical information maintained by the U.S. National Institutes of Health. 

With classical expert-driven models, on the other hand, specialists in a field manually input detailed knowledge about their subject. In developing these classical models, he says, for example, people know from experiments that a certain property of interest, say solubility, may relate to particular descriptors of the same molecules, “like molecular weight, or the number of oxygens that are present, or how branchy or bulky the molecule is.” 

With this team’s approach, they can start with an existing neural network architecture and train it to learn underlying principles. “We’re not training it for a specific property, but as a general model that understands some level of chemistry, so that even if you fine-tune it with just a few data points for the task you care about, you can still get some good performance,” he says. That’s thanks to the fact that the model is “not having to learn everything from scratch.”

To verify its usefulness, “We compared our model not only against other foundation models that are out there, but also with classical models leveraging expert-designed principles,” Zalte says. Comparing its performance across 58 test cases, “we see that our model comes out on top.”

Green adds, “The CheMeleon foundation model drastically reduces the number of molecules that need to be tested experimentally to accurately predict the properties of new molecules. This is a huge advantage, since synthesizing and testing a large number of molecules is slow and expensive."

Besides the MIT members, the team also included Jochen Sieg, Christian Feldmann, and Miriam Mathea, researchers at BASF SE in Germany. The work was supported by the Machine Learning for Pharmaceutical Discovery and Synthesis consortium, along with fellowship support from U.S. Department of Energy and MathWorks.

media:content.media:description: Like a chameleon changing colors, CheMeleon adapts a single pre-trained model to predict many different molecular properties, such as potency (pEC50), toxicity (LD50), and solubility (logS). The MIT-developed model first learns chemistry by predicting easy-to-compute molecular descriptors for about a million molecules, then fine-tunes to each new task.

item.title: Studying bacteria and the cells they infect
item.description: By exploring how bacteria hijack cell functions, Associate Professor Rebecca Lamason hopes to learn more about how host cells carry out those functions.
item.dc:creator: Anne Trafton | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
Most biologists who study pathogenic microbes have focused on strains such as Escherichia coli or Staphylococcus aureus, which are not only important for human health, but also relatively easy to grow in the lab. 

Rebecca Lamason, an MIT associate professor of biology, wants to take a more expansive approach that includes bacteria that are more challenging to study. Tackling those microbes, she says, can help scientists learn more about the huge diversity of strategies that pathogens have evolved to interact with their hosts. 

In her lab, she has devised new tools for analyzing pathogens such as Rickettsia parkeri, a tickborne bacterium that causes a mild form of spotted fever. She also studies Listeria monocytogenes, a microbe commonly linked to foodborne illnesses.

From studying these microbes, she hopes to learn more about the many strategies that pathogens have devised to take over host cell machinery, which also offers insight into the fundamental functions performed by those host cells.

“We cannot learn everything from a single type of bacterium or a single type of cell,” Lamason says. “There’s a rich diversity of biological mechanisms that are out there, and I think we have just barely scratched the surface on that.”

In just one recent example, her lab found that R. parkeri can form very tight connections with a cell structure called the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), which mimics some of the interactions that the host cell’s own organelles have with the ER. They’re still puzzling out the reason for this interaction, which hasn’t been seen with other microbes.

“It’s one of those things too where we had gone into the microscope room to look at something else to ask a different question, and we discovered this other unexpected interaction,” Lamason says. “This has been a really fun experience, and it’s also very common when you’re doing cell biology experiments: you see some phenomenon that you didn't expect.”

How systems interact

As a high school student, Lamason was drawn to cell biology and physiology, and she decided she wanted to pursue a PhD even before she knew exactly what that career path would look like.

“I didn’t have anybody in my family that had a PhD or worked in science, and so I didn’t really know what it took or what it was to get a PhD, but for some reason I wanted to do it,” she says. 

Her father was in the military, so her family moved quite a bit, mainly between Florida, California, and Virginia, before settling in Pennsylvania. After graduating from high school, where she was the editor-in-chief of the school newspaper, Lamason spent two years at a local community college before transferring to Millersville University to finish her bachelor’s degree.

At Millersville, she majored in molecular biology and biotechnology and worked in a lab studying chlorella viruses, which infect algae.

“We were characterizing different variants that we could isolate from a pond that was next to the building, so we were looking at very simple questions, but that experience allowed me to see what it was like to ask questions, what it was like to work regularly in a lab,” she recalls.

To gain more experience before applying to graduate school, she worked as a research technician at Hershey Medical Center for a couple of years, in a lab studying zebrafish as a model to understand the genetics of cancer.

As a PhD student at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, where she studied immunology, Lamason realized that what she liked most about biology was studying how different biological systems interact with each together.

“The immune system was an interesting way to get that, because there were all these moving parts, all these cells that had to talk to each other to mount an effective immune response,” she says. “Studying immunology helped me realize what I liked more and more was cell biology. How does the cell, a really complex environment, respond to these external signals and commit to a program or a response that then supports some kind of function?”

For her postdoc, she chose a lab where she could look at those questions through the lens of host-pathogen relationships, at the University of California at Berkeley. 

“What really excited me about pathogens is that they are these wonderful little cell biologists, who often have to navigate the complex environment of the host cell and have evolved unexpected ways to solve problems,” she says. “If they have to get through a barrier, or they have to tell the cell not to die or they have to turn off a response, they have evolved distinct ways to do this.”

Working with Matthew Welch, a cell biologist at Berkeley, she began studying the two organisms that are now the focus of her current research: R. parkeri and L. monocytogenes.

R. parkeri, similar to viruses, cannot survive outside of a host cell and is fully dependent on the host cell machinery to replicate itself. L. monocytogenes, on the other hand, can survive and replicate on its own.

“These constraints shape the biology and the types of interactions that these organisms can use to cause infection,” Lamason says. “That’s what really got me interested in these two very different bacteria and in studying the different cellular and bacterial factors that drive a specific outcome.”

Solving technical challenges

In her lab at MIT, which she started in 2017, Lamason has identified many of the host proteins and other factors that help those two species of bacteria perform functions such as moving between infected cells, which they each do in different ways. In order to do much of this work, Lamason and her students, postdocs, and technicians have had to develop new techniques for studying these microbes. 

Until recently, there was no way to target specific genes in R. parkeri cells, but using CRISPR, Lamason’s lab developed the first technique for doing so, in 2024. That has made it easier for them to delve into the roles of specific genes of interest. They also developed ways to label bacterial proteins that are secreted into the host cell, making it much easier to pick them out from the cells’ own proteins.

“My lab recognizes the technical challenges that face our field, and so sometimes we’re building things to solve problems and sometimes we’re just chasing down really interesting observations and trying to understand how it works,” Lamason says.

When looking for faculty jobs, Lamason was drawn to MIT by the sense of collaboration she found. When members of her lab need to learn a new technique, or explore the workings of a cell organelle the lab hasn’t studied before, they can find help from one of the many other MIT labs that have expertise in different aspects of biology.

“That’s been the key to our success — not only attempting and having these riskier ideas, but having the support of the community to help us think about how do we execute on those,” she says. “There’s this wonderful community of scientists to help you think through and complete the kind of work that you want to do and also to push you to think bigger about how to approach a problem.”

When she’s not puzzling out biology problems, Lamason likes to take to the ice as part of a women’s hockey league in Boston. She took up the sport as a beginner a few years ago, in part as a way to take her mind off the everyday stresses of academia.

“It’s a good challenge, and a good way to get out of the lab and the office and give you something else to think about. If my grant got rejected, if I was having a bad day at work, it was a good way to shut my brain off for a little bit and focus on staying upright,” she says.

item.title: Pinning down the structure of quark-gluon plasma, the universe’s first fluid
item.description: A new method picks up where Einstein left off, to predict how particles move through fluid under extreme conditions.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Chu | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
In the first fraction of a second following the Big Bang, matter existed as a trillion-degree plasma of quarks and gluons — subatomic particles that zinged around at close to the speed of light. This roiling soup lasted for just a few microseconds, before the particles coalesced into more stable protons and neutrons. 

To study this primordial fluid, scientists recreate quark-gluon plasma in large particle accelerators, where ions are smashed together at close to the speed of light. These collisions create droplets of plasma roughly the size of an atomic nucleus, that exist for only tens of septillionths of a second.

One way scientists study this plasma is by tracking other particles, such as heavy quarks, that are not part of the plasma but happen to move through it. The way a heavy particle moves through a fluid should tell something about the microscopic structure of the fluid itself. This general relationship was established famously by physicist Albert Einstein in 1905. 

But in such extreme conditions, where particles are moving at close to the speed of light, something in Einstein’s theory starts to break down; there are interactions within the plasma that the theory can’t quite capture.

Now, physicists at MIT and the University of California at Santa Barbara (UCSB) have taken up where Einstein’s theory left off. They have worked out a theory that predicts how a relativistic particle, moving at close to the speed of light, is likely to be pushed and pulled by a fluid as it flies through it. 

The researchers envision that the new theory could be applied to predict how a heavy quark will move through quark-gluon plasma. Such predictions could then be compared to experiments to characterize the microscopic structure of quark-gluon plasma, and what kind of fluid must have existed in the universe’s first moments.

“Our result reveals a new source of information carried by heavy quarks in rare, unusually large changes in their motion,” says Jean Du Plessis, a graduate student in MIT’s Center for Theoretical Physics – a Leinweber Institute. “How often those large changes occur depends on the microscopic nature of the plasma, raising the possibility that they could provide a new way to learn what the quark-gluon plasma is actually like inside.”

Du Plessis and Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld of the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics at UCSB report their findings today in Physical Review Letters. 

A path from pollen

In 1905, Einstein developed a theory to describe a particle’s motion through fluid and how that motion can reveal the fluid’s microscopic structure. His theory was inspired by the botanist Robert Brown. In 1827, Brown observed a surprising phenomenon: Grains of pollen appeared to randomly jiggle and swirl when suspended in seemingly still water. This curious jittering of particles in fluid was later named “Brownian motion.” 

Einstein’s 1905 theory showed that Brownian motion was a product of invisible, microscopic forces within the fluid. A particle’s motion is a balance between the drag that the fluid exerts on the particle to slow it down, and the random kicks within the fluid that keep the particle moving. These random kicks, Einstein argued, must come from microscopic forces within the fluid, exerted by none other than the atoms and molecules that make up the fluid. The energy of these microscopic particles can add up to kick and jostle larger particles. 

Since he first published his theory, scientists have applied Einstein’s explanation of Brownian motion to characterize a host of fluids, including quark-gluon plasma. Like most other fluids, it was assumed that a particle moving through quark-gluon plasma should experience a similar balance of microscopic kicks as a grain of pollen moving through water. 

This balance is represented by a bell-shaped probability distribution, where a particle is most likely to experience medium forces of kicks (the highest point of the bell), and an equally low probability of the most extreme kicks (the tail ends of the bell), as the particle moves through and eventually settles into a fluid. 

“Einstein showed that the drag and the random kicks must balance in just the right way for a particle eventually to come to the same temperature as its surroundings,” Du Plessis explains. “For the types of fluids he was thinking about, he was correct. But for particles that are moving at relativistic velocities, this relationship breaks down. And we’ve known for 20 years that something is missing. So we have to go beyond the work that Einstein did.”

Kick speed

In their new study, Du Plessis and Scheihing-Hitschfeld calculated the forces that a heavy quark would likely experience if it flew through a fluid at relativistic speeds, close to the speed of light. They did so by carrying out calculations of the strong nuclear force, which is the fundamental force that pulls together quarks and gluons. 

The team started with a scenario of a relativistic heavy quark flying through a gas of weakly interacting quarks and gluons. The weak interactions made this a manageable starting point for their calculations.

For this starting scenario, they calculated the heavy quark’s strong nuclear force and how much its momentum is likely to change as it moves through the gas of quarks and gluons. This calculation produced a curve, or a probability distribution of the quark’s changes in momentum. The same curve can represent the quark’s probability of being kicked with various force; stronger kicks cause bigger changes to the quark’s momentum. 

The curve that the researchers calculated was bell-shaped, similar to what Einstein found with other fluids, only for small kicks. And, unlike Einstein’s bell-shaped curve, what the team found showed a tilt for heavy quarks moving at relativistic speeds. The tails at either end of the curve were uneven, and revealed a surprising imbalance in the kinds of kicks that a heavy quark would experience.

“The usual Brownian picture assumes that large kicks become exceedingly rare,” Du Plessis says. “For heavy quarks, however, these rare kicks are more common than the bell curve predicts, and are not equally likely in opposite directions: A large kick that slows the quark down more than expected from drag is more likely than an equally large kick that leaves it moving faster than expected.”

The team carried out the same calculation in plasmas made up of different particles. They found that the same tilted curve applies, regardless of the makeup of the plasma. Furthermore, they found that this same structure was already hiding in an earlier calculation in a strongly coupled plasma, despite the differences in the microscopic physics.

“This is the first time that this seemingly universal structure was realized and really formalized,” Du Plessis says. “This gives a concrete path forward for how to better understand the quark-gluon plasma, using heavy quarks.”

In terms of what this means for the universe’s first fluid, Du Plessis says that primordial quark-gluon plasma is likely “more strongly interacting than this Brownian motion way of modeling it would suggest. It’s more like a liquid and less like a gas.” 

This research was supported, in part, by the Office of Nuclear Physics in the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Science, the U.S. National Science Foundation, and the Simons Foundation.
